hpo_input.name: Postural tremor
hpo_input.definition: "A type of tremors that is triggered by holding a limb in a fixed position." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Spastic dysarthria
hpo_input.definition: "A type of dysarthria related to bilateral damage of the upper motor neuron tracts of the pyramidal and extra- pyramidal tracts. Speech of affected individuals is slow, effortful, and has a harsh vocal quality." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Elbow flexion contracture
hpo_input.definition: "An elbow contracture that limits the ability of the elbow joint to be extended (straightened), meaning that the elbow is fixed in an flexed (bent) position." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Fixed flexion at the elbow joint

hpo_input.name: Gait disturbance
hpo_input.definition: "The term gait disturbance can refer to any disruption of the ability to walk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:27770207]

hpo_input.name: Dystonia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally increased muscular tone that causes fixed abnormal postures. There is a slow, intermittent twisting motion that leads to exaggerated turning and posture of the extremities and trunk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Increased circulating free fatty acid level
hpo_input.definition: "A higher than normal levels of the fatty acids which can occur in plasma as a result of lipolysis in adipose tissue or when plasma triacyglycerols are taken into tissues." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Autoimmunity
hpo_input.definition: "The occurrence of an immune reaction against the organism's own cells or tissues." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dementia
hpo_input.definition: "A loss of global cognitive ability of sufficient amount to interfere with normal social or occupational function. Dementia represents a loss of previously present cognitive abilities, generally in adults, and can affect memory, thinking, language, judgment, and behavior." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Gastroesophageal reflux
hpo_input.definition: "A condition in which the stomach contents leak backwards from the stomach into the esophagus through the lower esophageal sphincter." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypothermia
hpo_input.definition: "Reduced body temperature due to failed thermoregulation." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Otosclerosis
hpo_input.definition: "In otosclerosis, a callus of bone accumulates on the stapes creating a partial fixation. This limits the movement of the stapes bone, which results in hearing loss." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15931303]

hpo_input.name: Panhypopituitarism
hpo_input.definition: "A pituitary functional deficit affecting all the anterior pituitary hormones (growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and prolactin)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:12466332]

hpo_input.name: Muscular dystrophy
hpo_input.definition: "The term dystrophy means abnormal growth. However, muscular dystrophy is used to describe primary myopathies with a genetic basis and a progressive course characterized by progressive skeletal muscle weakness and wasting, defects in muscle proteins, and histological features of muscle fiber degeneration (necrosis) and regeneration. If possible, it is preferred to use other HPO terms to describe the precise phenotypic abnormalities." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9046-3540, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Spastic gait
hpo_input.definition: "Spasticity is manifested by increased stretch reflex which is intensified with movement velocity. This results in excessive and inappropriate muscle activation which can contribute to muscle hypertonia. Spastic gait is characterized by manifestations such as muscle hypertonia, stiff knee, and circumduction of the leg." [PMID:25649546]

hpo_input.name: Focal dystonia
hpo_input.definition: "A type of dystonia that is localized to a specific part of the body." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Hepatosplenomegaly
hpo_input.definition: "Simultaneous enlargement of the liver and spleen." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Diffuse cerebral atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Diffuse unlocalised atrophy affecting the cerebrum." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Secondary microcephaly
hpo_input.definition: "Head circumference which falls below 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender because of insufficient head growth after birth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Development of small head that was not present at birth

hpo_input.name: Decreased circulating ceruloplasmin concentration
hpo_input.definition: "Decreased concentration of ceruloplasmin in the blood." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:32119309]

hpo_input.name: Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum
hpo_input.definition: "Absence or underdevelopment of the corpus callosum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Complete or partial absence of the corpus callosum
Hypoplasia or absence of the corpus callosum

hpo_input.name: Generalized-onset seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A generalized-onset seizure is a type of seizure originating at some point within, and rapidly engaging, bilaterally distributed networks. The networks may include cortical and subcortical structures but not necessarily the entire cortex." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:20196795, PMID:23739099, PMID:28276060, PMID:28276064, PMID:6790275]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal size of pituitary gland
hpo_input.definition: "A deviation from the normal size of the pituitary gland." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Atypical behavior
hpo_input.definition: "Atypical behavior is an abnormality in a person's actions that can be controlled or modulated by the will of the individual. While abnormal behaviors can be difficult to control, they are distinct from other abnormal actions that cannot be affected by the individual's will." []

hpo_input.name: Pain
hpo_input.definition: "An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5208-3432]

hpo_input.name: Skin rash
hpo_input.definition: "A red eruption of the skin." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Decreased circulating vitamin E concentration
hpo_input.definition: "A reduced concentration of vitamin E in the blood circulation. Vitamin E is a lipophilic vitamin that is also known as alpha-tocopherol." [PMID:30559825]

hpo_input.name: Reduced circulating vitamin A concentration
hpo_input.definition: "Concentration of vitamin A below the lower limit of normal in the blood circulation." []

hpo_input.name: Cholecystitis
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of inflammatory changes in the gallbladder." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Laryngeal atresia
hpo_input.definition: "Congenital absence of the lumen of the larynx. Laryngeal atresia is a rare condition. If the laryngeal opening fails to develop, fluid secreted by the lungs cannot be expelled. In a fetus with laryngeal atresia, the lungs are either normal or hyperplastic, not hypoplastic. Mortality is reported as 100%. At obstetric US examination, views of the fetal neck demonstrate a dilated trachea filled with trapped fluid. Views of the fetal chest show enlarged, hyperechoic lungs, with dilated fluid-filled bronchi. Fetal ascites is usually present." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:10517457, PMID:17715321]

hpo_input.name: Chorioretinal scar
hpo_input.definition: "Fibrous connective tissue resulting from incomplete healing of a wound (i.e., a scar) located in the choroid and retina or the eye." []

hpo_input.name: Diaphragmatic paralysis
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of a paralyzed diaphragm." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:3612666]

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of the liver
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the liver." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Diabetes insipidus
hpo_input.definition: "A state of excessive water intake and hypotonic (dilute) polyuria. Diabetes insipidus may be due to failure of vasopressin (AVP) release (central or neurogenic diabetes insipidus) or to a failure of the kidney to respond to AVP (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum
hpo_input.definition: "Underdevelopment of the corpus callosum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21263138]
synonym: Underdevelopment of part of brain called corpus callosum

hpo_input.name: Generalized tonic seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A generalized tonic seizure is a type of generalized motor seizure characterized by bilateral limb stiffening or elevation, often with neck stiffening without a subsequent clonic phase. The tonic activity can be a sustained abnormal posture, either in extension or flexion, sometimes accompanied by tremor of the extremities." [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:jalbers, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:11580774, PMID:28276060, PMID:28276064]

hpo_input.name: Small pituitary gland
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally decreased size of the pituitary gland." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5208-3432]

# Analysis of HPO Terms for Disease Specificity and Clinical Relevance

## Global Developmental Delay (HP:0001263)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Global developmental delay is a **common but non-specific term**[1][2][3]. It affects approximately 1-3% of preschool-aged children worldwide[1][2], and according to the CDC, approximately 1 in 6 children (17%) in the United States has at least one developmental delay[9]. This high prevalence makes it less informative for identifying a specific disease, as it represents a symptom or manifestation rather than a diagnosis itself. GDD is defined as significant delay in two or more developmental domains including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive abilities, and social-emotional skills[1][2][3].

**Disease Specificity:**
In up to 50% of cases, the exact cause of GDD remains unknown even after thorough evaluation[3]. The condition can result from numerous etiologies including genetic factors (Down syndrome, Fragile X syndrome), prenatal complications, infections, brain trauma, metabolic disorders, and environmental factors like prenatal alcohol exposure or lead poisoning[1][2][3][4]. Because GDD is a general term and not a specific diagnosis, it serves as a clinical indicator requiring further investigation rather than pointing to a particular disease[2].

**Age and Gender Considerations:**
GDD is typically diagnosed between birth and five years of age when developmental milestones are expected to be achieved[1]. There is no gender-specific predisposition mentioned in the literature, though some underlying genetic causes (such as Fragile X syndrome) do show gender differences in prevalence[3].

---

## Rare and Informative Terms

### Decreased Circulating Ceruloplasmin Concentration (HP:0010837)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **rare and highly specific finding** that is particularly informative for Wilson disease, a rare genetic disorder of copper metabolism. Decreased serum ceruloplasmin is a hallmark laboratory finding in Wilson disease and is not commonly seen in other conditions[3].

**Disease Association:**
This finding is virtually pathognomonic for Wilson disease when combined with other clinical features, making it highly informative for diagnosis.

**Age and Gender:**
Wilson disease typically manifests in childhood to early adulthood, with symptoms usually appearing between ages 6-20 years. There is no significant gender predisposition.

### Decreased Circulating Vitamin E Concentration (HP:0100513)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **rare finding** that is informative for specific neurological conditions, particularly ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED), a rare autosomal recessive disorder[3].

**Disease Association:**
Low vitamin E levels are characteristic of AVED and certain other rare lipid malabsorption disorders, making this finding relatively specific when present.

**Age and Gender:**
AVED typically presents in childhood or adolescence with progressive neurological symptoms. No significant gender predisposition is noted.

### Reduced Circulating Vitamin A Concentration (HP:0004905)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **moderately rare finding** that can be informative for specific malabsorption disorders or nutritional deficiencies, though it is less specific than ceruloplasmin or vitamin E deficiencies[3].

**Disease Association:**
This finding is associated with conditions affecting fat-soluble vitamin absorption and certain genetic disorders of vitamin A metabolism.

**Age and Gender:**
Can occur across age groups but is more commonly associated with malnutrition in developing countries and specific genetic disorders in developed countries.

### Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the Corpus Callosum (HP:0007370)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **rare structural brain abnormality** that is moderately specific and informative. Corpus callosum abnormalities are associated with specific genetic syndromes and developmental disorders[3].

**Disease Association:**
This finding is characteristic of several rare genetic conditions including Aicardi syndrome, certain chromosomal abnormalities, and specific metabolic disorders. It is more informative than general developmental delay because it points to specific neurological etiologies.

**Age and Gender:**
Can be detected prenatally or in early childhood. Aicardi syndrome, which commonly features corpus callosum abnormalities, predominantly affects females.

### Secondary Microcephaly (HP:0005484)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **moderately rare finding** that is more specific than general developmental delay. Secondary (postnatal) microcephaly indicates abnormal head growth after birth and suggests specific acquired or progressive conditions[3].

**Disease Association:**
Secondary microcephaly is associated with progressive neurological disorders, infections (such as congenital infections), and metabolic disorders. It is more informative than primary microcephaly because it indicates the timing of the insult.

**Age and Gender:**
By definition, secondary microcephaly develops after birth and is detected during infancy or early childhood. No significant gender predisposition.

### Diffuse Cerebral Atrophy (HP:0002506)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
This is a **moderately rare finding** that is informative for progressive neurological disorders. Diffuse cerebral atrophy suggests ongoing neurodegeneration or significant brain damage[3].

**Disease Association:**
This finding is associated with progressive metabolic disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, and severe acquired brain injuries. It is more specific than general developmental delay as it indicates structural brain changes.

**Age and Gender:**
Can occur at any age depending on the underlying etiology. Progressive forms typically manifest in childhood or adolescence.

### Generalized-Onset Seizure (HP:0002197) and Generalized Tonic Seizure (HP:0010818)

**Rarity and Specificity:**
These are **moderately common findings** in children with developmental disorders but are **moderately informative** when combined with other features. Seizures are present in many genetic and metabolic disorders[3].

**Disease Association:**
Seizures are associated with numerous conditions including genetic epilepsies, metabolic disorders, and structural brain abnormalities. While not rare, they become more informative when characterized by specific seizure types and combined with other clinical features.

**Age and Gender:**
Seizures can manifest at any age but are more common in infants and young children. Certain genetic epilepsies show gender-specific inheritance patterns.

**Commonality:**
This is a **very common and non-specific finding** that can occur in numerous conditions including developmental delays, autism spectrum disorder, psychiatric conditions, and many genetic syndromes[3].

**Informativeness:**
Behavioral abnormalities are too broad to be informative for specific disease identification without additional clinical context.

This is a **relatively common finding** that is non-specific without further characterization. It can occur in metabolic disorders, infections, and genetic syndromes[3].

### Hepatosplenomegaly (HP:0001433)

**Commonality:**
This is a **moderately common finding** that, while more specific than general liver abnormality, still occurs in numerous conditions including metabolic storage disorders, infections, and hematologic disorders[3].

**Informativeness:**
More informative than general liver abnormality but still requires additional clinical features for specific diagnosis.

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Clinical Significance and Specificity

## Overview of the HPO Terms

The provided list contains 24 HPO (Human Phenotype Ontology) terms spanning metabolic, muscular, endocrine, and systemic conditions. Based on the search results and clinical knowledge, I'll analyze their specificity and diagnostic value.

## 1. Common and Less Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are relatively common and have broad differential diagnoses, making them less specific for identifying a particular disease:

**Elevated circulating creatine kinase concentration (HP:0003236)** is one of the most common and least specific findings on this list. CK elevation occurs in numerous conditions including intense exercise, muscle injuries, cardiac disease, stroke, and various medications[1][2][3]. CK levels can increase 5 to 30 times above baseline within 24 to 48 hours after intense exercise alone[2], making this finding non-specific without additional clinical context.

**Hyperlipidemia (HP:0003077)** is extremely common in the general population and associated with numerous metabolic conditions, lifestyle factors, and medications. It lacks specificity for any particular disease.

**Insulin resistance (HP:0000855)** is prevalent in metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and polycystic ovary syndrome, but occurs in many other conditions as well.

**Hearing impairment (HP:0000365)** has an exceptionally broad differential diagnosis, ranging from congenital conditions to age-related changes to infections to medication side effects.

**Thrombocytopenia (HP:0001873)** can result from numerous causes including bone marrow disorders, autoimmune conditions, infections, medications, and liver disease.

**Hepatomegaly (HP:0002240)** similarly has a very broad differential, including fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, infections, malignancy, and metabolic disorders.

## 2. Rare and Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are more specific and informative for particular disease categories:

**Rhabdomyolysis (HP:0003201)** is a relatively rare but highly significant finding that indicates severe muscle breakdown[2]. This term is informative because it represents a specific pathophysiological process with a defined set of causes including severe trauma, extreme physical exertion, heat stroke, certain infections, and specific medications[2]. The presence of rhabdomyolysis often requires urgent intervention to prevent acute kidney failure.

**Progressive external ophthalmoplegia (HP:0000590)** is a rare and highly specific finding that strongly suggests mitochondrial myopathy or other neuromuscular disorders affecting the extraocular muscles. This finding is particularly informative because the combination of progressive bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoplegia narrows the differential significantly.

**Optic atrophy (HP:0000648)** is relatively uncommon and, when present with other systemic features, can be informative for specific genetic or metabolic disorders, particularly mitochondrial diseases or inherited optic neuropathies.

**Aplasia cutis congenita (HP:0001057)** is a rare congenital finding that, while not disease-specific on its own, is highly informative when present as it indicates a developmental abnormality and can be associated with specific genetic syndromes.

**Proximal muscle weakness in upper and lower limbs (HP:0008997, HP:0008994)** becomes more informative when combined with elevated CK, as this pattern suggests myopathy rather than neuropathy. The proximal distribution is particularly characteristic of inflammatory myopathies, muscular dystrophies, and metabolic muscle diseases.

**Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection (HP:0032326)** is specific for a particular pathogen and is informative for identifying antibiotic-resistant infections, though it's not rare in hospitalized populations.

## 3. Gender and Age-Related Patterns

**Gender-specific patterns:**

**Polycystic ovaries (HP:0000147)** and **Oligomenorrhea (HP:0000876)** are female-specific findings. Polycystic ovary syndrome affects approximately 6-20% of women of reproductive age and is often associated with insulin resistance and hyperlipidemia[1].

**Premature thelarche (HP:0010314)** occurs exclusively in females and represents early breast development, typically before age 8.

**Age-related patterns:**

**Hearing impairment (HP:0000365)** increases significantly with age, with age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) becoming increasingly common after age 60, though it can occur at any age.

**Optic atrophy (HP:0000648)** can occur at any age but is more commonly associated with progressive inherited conditions that manifest in childhood or early adulthood.

**Proximal muscle weakness (HP:0008994, HP:0008997)** patterns vary by age depending on the underlying cause. Inflammatory myopathies like polymyositis and dermatomyositis typically present in adults, while muscular dystrophies often present in childhood.

**Elevated CK (HP:0003236)** can occur at any age but interpretation varies: in children, it may suggest muscular dystrophy; in adults, it more commonly reflects exercise, medication effects, or acquired myopathy.

**Rhabdomyolysis (HP:0003201)** can occur at any age but risk factors vary—crush injuries and trauma are more common in younger individuals, while medication-induced rhabdomyolysis (particularly from statins) is more common in older adults.

**Increased intraabdominal fat (HP:0008993)** and **Increased adipose tissue around the neck (HP:0000468)** are more prevalent in adults and increase with age, particularly in sedentary populations.

# Analysis of HPO Terms

## Overview

Among the HPO terms provided, only **one term is directly relevant to the search results**: bilateral choanal atresia. The remaining terms represent a mix of unrelated conditions and general symptoms that do not appear in the provided medical literature on choanal atresia. Below is a detailed analysis organized by relevance.

## Relevant HPO Term: Bilateral Choanal Atresia

**HP:0004502 - Bilateral choanal atresia**

### 1. Common vs. Informative Status

Bilateral choanal atresia is **rare but highly informative** for specific disease diagnosis. While choanal atresia overall affects approximately 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 7,000 live births[1][4], bilateral cases represent a medical emergency with distinctive clinical presentation. This term is highly specific and directly diagnostic rather than being a general symptom.

### 2. Rarity and Disease Specificity

Bilateral choanal atresia is a **rare and highly specific condition**. It is immediately life-threatening and requires emergency intervention[1][2][6]. The bilateral form is less common than unilateral atresia, which occurs in approximately 70% of cases, meaning bilateral cases represent only about 30% of all choanal atresia presentations[2]. This rarity combined with its acute presentation makes it extremely informative for diagnosis.

### 3. Gender and Age Group Predilection

**Age group**: Bilateral choanal atresia manifests **immediately at birth**[1][6]. Symptoms are evident in the neonatal period, with affected newborns requiring resuscitation or showing respiratory distress immediately after delivery[1].

**Gender**: Choanal atresia overall is **more common in females**, occurring approximately twice as often in girls as in boys[1][5]. This female predominance applies to both unilateral and bilateral forms.

## Unrelated HPO Terms

The following terms do not appear in the search results regarding choanal atresia and represent unrelated conditions:

- **HP:0000316** (Hypertelorism) - Wide-set eyes
- **HP:0000422** (Abnormal nasal bridge morphology) - General nasal bridge abnormality

- **HP:0008677** (Congenital nephrotic syndrome) - Kidney disease
- **HP:0012324** (Myeloid leukemia) - Blood cancer
- **HP:0005508** (Monoclonal immunoglobulin M proteinemia) - Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
- **HP:0000426** (Prominent nasal bridge) - Elevated nasal bridge

### Why These Terms Are Unrelated

While some terms reference nasal features (abnormal nasal bridge morphology, short nose, prominent nasal bridge), they are **general descriptors** that could apply to many conditions and are not specifically associated with choanal atresia in the provided literature. The remaining terms (cardiac, neurological, behavioral, hematological, and renal conditions) represent completely distinct pathologies unrelated to choanal atresia.

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Common vs. Rare and Informative Terms

### Common and Less Informative Terms

The following HPO terms are relatively common across multiple conditions and therefore less specific for identifying a particular disease:

**Seizure (HP:0001250)** - Seizures occur in numerous neurological and genetic conditions, making them a non-specific finding. They appear in epilepsy, metabolic disorders, brain malformations, and many other syndromes.

**Recurrent infections (HP:0002719)** - This term reflects immune system dysfunction and can occur in various conditions affecting immunity, including zinc deficiency, immunodeficiencies, and other systemic disorders.[3]

**Short stature (HP:0004322)** - Growth impairment is a common feature in many genetic syndromes, metabolic disorders, and chronic conditions, making it relatively non-specific.

**Hearing impairment (HP:0000365)** - While important clinically, hearing loss occurs in numerous genetic syndromes and acquired conditions.

**Low-set ears (HP:0000369)** - This dysmorphic feature appears in many genetic syndromes but is not specific to any particular condition.

**Nystagmus (HP:0000639)** - Involuntary eye movements can result from various neurological conditions affecting the visual or vestibular systems.

### Rare and Highly Informative Terms

The following HPO terms are more specific and informative for particular disease categories:

**Abnormal blood zinc concentration (HP:0008277)** - This term is highly specific and directly points toward zinc metabolism disorders, particularly acrodermatitis enteropathica, which results from mutations in genes like SLC39A4 affecting zinc absorption.[3][6][9] This finding is particularly informative because severe zinc deficiency is rare and has a limited differential diagnosis.

**Hypomanganesemia (HP:0032098)** - A reduction in blood manganese concentration is a rare finding that points toward specific metabolic disorders affecting trace metal homeostasis.

**Abnormality of mitochondrial metabolism (HP:0003287)** - This term indicates dysfunction in cellular energy production and is informative for identifying mitochondrial disorders, a specific class of genetic conditions.

**Cerebral atrophy (HP:0002059)** and **Cerebral cortical atrophy (HP:0002120)** - While brain atrophy can occur in several conditions, the specific pattern and timing of atrophy can be informative for certain progressive neurological disorders.

**Ventriculomegaly (HP:0002119)** - Enlarged cerebral ventricles can indicate specific developmental or degenerative processes affecting brain structure.

## Developmental and Neurological Specificity

**Profound intellectual disability (HP:0002187)** and **Profound global developmental delay (HP:0012736)** - These terms indicate severe neurodevelopmental impairment. While not disease-specific individually, they are highly informative when combined with other findings. They suggest early-onset brain dysfunction and are particularly relevant in pediatric presentations.[1][4]

**Severe muscular hypotonia (HP:0006829)** and **Poor head control (HP:0002421)** - Severe hypotonia with poor head control is characteristic of central nervous system dysfunction and is particularly informative in infants, where it suggests early developmental abnormalities.[2][5][8] The combination of these findings in infancy is more specific than either finding alone.

**Inability to walk (HP:0002540)** - When combined with other neurological findings like spasticity or severe hypotonia, this indicates significant motor system involvement.

## Age and Gender Patterns

### Age-Specific Patterns

**Infancy and Early Childhood** - Several HPO terms are predominantly identified in infants and young children:

- **Poor head control (HP:0002421)** - Typically identified by 3-4 months of age; head lag beyond this age is abnormal.[2]
- **Severe muscular hypotonia (HP:0006829)** - Most commonly detected at birth or during early infancy, often called "floppy baby syndrome."[2][8]
- **Failure to thrive in infancy (HP:0001531)** - By definition, occurs in the first year of life and reflects inadequate growth and development.
- **Profound global developmental delay (HP:0012736)** - Identified during infancy and early childhood as developmental milestones are not achieved.

**Zinc deficiency conditions** - Infants are particularly susceptible to zinc deficiency through multiple mechanisms, including lower intestinal absorption capacity, low zinc concentration in maternal breast milk, and dietary factors.[6] Acrodermatitis enteropathica typically manifests in infancy after weaning from breast milk or when zinc intake becomes inadequate.[3][15]

**Seizures (HP:0001250)** - While seizures can occur at any age, certain genetic conditions with seizures present in infancy or early childhood, such as infantile spasms or early infantile epileptic encephalopathies.

### Gender Patterns

The search results do not provide specific information indicating that most of these HPO terms show significant gender predilection. However, there is one notable exception:

**Zinc deficiency through maternal transmission** - Mutations in the ZnT2 transporter gene (SLC30A2) in mothers can result in zinc-deficient breast milk, causing severe zinc deficiency in breast-fed infants.[6][9] This creates a maternal-to-infant transmission pattern rather than a gender-specific predilection in affected individuals.

Most of the neurological and developmental HPO terms listed (intellectual disability, developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures) do not show strong gender predilection and affect both males and females similarly, though some underlying genetic conditions may show X-linked inheritance patterns not specifically detailed in these search results.

hpo_input.name: Dystonia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally increased muscular tone that causes fixed abnormal postures. There is a slow, intermittent twisting motion that leads to exaggerated turning and posture of the extremities and trunk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Head titubation
hpo_input.definition: "A head tremor of moderate speed (3 to 4 Hz) in the anterior-posterior direction." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Upper motor neuron dysfunction
hpo_input.definition: "A functional anomaly of the upper motor neuron. [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal reflex
hpo_input.definition: "Any anomaly of a reflex, i.e., of an automatic response mediated by the nervous system (a reflex does not need the intervention of conscious thought to occur)." []

hpo_input.name: Strabismus
hpo_input.definition: "A misalignment of the eyes so that the visual axes deviate from bifoveal fixation. hpo_input.name: Laryngeal web

hpo_input.name: Salivary gland neoplasm

hpo_input.definition: "A brighter than expected signal on magnetic resonance imaging emanating from the cerebral white matter." [PMID:15576652]

| **HP:0100684 Salivary gland neoplasm** | **Rare and informative:** Tumors of salivary glands are uncommon and informative for oncological diagnosis[1]. | More common in adults; no clear gender bias. |
| **HP:0030318 Angular cheilitis** | **Common but nonspecific:** Inflammation at mouth corners is common and usually nonspecific; less informative for genetic diseases unless syndromic[1]. | Any age; no gender bias. |
| **HP:0005110 Atrial fibrillation** | **Common in adults, informative for cardiac disease:** Atrial fibrillation is a common arrhythmia in adults, especially elderly; informative for cardiovascular risk[1]. | More common in older adults; no gender bias. |

hpo_input.name: Retinopathy of prematurity stage 5
hpo_input.definition: "Funnel detachment from the retina with generally traction in all four quadrants." [ISBN:978-3-319-52190-9]

hpo_input.name: Arthralgia
hpo_input.definition: "Joint pain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Diabetes insipidus
hpo_input.definition: "A state of excessive water intake and hypotonic (dilute) polyuria. Diabetes insipidus may be due to failure of vasopressin (AVP) release (central or neurogenic diabetes insipidus) or to a failure of the kidney to respond to AVP (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)." hpo_input.name: Parasomnia
hpo_input.definition: "An undesirable physical event or experience that occurs during the process of falling asleep, while asleep, or when waking up from sleep." [PMID:35956054]

hpo_input.definition: "Width of the forehead or distance between the frontotemporales is more than two standard deviations above the mean (objective); or apparently increased distance between the two sides of the forehead." [PMID:19125436]

### **1. Macrocephaly (HP:0000256)**
- **Common and less informative?**  
  Yes, macrocephaly is a very common finding and is often non-specific. It can be benign (familial) or associated with a wide range of genetic, metabolic, and neurological conditions. It is not diagnostic of any single disease.

- **Rare and informative?**  
  When present in combination with other features (e.g., developmental delay, seizures, or specific facial features), it can be informative for syndromes like Sotos syndrome, neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, or megalencephaly syndromes.

- **Gender or age group more likely?**  
  Macrocephaly is more commonly observed in males, especially in the context of autism spectrum disorder. It is usually detected in infancy or early childhood.

---

  Long philtrum is a relatively common facial feature and can be seen in several syndromes (e.g., fetal alcohol syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Sotos syndrome). It is not specific to one condition.

  When combined with other features (e.g., micrognathia, hypertelorism), it can be a clue to specific syndromes like Fryns syndrome or fetal alcohol syndrome.

# Analysis of HPO Terms for Disease Specificity and Informativeness

## Overview of Term Categories

The HPO terms provided span a range of clinical features from highly specific to relatively common manifestations. Below is a detailed analysis addressing each of your three questions.

## 1. Common and Less Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are relatively common across multiple conditions and therefore less specific for identifying a particular disease:

**Seizure (HP:0001250)** represents one of the most non-specific terms in this list. Seizures occur in numerous neurological conditions including epilepsy, metabolic disorders, infections, brain tumors, and many genetic syndromes. This symptom alone provides minimal diagnostic specificity.

**Strabismus (HP:0000486)** and **Abnormal conjugate eye movement (HP:0000549)** are common eye movement abnormalities that can result from various causes including developmental disorders, neurological conditions, and muscular problems. While strabismus is frequently observed, it lacks disease specificity[1].

**Hypertonia (HP:0001276)** (increased muscle tone) is a common finding in cerebral palsy, spastic paraplegia, and numerous neurological disorders. Its presence alone does not narrow the differential diagnosis significantly.

**Scoliosis (HP:0002650)** occurs in many conditions including neuromuscular disorders, connective tissue diseases, and idiopathic forms. It is relatively common and non-specific.

**Abnormal retinal morphology (HP:0000479)** and **Abnormality of retinal pigmentation (HP:0007703)** are broad categories that encompass many different retinal conditions and are therefore less informative without additional specification.

## 2. Rare and Highly Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are more specific and informative for particular disease categories:

**Nystagmus (HP:0000639)** is a rhythmic, involuntary oscillation of the eyes[1] that, while not exclusively rare, becomes highly informative when combined with other features. Congenital nystagmus typically appears between 6 weeks and 3 months of age and is often associated with specific conditions such as albinism, congenital cataracts, or underdeveloped optic nerves[1]. The presence of nystagmus in combination with other neurological features can significantly narrow diagnostic possibilities.

**Microcephaly (HP:0000252)** is a relatively specific finding indicating abnormal brain development. When present with other features, it strongly suggests genetic syndromes, intrauterine infections, or developmental disorders.

**Intrauterine growth retardation (HP:0001511)** combined with other features suggests prenatal-onset conditions, including genetic syndromes, infections (TORCH), or placental abnormalities. This term is informative particularly when clustered with other congenital anomalies.

**Cerebral cortical atrophy (HP:0002120)** is a more specific neuroimaging finding that indicates progressive neurological disease or developmental abnormality and helps narrow the differential diagnosis.

**Pointed chin (HP:0000307)** is a distinctive facial feature that, while subtle, can be characteristic of specific syndromes when combined with other facial features.

**Tracheal atresia (HP:0100682)** is a rare congenital anomaly that is highly specific and informative, as it occurs in only a limited number of genetic conditions.

**Cervical ribs (HP:0000891)** and **Spina bifida occulta (HP:0003298)** are skeletal anomalies that, while not extremely rare, are relatively specific findings that suggest particular developmental or genetic conditions.

**Webbed neck (HP:0000465)** is a distinctive feature associated with specific syndromes such as Turner syndrome and Noonan syndrome, making it informative when present.

## 3. Gender and Age-Related Patterns

**Age-Related Patterns:**

Several terms show clear age-related presentations:

- **Nystagmus (HP:0000639)**: Congenital nystagmus typically manifests between 6 weeks and 3 months of age[1]. Spasmus nutans, a specific form, usually occurs between 6 months and 3 years of age and often improves spontaneously between 2 and 8 years[1].

- **Seizures (HP:0001250)**: Can occur at any age but certain types are age-specific (infantile spasms, childhood absence epilepsy, etc.).

- **Intrauterine growth retardation (HP:0001511)**: By definition, this occurs prenatally and is identified at birth or during prenatal imaging.

- **Microcephaly (HP:0000252)**: Typically identified in infancy when head circumference measurements fall below normal ranges.

**Gender-Related Patterns:**

Most of these HPO terms do not show strong gender predilection. However, some exceptions exist:

- **Turner syndrome** (associated with webbed neck) predominantly affects females, making **Webbed neck (HP:0000465)** more informative in female patients.

- **Nystagmus (HP:0000639)**: Some forms of congenital nystagmus can be X-linked, making them more common in males, though many forms show no gender predilection.

- **Writer's cramp (HP:0002356)**: While not exclusively gender-specific, focal dystonias show variable gender prevalence depending on the underlying etiology.

- **Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000819)**: Type 1 diabetes shows relatively equal gender distribution, while Type 2 diabetes may show slight variations by gender and age.

Most other terms in this list (seizures, hypertonia, scoliosis, strabismus, retinal abnormalities) show no significant gender predilection.

hpo_input.definition: "Inability to walk in a person who previous had the ability to walk." []

hpo_input.name: Progressive gait ataxia
hpo_input.definition: "A type of gait ataxia displaying progression of clinical severity." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Overview of HPO Term Classification

The HPO (Human Phenotype Ontology) terms provided span a range of neurological and systemic manifestations. Here's a comprehensive analysis addressing your three questions:

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Spasticity (HP:0001257)** and **Upper motor neuron dysfunction (HP:0002493)** are among the most common and least specific terms in this set.[1] These represent broad categories of neurological dysfunction that appear across numerous conditions including cerebral palsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and traumatic brain injury.[1][5] While clinically important, they lack disease-specificity because they describe a mechanism rather than a unique presentation.

**Progressive neurologic deterioration (HP:0002344)** is similarly non-specific, as it characterizes the natural course of many neurodegenerative diseases rather than distinguishing between them.[4][12] This term applies to conditions ranging from Alzheimer's disease to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to Parkinson's disease.

**Anxiety (HP:0000739)** and **Bipolar affective disorder (HP:0007302)** are common psychiatric manifestations that occur across multiple neurological conditions but are not pathognomonic for any specific disease. These represent secondary psychological consequences rather than primary neurological pathology.

**Ataxia (HP:0001251)** and **Gait ataxia (HP:0002066)** are moderately common findings in cerebellar and sensory disorders but appear in diverse etiologies including multiple sclerosis, Friedreich ataxia, and various peripheral neuropathies.[14]

## Rare and Informative Terms

**Erythromelalgia (HP:0032147)** is a rare and highly specific term that characterizes a distinct syndrome of recurrent episodes of redness, burning pain, and warmth of the extremities.[32147] This condition is relatively uncommon and, when present, strongly suggests specific underlying pathologies such as myeloproliferative disorders or primary erythromelalgia.

**Partial albinism (HP:0007443)** is a rare congenital finding that, when combined with neurological symptoms, can be highly informative for specific genetic syndromes such as Sturge-Weber syndrome or other neurocutaneous disorders.[5]

**Coronary artery calcification (HP:0001717)** is a relatively rare finding in the context of neurological disease and, when present alongside neurological manifestations, may suggest specific metabolic or genetic conditions affecting both the nervous and cardiovascular systems.

**Spastic dysarthria (HP:0002464)** is more specific than general spasticity, as it indicates bilateral upper motor neuron involvement affecting speech production.[2464] This is particularly informative in progressive supranuclear palsy and other conditions with specific patterns of neurodegeneration.

**Progressive gait ataxia (HP:0007240)** is more informative than static gait ataxia because the progressive nature narrows the differential diagnosis toward degenerative conditions rather than static structural lesions.[7240]

## Gender and Age Group Associations

**Age-Related Patterns:**

Most of these HPO terms show age-dependent prevalence. **Progressive neurologic deterioration (HP:0002344)** and conditions manifesting **spasticity (HP:0001257)** increase significantly with age when caused by stroke or neurodegenerative diseases.[2][12] However, **spastic gait (HP:0002064)** and **upper motor neuron dysfunction (HP:0002493)** are notably common in children with cerebral palsy, representing congenital or perinatal etiologies.[5][7]

**Spastic diplegia** and other forms of cerebral palsy typically manifest in infancy and early childhood, making these HPO terms particularly relevant in pediatric populations.[7]

**Neurodegenerative conditions** causing **progressive gait ataxia (HP:0007240)** and **loss of ambulation (HP:0002505)** typically emerge in middle to late adulthood, with onset varying by specific disease (Huntington's disease typically appears in the 30s-40s, while Parkinson's disease more commonly presents after age 60).

**Gender Patterns:**

The search results provide limited explicit gender-specific information for most HPO terms. However, some conditions associated with these manifestations show gender differences:

- **Multiple sclerosis**, which commonly presents with **spasticity** and **gait ataxia**, shows a female predominance (approximately 2-3:1 female to male ratio).[1][5]
- **Parkinson's disease**, associated with postural tremor and progressive gait abnormalities, shows a slight male predominance.
- **Stroke**, a common cause of **spastic gait** and **upper motor neuron dysfunction**, shows variable gender patterns depending on age and risk factors.

**Psychiatric manifestations** like **anxiety (HP:0000739)** and **bipolar affective disorder (HP:0007302)** show higher prevalence in females across most populations, though this may reflect both biological and diagnostic bias factors.

The rarity of gender-specific data in the provided search results suggests that most HPO terms are relatively gender-neutral in their occurrence, with gender differences primarily reflecting the epidemiology of underlying diseases rather than the phenotypic manifestations themselves.

hpo_input.name: Seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A seizure is an intermittent abnormality of nervous system physiology characterized by a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15816939]

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Neurogenic bladder
hpo_input.definition: "A type of bladder dysfunction caused by neurologic damage. Neurogenic bladder can be flaccid or spastic. Common manifestatios of neurogenic bladder are overflow incontinence, frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, and retention." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:18095004, PMID:22400020]
synonym: Lack of bladder control due to nervous system injury

hpo_input.name: Optic atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the optic nerve. Optic atrophy results from the death of the retinal ganglion cell axons that comprise the optic nerve and manifesting as a pale optic nerve on fundoscopy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Absent speech
hpo_input.definition: "Complete lack of development of speech and language abilities." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Constipation
hpo_input.definition: "Infrequent or difficult evacuation of feces." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Ventriculomegaly
hpo_input.definition: "An increase in size of the ventricular system of the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal periventricular white matter morphology
hpo_input.definition: "A structural abnormality of the myelinated axons (white matter) located near the cerebral ventricles." []
synonym: Abnormality of the periventricular white matter

hpo_input.name: Oromotor apraxia
hpo_input.definition: "Oral-motor apraxia is the inability to volitionally sequence oral movements of the speech structure for nonspeech tasks in the absence of neuromuscular deficits such as paralysis or muscle weakness. Oral-motor apraxia is diagnosed when, despite intact sensory motor function an individual is unable to use these effector systems under voluntary control." [PMID:26275812]

hpo_input.name: Visual impairment
hpo_input.definition: "Visual impairment (or vision impairment) is vision loss (of a person) to such a degree as to qualify as an additional support need through a significant limitation of visual capability resulting from either disease, trauma, or congenital or degenerative conditions that cannot be corrected by conventional means, such as refractive correction, medication, or surgery." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8727-6592]

hpo_input.name: Delayed myelination
hpo_input.definition: "Delayed myelination." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5208-3432]

hpo_input.name: Cerebellar atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Cerebellar atrophy is defined as a cerebellum with initially normal structures, in a posterior fossa with normal size, which displays enlarged fissures (interfolial spaces) in comparison to the foliae secondary to loss of tissue. Cerebellar atrophy implies irreversible loss of tissue and result from an ongoing progressive disease until a final stage is reached or a single injury, e.g. an intoxication or infectious event." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:12169461, PMID:26331051]

hpo_input.name: Exotropia
hpo_input.definition: "A form of strabismus with one or both eyes deviated outward." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Aggressive behavior
hpo_input.definition: "Behavior or an act aimed at harming a person, animal, or physical property (e.g., acts of physical violence; shouting, swearing, and using harsh language; slashing someone's tires)." []

hpo_input.name: Chronic rhinitis
hpo_input.definition: "Chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Supernumerary tooth
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of one or more teeth additional to the normal number." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9338-3017, PMID:31468724]

hpo_input.name: Muscular dystrophy
hpo_input.definition: "The term dystrophy means abnormal growth. However, muscular dystrophy is used to describe primary myopathies with a genetic basis and a progressive course characterized by progressive skeletal muscle weakness and wasting, defects in muscle proteins, and histological features of muscle fiber degeneration (necrosis) and regeneration. If possible, it is preferred to use other HPO terms to describe the precise phenotypic abnormalities." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9046-3540, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of the outer ear
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the external ear." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Multicystic kidney dysplasia
hpo_input.definition: "Multicystic dysplasia of the kidney is characterized by multiple cysts of varying size in the kidney and the absence of a normal pelvicaliceal system. The condition is associated with ureteral or ureteropelvic atresia, and the affected kidney is nonfunctional." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

# Analysis of HPO Terms in Relation to Genetic Neurodevelopmental Disorders

## Overview

Based on the search results, I can provide analysis of these HPO terms in the context of genetic causes of intellectual disability, seizures, and developmental disorders. The terms cluster into three categories: highly common but non-specific, rare and informative, and those with age/gender associations.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)** and **Seizure (HP:0001250)** are the most prevalent but least specific terms in this set. Intellectual disability occurs in approximately 22% of individuals with epilepsy, and this prevalence increases with severity of intellectual disability.[3] These two conditions frequently co-occur, with seizures being a common comorbidity rather than a distinguishing feature. The co-occurrence is so frequent that it has become a recognized pattern in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs).[1]

**Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** is similarly non-specific, as it represents a broad category of early childhood developmental impairment that can result from numerous genetic and environmental causes.[6] This term is particularly common in early childhood presentations but lacks diagnostic specificity.

**Constipation (HP:0002019)**, **Chronic rhinitis (HP:0002257)**, and **Abnormality of the outer ear (HP:0000356)** are general medical findings that occur across many conditions and populations, making them poor discriminators for specific genetic disorders.

## Rare and Informative Terms

**SCN2A-related variants** emerge as highly informative markers from the search results, though not explicitly listed as a separate HPO term. Mutations in SCN2A are associated with a specific spectrum of presentations: infantile seizures, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability.[2] Importantly, the functional consequence of SCN2A variants predicts clinical presentation—hyperactive channels correlate with early seizure onset (first week of life), while completely inactive channels are associated with intellectual disability without seizures.[2]

**Optic atrophy (HP:0000648)** and **Visual impairment (HP:0000505)** are more informative when present, as they suggest specific genetic etiologies. For example, CEP290-associated neurodevelopmental and epileptic disorders present with visual impairment as a distinguishing feature.[3]

**Absent speech (HP:0001344)** and **Poor speech (HP:0002465)** are informative markers, particularly when combined with other features. Speech and language impairments are core features of specific genetic syndromes and correlate with severity of underlying genetic mutations.[2]

**Ventriculomegaly (HP:0002119)**, **Abnormal periventricular white matter morphology (HP:0002518)**, **Delayed myelination (HP:0012448)**, and **Cerebellar atrophy (HP:0001272)** are neuroimaging findings that provide structural evidence of specific neurodevelopmental processes. These are particularly informative because they suggest specific patterns of brain development disruption associated with particular genetic etiologies.

**Oromotor apraxia (HP:0007301)** is a relatively rare and specific finding that, when present alongside seizures and intellectual disability, can narrow the differential diagnosis significantly.

## Age and Gender Associations

**Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** is definitionally restricted to children younger than five years of age, making it age-specific by definition.[1] This term is most relevant during early childhood assessment.

**Seizure onset age** shows strong gender and age patterns in specific genetic conditions. In SCN2A-related disorders, hyperactive channel variants typically present with seizure onset in the first week of life, while more impaired channel function correlates with later seizure onset.[2] However, the search results do not indicate strong gender differences in seizure presentation for most genetic forms.

**Fragile X syndrome**, mentioned in the search results as a common genetic cause of intellectual disability and autism, shows **gender-related severity differences**: males typically present with moderate to severe developmental delay and intellectual disability, while females often have milder disability.[6] This represents one of the clearest gender-based phenotypic differences in the genetic neurodevelopmental disorder spectrum.

**Intellectual disability severity** correlates with age of presentation and diagnostic yield. Diagnostic yield from genetic testing is higher in individuals with moderate (57.1%) and severe to profound (50.0%) intellectual disability compared with mildly affected individuals (34.0%).[3] This suggests that more severe presentations, which may manifest earlier in development, have clearer genetic etiologies.

The search results do not provide specific information regarding gender associations for most of the other HPO terms listed, though the general prevalence of epilepsy in intellectual disability appears consistent across genders in the available data.

hpo_input.name: Abnormal superficial reflex
hpo_input.definition: "An anomaly of a reflex that is elicited as a motor response to scraping of the skin. They are generally graded as present or absent. hpo_input.name: Inability to walk
hpo_input.definition: "Incapability to ambulate." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Generalized hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Generalized muscular hypotonia (abnormally low muscle tone)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Intellectual disability
hpo_input.definition: "Intellectual disability, previously referred to as mental retardation, is characterized by subnormal intellectual functioning that occurs during the developmental period. It is defined by an IQ score below 70." []

hpo_input.name: Failure to thrive
hpo_input.definition: "Failure to thrive (FTT) refers to a child whose physical growth is substantially below the norm." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: EEG abnormality
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormality observed by electroencephalogram (EEG), which is used to record of the brain's spontaneous electrical activity from multiple electrodes placed on the scalp." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Expressive language delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the acquisition of the ability to use language to communicate needs, wishes, or thoughts." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Nystagmus
hpo_input.definition: "Rhythmic, involuntary oscillations of one or both eyes related to abnormality in fixation, conjugate gaze, or vestibular mechanisms." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Interictal epileptiform activity
hpo_input.definition: "Epileptiform activity refers to distinctive EEG waves or complexes distinguished from background activity found in in a proportion of human subjects with epilepsy, but which can also be found in subjects without seizures. Interictal epileptiform activity refers to such activity that occurs in the absence of a clinical or subclinical seizure." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Polymicrogyria
hpo_input.definition: "Polymicrogyria is a congenital malformation of the cerebral cortex characterized by abnormal cortical layering (lamination) and an excessive number of small gyri (folds)." [http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q90573458, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:24888723]

hpo_input.name: Seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A seizure is an intermittent abnormality of nervous system physiology characterized by a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15816939]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal circulating cholesterol concentration
hpo_input.definition: "Any deviation from the normal concentration of cholesterol in the blood circulation." []

hpo_input.name: Amenorrhea
hpo_input.definition: "Absence of menses for an interval of time equivalent to a total of more than (or equal to) 3 previous cycles or 6 months." [PMID:22594864]

hpo_input.name: Miscarriage
hpo_input.definition: "A pregnancy that ends at a stage in which the fetus is incapable of surviving on its own, defined as the spontaneous loss of a fetus before the 22th week of pregnancy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Strabismus
hpo_input.definition: "A misalignment of the eyes so that the visual axes deviate from bifoveal fixation. The classification of strabismus may be based on a number of features including the relative position of the eyes, whether the deviation is latent or manifest, intermittent or constant, concomitant or otherwise and according to the age of onset and the relevance of any associated refractive error." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0986-4123, PMID:26319345]

hpo_input.name: Overfolded helix
hpo_input.definition: "A condition in which the helix is folded over to a greater degree than normal. That is, excessive curling of the helix edge, whereby the free edge is parallel to the plane of the ear." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19152421]

hpo_input.name: Aneurysmal bone cyst
hpo_input.definition: "Radiographic features include a dilated, radiolucent lesion typically located eccentrically within the metaphyseal portion of the bone, with fluid levels visible on magnetic resonance imaging." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:22474093, PMID:7863874]

hpo_input.name: Sacral dimple
hpo_input.definition: "A cutaneous indentation resulting from tethering of the skin to underlying structures (bone) of the intergluteal cleft." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:28245993]

hpo_input.name: Insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus
hpo_input.definition: "A type of diabetes mellitus related not to lack of insulin but rather to lack of response to insulin on the part of the target tissues of insulin such as muscle, fat, and liver cells. This type of diabetes is typically associated with increases both in blood glucose concentrations as well as in fasting and postprandial serum insulin levels." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:7706500]

hpo_input.name: Mandibular pain
hpo_input.definition: "An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the mandible." []

hpo_input.name: Tracheoesophageal fistula
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormal connection (fistula) between the esophagus and the trachea." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Overview of Term Categories

The HPO terms provided span a wide range of clinical manifestations, from highly common and non-specific symptoms to rare and disease-specific findings. Below is a detailed analysis addressing each of your three questions.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Inability to walk (HP:0002540)** is a relatively common symptom that appears across numerous neurological and genetic conditions[1][2]. While it indicates significant motor impairment, it lacks specificity because it can result from diverse underlying causes including muscle weakness, balance disorders, neurological damage, or developmental delays[1].

**Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** is another broadly applicable term that appears in many pediatric genetic syndromes and neurological conditions. This term describes delayed achievement of motor or mental milestones in children under five years old, but the underlying etiology varies widely[6].

**Seizure (HP:0001250)** and **EEG abnormality (HP:0002353)** are common in neurological disorders but lack specificity. While they indicate nervous system dysfunction, they occur in numerous conditions ranging from epilepsy to metabolic disorders to genetic syndromes.

**Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)** is similarly non-specific, appearing in hundreds of genetic and acquired conditions. It represents a broad category of cognitive impairment rather than a distinctive diagnostic feature.

**Generalized hypotonia (HP:0001290)** is a common finding in neuromuscular and neurological disorders but does not point to a specific diagnosis without additional clinical context.

**Failure to thrive (HP:0001508)** is a general indicator of poor growth that can result from nutritional, metabolic, or systemic causes, making it non-specific for disease diagnosis.

## Rare and Informative Terms

**Polymicrogyria (HP:0002126)** is a rare congenital malformation of the cerebral cortex characterized by abnormal cortical layering and excessive small gyri. This is a highly specific neuroimaging finding that, when present, significantly narrows the differential diagnosis and suggests specific genetic or developmental etiologies.

**Aneurysmal bone cyst (HP:0012063)** is a rare skeletal lesion with distinctive radiographic features including eccentric metaphyseal location and fluid levels on MRI. Its presence is highly informative for specific bone pathologies.

**Tracheoesophageal fistula (HP:0002575)** is a rare congenital malformation representing an abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus. This specific anatomical defect is highly informative and associated with particular genetic syndromes.

**Interictal epileptiform activity (HP:0011182)** is more specific than general EEG abnormality, as it represents distinctive epileptiform discharges on EEG that are characteristic of epilepsy, though not pathognomonic.

**Nystagmus (HP:0000639)** indicates rhythmic involuntary eye movements related to specific neurological or vestibular abnormalities, making it more informative than general developmental delay.

## Gender and Age-Specific Patterns

**Age-specific terms:**

**Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** is definitionally restricted to children younger than five years of age, as it describes delayed achievement of developmental milestones during early childhood[6].

**Failure to thrive (HP:0001508)** primarily affects infants and young children, as it describes substantially below-normal physical growth during the developmental period.

**Expressive language delay (HP:0002474)** is most relevant in young children during the language acquisition period, typically identified in the first few years of life.

**Gender-specific terms:**

**Amenorrhea (HP:0000141)** is exclusively relevant to females of reproductive age, defined as absence of menses for three or more cycles or six months.

**Miscarriage (HP:0005268)** is specific to pregnant individuals, representing spontaneous pregnancy loss before 22 weeks gestation.

**Vulvodynia (HP:0030943)** is specific to individuals with vulvae, representing pain in the vulvar area.

**Insulin-resistant diabetes mellitus (HP:0000831)** and most other metabolic and neurological terms show no inherent gender predisposition, though specific genetic syndromes associated with these features may show sex-linked inheritance patterns.

**Mandibular pain (HP:0200025)** and **Strabismus (HP:0000486)** are not gender or age-specific, occurring across all demographics depending on underlying etiology.

**Sacral dimple (HP:0000960)** and **Overfolded helix (HP:0000396)** are congenital features present from birth and are not gender or age-specific in their occurrence.

Here is a detailed analysis for each of the provided HPO terms, addressing the three questions:

---

### **1. Hypertriglyceridemia (HP:0002155)**
- **Common/Less Informative:** Yes, hypertriglyceridemia is a common finding in many metabolic disorders (e.g., metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, and certain medications). It is not specific to a single disease.
- **Rare/Informative:** No, it is not rare. However, extremely high levels (severe hypertriglyceridemia) can be seen in rare genetic disorders like familial chylomicronemia syndrome (lipoprotein lipase deficiency).
- **Gender/Age Group:** More common in adults, especially those with obesity, metabolic syndrome, or type 2 diabetes. No strong gender predilection, but can be more prevalent in men with metabolic syndrome.

---

### **2. Hepatomegaly (HP:0002240)**
- **Common/Less Informative:** Yes, hepatomegaly is a common finding in many liver diseases (e.g., fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis, heart failure, infections, metabolic disorders, and malignancies). It is not specific to a single disease.
- **Rare/Informative:** No, it is not rare. However, in rare genetic or metabolic diseases (e.g., glycogen storage diseases, lysosomal storage disorders), hepatomegaly can be a key feature.
- **Gender/Age Group:** Can occur at any age. More common in adults with metabolic syndrome, alcohol-related liver disease, or heart failure. In children, it may be seen in metabolic or infectious diseases.

---

### **3. Elevated circulating creatine kinase concentration (HP:0003236)**
- **Common/Less Informative:** Yes, elevated CK is common in many muscle disorders (e.g., muscular dystrophies, rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise, trauma, hypothyroidism, and some medications). It is not specific to a single disease.
- **Rare/Informative:** No, it is not rare. However, persistently high CK levels can be informative in rare muscle diseases (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy).

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Exercise Intolerance (HP:0003546)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Exercise intolerance is a relatively common symptom that appears across numerous medical conditions, making it less specific for diagnosing a particular disease[1][4][5]. Approximately 50% of the more than 6 million people in the U.S. with heart failure experience exercise intolerance[6]. The symptom can result from cardiopulmonary issues (60% of cases), metabolic disorders (25%), or neuromuscular conditions[5].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
While exercise intolerance itself is common, certain underlying causes are rare and highly informative. Metabolic myopathies, mitochondrial disorders like McArdle disease, and specific genetic conditions causing exercise intolerance are rare and provide strong diagnostic clues[1][4][5].

**Demographics:**
Exercise intolerance can affect any age group, including children with asthma, congenital heart disease, or iron deficiency[5]. It is particularly common in women over 60 with hypertension who develop heart failure with preserved ejection fraction[5].

**Commonality and Informativeness:**

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
The specific type of dysarthria (spastic, flaccid, ataxic, hyperkinetic, hypokinetic, or mixed) becomes more informative for identifying the underlying neurological disorder[1]. Certain patterns of dysarthria are associated with specific rare neurological conditions.

**Demographics:**
Dysarthria can occur across all age groups but is particularly associated with motor neuron diseases, which may present differently depending on age of onset.

When dysphagia appears in combination with other symptoms (such as dysarthria and muscle weakness), it becomes more informative for identifying specific neuromuscular or motor neuron diseases.

Dysphagia becomes increasingly common with age and is frequently seen in elderly populations. It can also occur in children with feeding difficulties related to neuromuscular conditions.

Neurogenic muscle atrophy, particularly when localized to specific muscle groups or appearing in combination with other symptoms, becomes more informative for identifying motor neuron diseases, spinal cord disorders, or specific myopathies.

Muscle atrophy increases with age and sedentary lifestyle. It is more prevalent in elderly populations but can occur at any age depending on the underlying cause.

Hip subluxation can occur at any age but is more commonly associated with progressive neuromuscular diseases that develop in childhood or early adulthood.

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Primary CNS lymphoma is a rare malignancy, making it highly specific when present. However, as a symptom or finding, it is not commonly encountered in general practice.

This is a rare and highly specific diagnosis. Its presence is highly informative for identifying a specific type of cancer.

Primary CNS lymphoma typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals (particularly those with HIV/AIDS) or in elderly populations. It is rare in immunocompetent younger individuals.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a relatively rare lung condition, making it more specific when present. It requires exposure to a specific antigen.

This is a rare condition that is highly informative when identified, as it indicates a specific environmental exposure and immune response pattern.

**Demographics:**
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis can occur at any age but is more common in occupational settings with specific antigen exposures (farmers, bird handlers, etc.).

Natal teeth are relatively rare, occurring in approximately 1 in 2,000 to 3,000 births, making them more specific and informative when present.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Natal teeth are rare and can be associated with specific genetic syndromes, making them informative for identifying certain rare genetic conditions.

Natal teeth are identified at birth or within the first month of life by definition. They occur equally across genders.

Chiari malformation is a relatively rare structural brain abnormality, making it more specific and informative when identified. It can cause various neurological symptoms.

Chiari malformation is rare and highly informative for identifying a specific structural CNS abnormality. When present with other symptoms, it helps guide diagnosis and management.
