hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.definition: "Cerebellar atrophy is defined as a cerebellum with initially normal structures, in a posterior fossa with normal size, which displays enlarged fissures (interfolial spaces) in comparison to the foliae secondary to loss of tissue. Cerebellar atrophy implies irreversible loss of tissue and result from an ongoing progressive disease until a final stage is reached or a single injury, e.g. an intoxication or infectious event." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:12169461, PMID:26331051]

hpo_input.name: Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the cerebral white matter
hpo_input.definition: "Absence or underdevelopment of the cerebral white matter." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Perisylvian polymicrogyria
hpo_input.definition: "Polymicrogyria (an excessive number of small gyri or convolutions) that is maximal in perisylvian regions (the regions that surround the Sylvian fissures), which may be symmetric or asymmetric and may extend beyond perisylvian regions. The Sylvian fissures often extend posteriorly and superiorly." [http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q90573458, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15159468, PMID:20301504]

hpo_input.name: Cognitive impairment
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormal cognition is characterized by deficits in thinking, reasoning, or remembering." []

hpo_input.name: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita
hpo_input.definition: "Multiple congenital contractures in different body areas." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:23050160]

hpo_input.name: Neurodevelopmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "Neurodevelopmental delay (NDD) refers to delays in the maturation of the brain and central nervous system; infants and young children with NDD may experience delays in the development of one or more skills including gross motor abilities, fine-motor coordination, language abilities and ability to solve increasingly complex problems." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6670-9157, PMID:31783983]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal speech pattern
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality in the sound (volume) or cadence (rate) of speech." []

hpo_input.name: Micrognathia
hpo_input.definition: "Developmental hypoplasia of the mandible." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dysarthria
hpo_input.definition: "Dysarthric speech is a general description referring to a neurological speech disorder characterized by poor articulation. Depending on the involved neurological structures, dysarthria may be further classified as spastic, flaccid, ataxic, hyperkinetic and hypokinetic, or mixed." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Sensorineural hearing impairment
hpo_input.definition: "A type of hearing impairment in one or both ears related to an abnormal functionality of the cochlear nerve." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abetalipoproteinemia
hpo_input.definition: "An absence of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Chronic sinusitis
hpo_input.definition: "A chronic form of sinusitis." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Histrionic personality disorder
hpo_input.definition: "A personality disorder characterized by shallow and labile affectivity, self-dramatization, theatricality, exaggerated expression of emotions, suggestibility, egocentricity, self-indulgence, lack of consideration for others, easily hurt feelings, and continuous seeking for appreciation, excitement and attention." [ICD-10:F60.4]

hpo_input.name: Citrullinuria
hpo_input.definition: "The amount of citrulline in the urine, when normalized for urine concentration, is above the upper limit of normal." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8169-9049, PMID:29695388]

hpo_input.name: Lactose intolerance
hpo_input.definition: "An inability to digest lactose." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: High palate

hpo_input.name: Strabismus
hpo_input.definition: "A misalignment of the eyes so that the visual axes deviate from bifoveal fixation. hpo_input.definition: "A bilateral tonic-clonic seizure is a seizure defined by a tonic (bilateral increased tone, lasting seconds to minutes) and then a clonic (bilateral sustained rhythmic jerking) phase." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:28276060]
synonym: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure (without specification of onset)
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure (without specification of onset)

hpo_input.name: Neurodegeneration
hpo_input.definition: "Progressive loss of neural cells and tissue." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Increased CSF lactate
hpo_input.definition: "Increased concentration of lactate in the cerebrospinal fluid." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Gastrointestinal dysmotility
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormal intestinal contractions, such as spasms and intestinal paralysis, related to the loss of the ability of the gut to coordinate muscular activity because of endogenous or exogenous causes." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Increased CSF protein concentration
hpo_input.definition: "Increased concentration of protein in the cerebrospinal fluid." [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:KI_phemming, PMID:29114301]

hpo_input.name: Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex I
hpo_input.definition: "A reduction in the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I, which is part of the electron transport chain in mitochondria." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal autonomic nervous system physiology
hpo_input.definition: "A functional abnormality of the autonomic nervous system." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Diffuse cerebellar atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Diffuse unlocalised atrophy affecting the cerebellum." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal cerebral ventricle morphology
hpo_input.definition: "Any structural abnormality of the cerebral ventricles." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Feeding difficulties in infancy
hpo_input.definition: "Impaired feeding performance of an infant as manifested by difficulties such as weak and ineffective sucking, brief bursts of sucking, and falling asleep during sucking. There may be difficulties with chewing or maintaining attention." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Intermittent claudication
hpo_input.definition: "Intermittent claudication is a symptom of peripheral arterial occlusive disease. After having walked over a distance which is individually characteristic, the patients experience pain or cramps in the calves, feet or thighs which typically subsides on standing still." [PMID:27770207]

hpo_input.name: Polycystic kidney dysplasia
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of multiple cysts in both kidneys." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypocalcemia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally decreased calcium concentration in the blood." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Epileptic spasm
hpo_input.definition: "A sudden flexion, extension, or mixed extension-flexion of predominantly proximal and truncal muscles that is usually more sustained than a myoclonic movement but not as sustained as a tonic seizure. Limited forms may occur: Grimacing, head nodding, or subtle eye movements. Epileptic spasms frequently occur in clusters. Infantile spasms are the best known form, but spasms can occur at all ages" [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:jalbers, PMID:28276060]

hpo_input.name: Sinusitis
hpo_input.definition: "Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses owing to a viral, bacterial, or fungal infection, allergy, or an autoimmune reaction." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypertension
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of chronic increased pressure in the systemic arterial system." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Peripheral opacification of the cornea
hpo_input.definition: "Reduced transparency of the peripheral region of the cornea." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Ranula
hpo_input.definition: "A ranula is a mucocele that occurs in the floor of the mouth and usually involve the major salivary glands. Specifically, the ranula originates in the body of the sublingual gland, in the ducts of the sublingual gland, in the Wharton's duct of the submandibular gland or infrequently from the minor salivary glands at this location." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0003-6754, PMID:23291329]

hpo_input.name: White forelock
hpo_input.definition: "A triangular depigmented region of white hairs located in the anterior midline of the scalp." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: White part of hair above forehead

Here is an analysis of the provided HPO terms regarding their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and any known gender or age predilections:

---

### 1. **Retinopathy (HP:0000488)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Retinopathy is a broad, nonspecific term describing any noninflammatory retinal disease. It is common in conditions like diabetes and hypertension, making it less specific for a particular disease diagnosis[1][3][5][7][9].
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific types such as diabetic retinopathy or hypertensive retinopathy are more informative as they indicate underlying systemic diseases[1][3][5].
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in adults, especially those with diabetes or hypertension. No specific gender predilection noted[1][3][5].

---

### 2. **Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (HP:0002069)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** This seizure type is common in epilepsy and can occur in many neurological conditions, making it less specific alone[2][6][10][16].
- **Rare and Informative:** When linked to specific epilepsy syndromes or focal onset seizures spreading bilaterally, it becomes more informative[2][4][12].
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age; no strong gender bias. Some epilepsy syndromes with tonic-clonic seizures have pediatric onset[2][6][10].

---

### 3. **Neurodegeneration (HP:0002180)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Neurodegeneration is a broad term describing progressive neural loss, common in many neurological diseases, thus less specific[HPO definition].
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) are informative, but the general term is nonspecific.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Typically affects older adults but can occur at any age depending on the disorder.

---

### 4. **Poor coordination (HP:0002370)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** A nonspecific symptom seen in many neurological and systemic diseases.
- **Rare and Informative:** When associated with specific syndromes or genetic disorders, it gains informativeness.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 5. **Increased CSF lactate (HP:0002490)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Elevated CSF lactate is a relatively rare finding, often indicating mitochondrial disorders or metabolic dysfunction, thus informative[HPO definition].
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in infants and children with mitochondrial diseases.

---

### 6. **Gastrointestinal dysmotility (HP:0002579)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Abnormal gut motility is less common and often points to specific neuromuscular or systemic diseases, making it informative[HPO definition].
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age; no specific gender bias.

---

### 7. **Increased CSF protein concentration (HP:0002922)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Elevated CSF protein is a common nonspecific marker of CNS pathology (infection, inflammation, malignancy), less informative alone[HPO definition].
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific patterns or associated findings can be informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 8. **Myoclonic spasms (HP:0003739)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Myoclonic spasms are less common and often associated with specific epileptic syndromes (e.g., infantile spasms), thus informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in infants and young children.

---

### 9. **Abnormal muscle tone (HP:0003808)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** A nonspecific finding in many neurological disorders.
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific patterns (e.g., spasticity vs. hypotonia) can be more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 10. **Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex I (HP:0011923)**
- **Rare and Informative:** This is a specific biochemical abnormality indicative of mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders, highly informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in pediatric mitochondrial disease presentations.

---

### 11. **Abnormal autonomic nervous system physiology (HP:0012332)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Autonomic dysfunction is less common and can be a key feature in specific diseases (e.g., dysautonomia syndromes), informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can affect all ages; some forms more common in adults.

---

### 12. **Diffuse cerebellar atrophy (HP:0100275)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Cerebellar atrophy is a specific neuroimaging finding that can narrow differential diagnosis, informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age depending on etiology.

---

### 13. **Abnormal cerebral ventricle morphology (HP:0002118)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Ventricular abnormalities are common in many CNS disorders and nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific malformations or patterns can be informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 14. **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** A common pediatric finding, nonspecific for many genetic and acquired disorders.
- **Rare and Informative:** Specific associated features or genetic causes increase informativeness.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Only used for children under 5 years.

---

### 15. **Feeding difficulties in infancy (HP:0008872)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Common in many infant disorders, nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** When linked to specific syndromes, more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Infants only.

---

### 16. **Intermittent claudication (HP:0004417)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A specific symptom of peripheral arterial disease, informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in older adults, especially smokers and those with cardiovascular risk factors.

---

### 17. **Hepatic cysts (HP:0001407)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Presence of liver cysts can be informative for polycystic liver disease or systemic cystic disorders.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age; some cystic diseases have adult onset.

---

### 18. **Polycystic kidney dysplasia (HP:0000113)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Highly informative for polycystic kidney disease and related syndromes.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can present in childhood or adulthood depending on type.

---

### 19. **Hypocalcemia (HP:0002901)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Hypocalcemia is a common metabolic abnormality with many causes, less specific.
- **Rare and Informative:** When persistent or congenital, can be informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age.

---

### 20. **Hypercalciuria (HP:0002150)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Elevated urine calcium is less common and can indicate specific metabolic or renal disorders.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 21. **Epileptic spasm (HP:0011097)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Characteristic of infantile spasms (West syndrome), highly informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Primarily infants.

---

### 22. **Sinusitis (HP:0000246)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Very common and nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** Chronic or unusual forms may be more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** All ages.

---

### 23. **Hypertension (HP:0000822)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Very common, especially in adults, nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** Secondary hypertension forms are more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in adults and elderly.

---

### 24. **Peripheral opacification of the cornea (HP:0008011)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A specific ocular finding, informative for corneal diseases.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 25. **Ranula (HP:0030706)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A specific cystic lesion of the mouth floor, informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in young adults.

---

### 26. **White forelock (HP:0002211)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A distinctive pigmentary feature, informative for syndromes like Waardenburg syndrome.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Present from birth; no gender bias.

---

|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Retinopathy                    | Yes (broad term)                         | Specific types (diabetic, hypertensive)   | Adults with diabetes/hypertension   |
| Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure | Yes                                      | Focal onset spreading bilateral            | Any age; some pediatric syndromes   |
| Neurodegeneration              | Yes                                      | Specific disorders                         | Mostly older adults                  |
| Increased CSF lactate          | No                                       | Yes (mitochondrial/metabolic disorders)   | Infants/children                    |
| Gastrointestinal dysmotility  | No                                       | Yes                                        | Any age                            |
| Increased CSF protein          | Yes                                      | Specific patterns                          | Any age                            |
| Myoclonic spasms              | No                                       | Yes (infantile spasms)                     | Infants/young children             |
| Decreased mitochondrial complex I | No                                   | Yes                                        | Pediatric mitochondrial disease    |
| Global developmental delay     | Yes                                      | Yes (with associated features)             | Children <5 years                  |
| Epileptic spasm               | No                                       | Yes                                        | Infants                          |
| Hypertension                  | Yes                                      | Secondary forms                            | Adults/elderly                    |
| White forelock                | No                                       | Yes                                        | Congenital, no gender bias        |

---

This classification helps distinguish broad, common phenotypes that are less specific from rare, more disease-informative features, as well as highlighting relevant age or gender associations where known.

- **Rare and Informative:** Presence of liver cysts can be informative for polycystic liver disease or systemic cystic disorders.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age; some cystic diseases have adult onset.

---

### 18. **Polycystic kidney dysplasia (HP:0000113)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Highly informative for polycystic kidney disease and related syndromes.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can present in childhood or adulthood depending on type.

---

### 19. **Hypocalcemia (HP:0002901)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Hypocalcemia is a common metabolic abnormality with many causes, less specific.
- **Rare and Informative:** When persistent or congenital, can be informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Can occur at any age.

---

### 20. **Hypercalciuria (HP:0002150)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Elevated urine calcium is less common and can indicate specific metabolic or renal disorders.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 21. **Epileptic spasm (HP:0011097)**
- **Rare and Informative:** Characteristic of infantile spasms (West syndrome), highly informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Primarily infants.

---

### 22. **Sinusitis (HP:0000246)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Very common and nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** Chronic or unusual forms may be more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** All ages.

---

### 23. **Hypertension (HP:0000822)**
- **Common and Less Informative:** Very common, especially in adults, nonspecific.
- **Rare and Informative:** Secondary hypertension forms are more informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in adults and elderly.

---

### 24. **Peripheral opacification of the cornea (HP:0008011)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A specific ocular finding, informative for corneal diseases.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** No specific predilection.

---

### 25. **Ranula (HP:0030706)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A specific cystic lesion of the mouth floor, informative.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** More common in young adults.

---

### 26. **White forelock (HP:0002211)**
- **Rare and Informative:** A distinctive pigmentary feature, informative for syndromes like Waardenburg syndrome.
- **Age/Gender Predilection:** Present from birth; no gender bias.

# Analysis of HPO Terms for Disease Specificity and Informativeness

## Overview of Term Categories

Based on the search results and clinical literature, these HPO terms can be stratified by their diagnostic utility and specificity to particular genetic syndromes and disorders.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Hypertelorism (HP:0000316)** is among the most common and least specific terms in this list. It appears as a feature in numerous genetic syndromes including Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), DiGeorge syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome, Apert syndrome, Crouzon syndrome, and many others.[1][2][5] While hypertelorism is clinically recognizable and important for initial assessment, its presence alone provides limited diagnostic specificity because it occurs across such a broad range of conditions.

**Wide nasal bridge (HP:0000431)** similarly lacks specificity, appearing in multiple syndromes including Down syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome, and various craniofacial dysplasias.[1][3] This feature is often associated with hypertelorism and represents a common facial dysmorphism across many genetic conditions.

**Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)** and **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** are extremely common features across numerous genetic syndromes but provide minimal diagnostic specificity on their own. These terms describe functional outcomes rather than specific anatomical or pathological features.

**Abnormal eyelid morphology (HP:0000492)**, **Abnormal mandible morphology (HP:0000277)**, and **Abnormality of the gingiva (HP:0000168)** are broad categorical terms that encompass many different specific abnormalities without pointing to particular diagnoses.

**Hearing impairment (HP:0000365)** occurs in many syndromes but is nonspecific without additional clinical context.

**Scoliosis (HP:0002650)** and **Frontal balding (HP:0002292)** are relatively common findings in various conditions but lack strong diagnostic specificity.

## Rare and Highly Informative Terms

**Micromelia (HP:0002983)** combined with facial dysmorphism is more specific and appears in particular skeletal dysplasias and genetic syndromes. When present alongside other features, it narrows the differential diagnosis considerably.

**Sacrococcygeal pilonidal abnormality (HP:0010767)** is a rare and distinctive finding that, when present, significantly narrows the diagnostic possibilities.

**Hypoplasia of penis (HP:0008736)**, **Hypoplastic labia majora (HP:0000059)**, and **Clitoral hypoplasia (HP:0000060)** are specific genital abnormalities that, when combined with other features, can be highly informative. For example, these genital findings combined with frontonasal dysplasia features suggest FND-2 caused by *ALX4* mutations, which specifically includes genital malformations.[9]

**Hemivertebrae (HP:0002937)** is a specific skeletal abnormality that, when present with other features, can help identify particular skeletal dysplasias or genetic syndromes.

**Meconium peritonitis (HP:0030717)** is a rare prenatal finding that appears in specific genetic conditions like Fryns syndrome and indicates severe developmental abnormalities.

**Band keratopathy (HP:0000585)** is a specific ocular finding that, when present, suggests particular metabolic or genetic conditions.

**Premature ovarian insufficiency (HP:0008209)** is a specific reproductive finding that narrows diagnostic possibilities when present.

## Gender and Age-Specific Patterns

**Gender-specific considerations:**

Genital abnormalities including **Hypoplasia of penis (HP:0008736)**, **Hypoplastic labia majora (HP:0000059)**, and **Clitoral hypoplasia (HP:0000060)** are obviously sex-specific findings. In FND-2, these genital malformations occur in affected individuals regardless of sex, though they manifest differently.[9]

**Age-specific considerations:**

**Frontal balding (HP:0002292)** and **Alopecia (HP:0001596)** are age-dependent features that become more apparent with advancing age. In FND-2, total alopecia or unusual hair growth patterns may be present from birth or early childhood, but progressive hair loss would manifest over time.[9]

**Premature ovarian insufficiency (HP:0008209)** by definition affects reproductive-age females (typically before age 40), making it age and gender-specific.

**Developmental and behavioral terms** like **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)**, **Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)**, **Hyperactivity (HP:0000752)**, and **Hyperkinetic movements (HP:0002487)** are most evident and diagnosable in childhood and early development, though they persist into adulthood.

**Craniofacial features** including **Hypertelorism (HP:0000316)**, **Wide nasal bridge (HP:0000431)**, **Micrognathia (HP:0000347)**, and **Prominent forehead (HP:0011220)** are present from birth and remain relatively stable throughout life, though their relative prominence may change with facial growth and development. Surgical correction of hypertelorism is typically performed between ages 5-8 years.[2][11]

**Skeletal findings** like **Scoliosis (HP:0002650)** and **Hemivertebrae (HP:0002937)** may develop or become more apparent during periods of rapid skeletal growth, particularly during childhood and adolescence.

**Addictive behavior (HP:0030858)** and **Head-banging (HP:0012168)** are behavioral manifestations that typically emerge during childhood and may persist or change with age and development.

Here is a detailed analysis of the given HPO terms related to sperm abnormalities and other selected terms, addressing the three questions for each:

---

### 1. Oligozoospermia (HP:0000798)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Oligozoospermia, defined as a sperm count below 20 million/mL, is a relatively common cause of male infertility, accounting for a significant portion of male factor infertility cases (around 7% of men affected) and is often considered less specific because it can result from many causes such as varicocele, infections, hormonal imbalances, environmental toxins, and genetic factors[1][4][6][7][10][16][19].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  While oligozoospermia itself is common, cases caused by rare genetic syndromes or specific endocrine disorders (e.g., adrenal steroidogenesis abnormalities) are more informative for diagnosis[10].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  This condition is male-specific (affects males only) and typically diagnosed in reproductive-age men presenting with infertility[1][4][7][19].

---

### 2. Abnormal sperm head morphology (HP:0012865)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Abnormal sperm head morphology is common among infertile men and is a key parameter in semen analysis. However, mild abnormalities are frequent even in fertile men, making it less specific alone[2][14][20][27].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific morphological abnormalities like macrocephaly, microcephaly, globozoospermia, or multiple heads are rarer and more informative, often linked to genetic mutations or severe testicular damage[2][5][11][17][23].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Male-specific, typically identified in adult men undergoing fertility evaluation[2][14].

---

### 3. Abnormal sperm motility (HP:0012206)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Low sperm motility (asthenozoospermia) is a common cause of male infertility, affecting up to 2% of men and contributing to about 40-50% of infertility cases. It is less specific as it can be caused by many factors including genetics, infections, lifestyle, and varicocele[3][6][8][9][18][21].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe motility defects due to genetic causes or structural flagellar abnormalities are rarer and more informative diagnostically[15].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Male-specific, mostly diagnosed in reproductive-age men[3][6].

---

### 4. Focal sensory seizure (HP:0011157)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Focal sensory seizures are a type of partial seizure characterized by sensory symptoms. They are relatively common among epilepsy types but less common than generalized seizures[5]. They are informative for localization of seizure onset in the brain.  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific sensory aura types can be rare and highly informative for diagnosis and surgical planning[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can occur at any age and in both genders, with no strong gender predilection[5].

---

### 5. Acantholysis (HP:0100792)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Acantholysis, loss of keratinocyte cohesion, is a histopathological feature seen in certain blistering skin diseases (e.g., pemphigus). It is relatively rare and highly informative for diagnosing specific dermatological conditions[6].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence is diagnostic for diseases like pemphigus vulgaris, making it very informative[6].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages and genders, though some diseases have age/gender predilections.

---

### 6. Generalized non-motor (absence) seizure (HP:0002121)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Absence seizures are common in childhood epilepsy syndromes and are well-characterized clinically. They are informative for diagnosis of specific epilepsy syndromes[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  While common in children, their persistence or adult onset is less common and more informative[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Most common in children, with no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 7. Pain (HP:0012531)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Pain is a very common symptom and generally non-specific, thus less informative for specific diseases without context[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific types or patterns of pain can be informative but the term itself is broad[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Affects all ages and genders.

---

### 8. Pruritus (HP:0000989)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Itching is common and non-specific, often associated with many dermatologic and systemic diseases[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe or localized pruritus can be more informative diagnostically[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Affects all ages and genders.

---

### 9. Vascular dilatation (HP:0002617)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vascular dilatation (aneurysm) is less common and highly informative for vascular diseases, including aneurysmal disease[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific aneurysm locations or types can be rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  More common in older adults; some aneurysms have gender predilections (e.g., abdominal aortic aneurysm more common in males)[5].

---

### 10. Osteopetrosis (HP:0011002)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Osteopetrosis is a rare genetic bone disorder, highly informative for diagnosis due to its distinctive phenotype[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  The condition itself is rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Typically presents in childhood but can vary; no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 11. Dilatation of the ventricular cavity (HP:0006698)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Ventricular aneurysm is a rare cardiac condition, informative for cardiac pathology diagnosis[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence is highly informative for myocardial infarction complications or cardiomyopathies[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  More common in adults with cardiac disease; no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 12. Arthralgia of the hip (HP:0003365)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Hip joint pain is common and non-specific, less informative without additional context[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific causes (e.g., juvenile arthritis) may be informative[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages; some conditions have gender predilections.

---

### 13. Decreased circulating vitamin C concentration (HP:0100510)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vitamin C deficiency is uncommon in developed countries but informative when present, indicating nutritional deficiency or malabsorption[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe deficiency (scurvy) is rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages and genders, more common in malnourished populations[5].

---

### 14. Hematemesis (HP:0002248)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vomiting blood is less common and highly informative for gastrointestinal bleeding or severe pathology[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence usually indicates serious disease and is diagnostically important[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can occur at any age or gender but more common in adults with GI disease[5].

  While oligozoospermia itself is common, cases caused by rare genetic syndromes or specific endocrine disorders (e.g., adrenal steroidogenesis abnormalities) are more informative for diagnosis[10].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  This condition is male-specific (affects males only) and typically diagnosed in reproductive-age men presenting with infertility[1][4][7][19].

---

### 2. Abnormal sperm head morphology (HP:0012865)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Abnormal sperm head morphology is common among infertile men and is a key parameter in semen analysis. However, mild abnormalities are frequent even in fertile men, making it less specific alone[2][14][20][27].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific morphological abnormalities like macrocephaly, microcephaly, globozoospermia, or multiple heads are rarer and more informative, often linked to genetic mutations or severe testicular damage[2][5][11][17][23].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Male-specific, typically identified in adult men undergoing fertility evaluation[2][14].

---

### 3. Abnormal sperm motility (HP:0012206)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Low sperm motility (asthenozoospermia) is a common cause of male infertility, affecting up to 2% of men and contributing to about 40-50% of infertility cases. It is less specific as it can be caused by many factors including genetics, infections, lifestyle, and varicocele[3][6][8][9][18][21].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe motility defects due to genetic causes or structural flagellar abnormalities are rarer and more informative diagnostically[15].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Male-specific, mostly diagnosed in reproductive-age men[3][6].

---

### 4. Focal sensory seizure (HP:0011157)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Focal sensory seizures are a type of partial seizure characterized by sensory symptoms. They are relatively common among epilepsy types but less common than generalized seizures[5]. They are informative for localization of seizure onset in the brain.  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific sensory aura types can be rare and highly informative for diagnosis and surgical planning[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can occur at any age and in both genders, with no strong gender predilection[5].

---

### 5. Acantholysis (HP:0100792)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Acantholysis, loss of keratinocyte cohesion, is a histopathological feature seen in certain blistering skin diseases (e.g., pemphigus). It is relatively rare and highly informative for diagnosing specific dermatological conditions[6].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence is diagnostic for diseases like pemphigus vulgaris, making it very informative[6].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages and genders, though some diseases have age/gender predilections.

---

### 6. Generalized non-motor (absence) seizure (HP:0002121)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Absence seizures are common in childhood epilepsy syndromes and are well-characterized clinically. They are informative for diagnosis of specific epilepsy syndromes[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  While common in children, their persistence or adult onset is less common and more informative[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Most common in children, with no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 7. Pain (HP:0012531)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Pain is a very common symptom and generally non-specific, thus less informative for specific diseases without context[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific types or patterns of pain can be informative but the term itself is broad[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Affects all ages and genders.

---

### 8. Pruritus (HP:0000989)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Itching is common and non-specific, often associated with many dermatologic and systemic diseases[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe or localized pruritus can be more informative diagnostically[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Affects all ages and genders.

---

### 9. Vascular dilatation (HP:0002617)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vascular dilatation (aneurysm) is less common and highly informative for vascular diseases, including aneurysmal disease[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific aneurysm locations or types can be rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  More common in older adults; some aneurysms have gender predilections (e.g., abdominal aortic aneurysm more common in males)[5].

---

### 10. Osteopetrosis (HP:0011002)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Osteopetrosis is a rare genetic bone disorder, highly informative for diagnosis due to its distinctive phenotype[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  The condition itself is rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Typically presents in childhood but can vary; no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 11. Dilatation of the ventricular cavity (HP:0006698)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Ventricular aneurysm is a rare cardiac condition, informative for cardiac pathology diagnosis[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence is highly informative for myocardial infarction complications or cardiomyopathies[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  More common in adults with cardiac disease; no strong gender bias[5].

---

### 12. Arthralgia of the hip (HP:0003365)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Hip joint pain is common and non-specific, less informative without additional context[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Specific causes (e.g., juvenile arthritis) may be informative[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages; some conditions have gender predilections.

---

### 13. Decreased circulating vitamin C concentration (HP:0100510)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vitamin C deficiency is uncommon in developed countries but informative when present, indicating nutritional deficiency or malabsorption[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Severe deficiency (scurvy) is rare and diagnostic[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can affect all ages and genders, more common in malnourished populations[5].

---

### 14. Hematemesis (HP:0002248)  
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Vomiting blood is less common and highly informative for gastrointestinal bleeding or severe pathology[5].  
- **Rare and informative aspects:**  
  Its presence usually indicates serious disease and is diagnostically important[5].  
- **Gender/Age specificity:**  
  Can occur at any age or gender but more common in adults with GI disease[5].

Here is a detailed analysis of the given HPO terms regarding their prevalence, informativeness for specific diseases, and any gender or age predilections, based on the search results and known clinical knowledge:

---

### 1. Progressive spastic paraplegia (HP:0007020) and Progressive spasticity (HP:0002191)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Progressive spastic paraplegia and progressive spasticity are hallmark features of **Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia (HSP)**, a group of rare inherited neurological disorders characterized by progressive stiffness and weakness of the legs[1][2][3][4]. While spasticity is a relatively common neurological sign, its progressive form combined with paraplegia is more specific and informative for diagnosing HSP and related genetic disorders.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  The presence of progressive spastic paraplegia with additional neurological symptoms (complicated HSP) such as intellectual disability, peripheral neuropathy, or retinal abnormalities is rarer and more informative for specific subtypes of HSP or syndromes like Troyer syndrome[3][5].  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  HSP affects both sexes equally and can present at any age, from infancy to old age, depending on the genetic subtype[2][4]. Early childhood onset is seen in some complex forms like Troyer syndrome[5].

---

### 2. Microcephaly (HP:0000252)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Microcephaly, defined as head circumference below 2 SD of the mean, is a relatively common clinical finding in various genetic, infectious, and developmental disorders. It is **less informative alone** because it occurs in many conditions but is **informative when combined with other features** to narrow down diagnoses[HPO definition].  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Severe or syndromic microcephaly with additional neurological or systemic features is more specific and informative for particular genetic syndromes.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Microcephaly is typically identified in infancy or early childhood. It is not gender-specific.

---

### 3. Moderately short stature (HP:0008848)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Short stature is a common clinical feature seen in many genetic and non-genetic conditions and is generally **less informative alone** for specific diseases.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  When combined with other features like intellectual disability or spasticity, it may indicate syndromic conditions such as Troyer syndrome[5].  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Usually identified in childhood or adolescence during growth assessment; no specific gender predilection.

---

### 4. Intellectual disability, mild (HP:0001256)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Mild intellectual disability is relatively common in various neurodevelopmental disorders and genetic syndromes; alone, it is **less specific** but important when combined with other neurological signs.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Intellectual disability with progressive spasticity or neuropathy is informative for complex HSP types or syndromes like Troyer syndrome[5].  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Diagnosed in childhood; no strong gender bias.

---

### 5. Nasal dysarthria (HP:0008376)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Nasal dysarthria (breathy speech) is a less common and more specific symptom, often indicating neurological or muscular involvement affecting speech. It is **informative** in the context of neurological syndromes with bulbar involvement.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  More informative when present with other neurological deficits in complex HSP or related disorders.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Can occur at any age depending on disease onset; no gender predilection.

---

### 6. Ankle clonus (HP:0011448)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Ankle clonus is a classic sign of upper motor neuron dysfunction and spasticity, **common in spastic paraplegia** and other neurological disorders[2]. It is **informative** for confirming upper motor neuron involvement.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Not rare in spastic paraplegia but informative in neurological examination.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Occurs in affected individuals regardless of gender or age.

---

### 7. Bifid uvula (HP:0000193)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Bifid uvula is a relatively uncommon anatomical variant and can be a minor feature in syndromes involving cleft palate or connective tissue disorders. It is **informative** in syndromic diagnoses involving craniofacial anomalies.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Rare and more informative when combined with other craniofacial or developmental anomalies.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Present from birth; no gender bias.

---

### 8. Retinal pigment epithelial mottling (HP:0007814) and Central retinal vessel vascular tortuosity (HP:0007768)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  These retinal findings are **rare and informative** signs of retinal or systemic diseases affecting the eye, including some complex HSP forms with optic involvement[3].  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Highly informative for syndromes with retinal involvement or systemic vascular/connective tissue disorders.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Can be detected at any age depending on disease progression; no gender bias.

---

### 9. Demyelinating motor neuropathy (HP:0007220)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Demyelinating motor neuropathy is a **rare and informative** neurological sign indicating peripheral nerve involvement, seen in complex HSP or other neuropathies[3].  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Informative for distinguishing complex HSP from pure forms.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Can present at any age; no gender specificity.

---

### 10. Motor delay (HP:0001270)
- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Motor delay is common in many neurodevelopmental disorders and is **less specific** alone but important in early diagnosis.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  More informative when combined with progressive spasticity or intellectual disability.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Identified in infancy or early childhood; no gender bias.

- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  This is a specialized ophthalmologic finding, **rare and informative** for retinal or neurodegenerative diseases.

  Highly informative for specific retinal or neurodegenerative syndromes.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Depends on disease onset; no gender bias.

  These are **common and informative** neurological signs in HSP and other upper motor neuron diseases[2].  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  Not rare in the context of spastic paraplegia; very informative diagnostically.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Occurs in affected individuals regardless of gender or age.

  Functional motor deficits are common but **less specific** as they can result from various neurological or musculoskeletal causes.

  Less informative alone; context-dependent.

  No specific predilection.

- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Premature ovarian insufficiency is a **rare and informative** endocrine disorder, often genetic or syndromic in origin.

  Highly informative for syndromes with gonadal dysfunction.

  Occurs in females, typically before age 40.

  Hemoptysis is a **less common but non-specific** symptom related to respiratory or cardiovascular diseases, generally less informative for neurological syndromes.

  Rare in neurological genetic syndromes; informative for pulmonary or vascular conditions.

  No specific predilection.

- **Commonality and informativeness:**  
  Premature graying is relatively common in the general population and **less informative** alone but can be part of syndromic features in some genetic disorders.  
- **Rare and informative:**  
  More informative when combined with other systemic features.  
- **Gender/Age predilection:**  
  Can occur in both genders, usually noticeable in young adults or earlier.

# Analysis of HPO Terms for Disease Specificity

## Overview of Term Categories

Based on the search results and clinical relevance, these HPO terms can be categorized by their diagnostic utility and specificity to particular conditions.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Progressive spastic paraplegia** (HP:0007020), **Progressive spasticity** (HP:0002191), and **Upper motor neuron dysfunction** (HP:0002493) are relatively common findings across multiple neurological conditions[1][3][5]. These terms are particularly prevalent in hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), but they also appear in other neurodegenerative disorders, cerebral palsy, and various spinal cord pathologies[1]. Their broad applicability makes them less specific for distinguishing between particular diseases.

**Seizure** (HP:0001250) is another non-specific term that appears in many neurological conditions. While it can occur in complicated HSP forms, it is also a feature of numerous other genetic and acquired neurological disorders[3].

**Babinski sign** (HP:0003487) and **Delayed gross motor development** (HP:0002194) are also relatively common findings in upper motor neuron disorders and developmental neurological conditions, though they provide some clinical utility in identifying central nervous system involvement[5][12].

## Rare and Informative Terms

**Nasal dysarthria** (HP:0008376) is a more specific finding that relates to velopharyngeal dysfunction and can indicate particular patterns of neurological involvement[2][4]. When present alongside spastic paraplegia, it suggests involvement of specific neural pathways affecting speech production[6][10].

**Bifid uvula** (HP:0000193) and **Abnormal hard palate morphology** (HP:0100737) are structural findings that, while not exclusively diagnostic, can indicate specific genetic syndromes or developmental patterns. These are relatively uncommon in the general population and may point toward particular genetic subtypes of HSP or other syndromic conditions[3].

**Retinal pigment epithelial mottling** (HP:0007814) and **Central retinal vessel vascular tortuosity** (HP:0007768) are ophthalmologic findings that appear in specific forms of complicated HSP and other neurodegenerative conditions[3]. Their presence is more informative for narrowing the differential diagnosis.

**Microcephaly** (HP:0000252), **Lactic acidosis** (HP:0003128), and **Respiratory acidosis** (HP:0005972) are relatively rare in typical HSP presentations and would suggest alternative diagnoses or specific metabolic subtypes of neurological disease.

**Blue sclerae** (HP:0000592) and **Cerebral hemorrhage** (HP:0001342) are uncommon findings that would be highly informative if present, as they would suggest specific genetic syndromes or acute complications rather than primary HSP.

## Gender and Age Considerations

Hereditary spastic paraplegia **affects both sexes equally**[5], so most of these HPO terms do not show strong gender predilection. However, the mode of inheritance varies—X-linked forms would show different patterns of male versus female involvement depending on the specific genetic type[1][3].

**Age of onset varies considerably** depending on the specific genetic form of HSP. Some forms present in the first year of life, while others manifest in adulthood or old age[5]. Terms like **Delayed gross motor development** are more relevant for early-onset forms presenting in infancy and childhood, whereas progressive symptoms in adults would emphasize the degenerative nature of the condition[3][7].

**Microcephaly** would be apparent from birth or early infancy if present, making it informative for distinguishing early-onset genetic syndromes. **Seizures** can occur at any age but are more commonly associated with complicated HSP forms that may present earlier in life[3].

The ophthalmologic findings (**retinal pigment epithelial mottling** and **central retinal vessel vascular tortuosity**) would be detectable at any age but may become more apparent with disease progression and longer disease duration.

### 2. **Rare and informative HPO terms for specific diseases**

These terms are less common and more indicative of particular syndromes or rare diseases, thus more informative diagnostically:

### Examples of syndromes illustrating informative terms:

- **Robinow syndrome**: Anteverted nares, short nose, scoliosis, vertebral anomalies, short stature; affects both genders equally; onset in infancy[3].

### 2. **Rare and informative HPO terms for specific diseases**

- **Depressed nasal bridge (HP:0005280)**: Informative in syndromes such as Cornelia de Lange and Williams syndrome[4][5][6][8].

### 3. **Specific gender or age group predispositions**

- **Epicanthus (HP:0000286)**: More common in infants and young children; often diminishes with age; no strong gender bias.

Here is a detailed analysis of the provided Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms based on their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and any gender or age predilections, focusing especially on the extensively documented term "Nystagmus" from the search results and general HPO knowledge:

---

### 1. Common and Less Informative HPO Terms for Specific Diseases

These terms are relatively **common** in clinical practice or broad conditions and thus are **less specific** or less informative for pinpointing a particular disease:

- **Nystagmus (HP:0000639):**  
  Nystagmus is a relatively common symptom seen in various neurological, ophthalmological, and vestibular disorders. It occurs in congenital forms (infantile nystagmus syndrome) and acquired forms due to many causes such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, inner ear disorders, drug toxicity, or brain injury[1][3][4][5][6]. Because it appears in many conditions, it is less specific for a particular disease.

- **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263):**  
  This is a broad term describing delayed achievement of developmental milestones in children under five years. It is common in many genetic, metabolic, and environmental conditions, making it less informative for a specific diagnosis.

- **Failure to thrive (HP:0001508):**  
  Failure to thrive is a common pediatric symptom reflecting poor growth and can result from numerous underlying causes, including nutritional, metabolic, or chronic diseases.

- **Skin rash (HP:0000988):**  
  A red eruption on the skin is a very common symptom with many possible causes, from infections to allergies, making it nonspecific.

- **Proteinuria (HP:0000093):**  
  Increased protein in urine is common in many kidney diseases and systemic conditions, thus less specific.

- **Hyperactivity (HP:0000752):**  
  Hyperactivity is a behavioral symptom seen in various neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders, common but nonspecific.

- **Hyperkinetic movements (HP:0002487):**  
  Excessive involuntary movements are common in many neurological disorders, including chorea, dystonia, and others, thus less specific.

- **Abnormal circulating carnitine concentration (HP:0010967) and Decreased circulating carnitine concentration (HP:0003234):**  
  These metabolic abnormalities can occur in various metabolic disorders but are relatively nonspecific alone.

- **Abnormal circulating lysine concentration (HP:0010908):**  
  Metabolic abnormalities in amino acids are common in metabolic disorders but not highly specific without additional context.

---

### 2. Rare and Informative HPO Terms for Specific Diseases

These terms are **less common** and more **informative or specific** for certain diseases or conditions:

- **Choreoathetosis (HP:0001266):**  
  Involuntary movements combining chorea and athetosis are relatively rare and often point to specific neurological or genetic disorders such as certain neurodegenerative diseases or metabolic disorders.

- **Cerebellar atrophy (HP:0001272):**  
  Cerebellar atrophy is a specific neuroimaging finding indicating irreversible tissue loss, often seen in progressive neurodegenerative diseases, intoxications, or infections. It is a more informative sign for specific diagnoses.

- **Pancreatitis (HP:0001733):**  
  Inflammation of the pancreas is relatively specific and can be linked to genetic, metabolic, or autoimmune conditions.

- **Renal tubular acidosis (HP:0001947):**  
  This metabolic kidney disorder is relatively rare and informative for specific inherited or acquired renal tubular dysfunctions.

- **Organic aciduria (HP:0001992):**  
  The excretion of non-amino organic acids in urine is a hallmark of rare inherited metabolic disorders.

- **Progressive encephalopathy (HP:0002448):**  
  Progressive brain disease is a serious and relatively rare condition, informative for neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders.

- **Stress/infection-induced lactic acidosis (HP:0004897):**  
  This is a rare metabolic crisis often seen in mitochondrial or metabolic disorders triggered by stress or infection.

- **Abnormal basal ganglia morphology (HP:0002134):**  
  Structural abnormalities of the basal ganglia are relatively rare and informative for specific neurodevelopmental or neurodegenerative diseases.

- **Abnormal external genitalia morphology (HP:0000811):**  
  Structural anomalies of external genitalia are relatively rare and often informative for specific genetic syndromes or endocrine disorders.

- **Abnormal posturing (HP:0002533):**  
  Involuntary flexion or extension postures are relatively rare and can indicate specific neurological or metabolic conditions.

- **Vasculitis in the skin (HP:0200029):**  
  Cutaneous vasculitis is a rare inflammatory condition, informative for autoimmune or systemic vasculitis diseases.

- **Cubitus valgus (HP:0002967):**  
  Abnormal elbow positioning is rare and can be a clue to specific skeletal dysplasias or syndromes.

- **Vaginitis (HP:0030683):**  
  Inflammation of the vagina is relatively uncommon in systemic genetic diseases but can be informative in specific infectious or inflammatory conditions.

- **Ankyloglossia (HP:0010296):**  
  Tongue-tie is a rare congenital anomaly that can be informative in syndromic contexts.

---

### 3. Gender or Age Group Predilections

- **Nystagmus (HP:0000639):**  
  - *Age:* Infantile (congenital) nystagmus typically presents in infancy (6 weeks to 3 months) and is usually stable throughout life[3][6]. Acquired nystagmus can develop at any age but is more common in adults due to neurological or vestibular causes[1][3][6].  
  - *Gender:* No strong gender predilection reported.

- **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263):**  
  - *Age:* By definition, applies to children under 5 years old.  
  - *Gender:* Slight male predominance reported in some studies but generally affects both genders.

- **Failure to thrive (HP:0001508):**  
  - *Age:* Primarily infants and young children.  
  - *Gender:* No specific gender predilection.

- **Hyperactivity (HP:0000752):**  
  - *Age:* Typically diagnosed in childhood.  
  - *Gender:* More commonly diagnosed in males.

- **Spasmus nutans (a subtype of nystagmus mentioned in sources):**  
  - *Age:* Occurs between 6 months and 3 years, usually resolves by 8 years[5][6].

- **Other terms (e.g., pancreatitis, renal tubular acidosis, organic aciduria, progressive encephalopathy):**  
  - Often present in pediatric populations when genetic/metabolic in origin but can also occur in adults depending on etiology.  
  - Gender predilections are generally not prominent unless linked to sex chromosome-related syndromes.

- **Ankyloglossia (HP:0010296):**  
  - *Age:* Present at birth (congenital).  
  - *Gender:* Slight male predominance reported.

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Visual Impairment (HP:0000505)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Visual impairment is a **broad, non-specific term** that represents a symptom rather than a diagnosis[1][3][4]. It encompasses numerous underlying conditions including age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, retinitis pigmentosa, and cataracts[1]. Because it describes the end result of many different diseases, it is **less informative for identifying a specific disease** and requires additional clinical investigation to determine the underlying cause.

**Rarity:**

Visual impairment is **common**, not rare. It affects millions of people worldwide across various age groups and conditions.

**Demographics:**

Visual impairment shows strong **age-related prevalence**, with age-related macular degeneration being the leading cause of vision loss in older Americans, affecting an estimated 6% of people aged 40 and older[3]. However, visual impairment can occur at any age due to congenital conditions, injuries, or genetic diseases like retinitis pigmentosa[1].

---

## Intellectual Disability (HP:0001249)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Intellectual disability is a **non-specific, common finding** that appears in numerous genetic and developmental disorders. It is defined by an IQ score below 70 and represents a functional outcome rather than a specific disease etiology. This makes it **less informative for disease identification** without additional clinical context.

**Rarity:**

Intellectual disability is **relatively common** in the general population and appears as a feature in hundreds of different genetic syndromes and conditions.

**Demographics:**

Intellectual disability is present **from childhood or early developmental periods** by definition, as it is characterized by subnormal intellectual functioning occurring during the developmental period. It affects both males and females, though some genetic causes (such as X-linked intellectual disability) show male predominance.

---

## Ataxia (HP:0001251)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Ataxia is a **moderately specific neurological sign** indicating cerebellar dysfunction or related neurological pathology. While it narrows the differential diagnosis to cerebellar or related neurological disorders, it still appears in multiple conditions including cerebellar ataxias, leukodystrophies, and mitochondrial disorders. It is **more informative than broad symptoms** but still requires additional testing for specific diagnosis.

**Rarity:**

Ataxia itself is **relatively uncommon** in the general population, making it more informative than non-specific symptoms. However, it appears in numerous rare genetic conditions.

**Demographics:**

Ataxia can present at various ages depending on the underlying cause. Inherited cerebellar ataxias typically manifest in childhood or early adulthood, while acquired ataxias can occur at any age following brain injury or disease.

---

## Choreoathetosis (HP:0001266)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Choreoathetosis is a **relatively specific neurological sign** characterized by involuntary movements combining athetosis and chorea. This finding is **more informative** as it points toward specific movement disorders and neurological conditions affecting motor control, such as certain mitochondrial disorders or leukodystrophies.

**Rarity:**

Choreoathetosis is **rare** in the general population, making it a **more informative finding** for disease identification. Its presence should prompt investigation into specific neurological and metabolic disorders.

**Demographics:**

Choreoathetosis can present across various ages depending on the underlying etiology, though many genetic causes present in childhood or early adulthood.

---

## Abnormality of Mitochondrial Metabolism (HP:0003287)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

This term is **moderately specific**, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction. While it narrows the differential to mitochondrial disorders, many different genetic mutations can cause mitochondrial dysfunction, making it **less informative for identifying a specific disease** without additional metabolic and genetic testing.

**Rarity:**

Mitochondrial disorders are **relatively rare**, making this finding **more informative** than common non-specific symptoms.

**Demographics:**

Mitochondrial disorders can present at any age, though many manifest in childhood. Both males and females are affected, though some mitochondrial conditions show maternal inheritance patterns due to maternal transmission of mitochondrial DNA.

---

## Ichthyosis (HP:0008064)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Ichthyosis is a **moderately specific dermatological finding** indicating abnormal keratinization. While it appears in multiple conditions, its presence is **more informative** than general skin abnormalities and can help narrow the differential diagnosis to specific genetic skin disorders and systemic conditions.

**Rarity:**

Ichthyosis is **relatively uncommon**, making it a **more informative finding** for disease identification.

**Demographics:**

Ichthyosis typically presents from **birth or early childhood** in inherited forms. Both males and females are affected, though some forms show sex-linked inheritance patterns.

---

## Obesity (HP:0001513)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Obesity is a **non-specific, common finding** that results from multiple genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors. It appears in numerous genetic syndromes and metabolic disorders but is also extremely common in the general population. This makes it **less informative for disease identification** without additional clinical context.

**Rarity:**

Obesity is **very common** in modern populations, making it **non-specific and less informative** for identifying rare genetic diseases.

**Demographics:**

Obesity can develop at any age but is increasingly prevalent in childhood and adulthood. Both males and females are affected, though some genetic obesity syndromes may show different prevalence patterns between sexes.

---

## Frontal Balding (HP:0002292)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Frontal balding is a **non-specific finding** that occurs commonly in the general population due to androgenetic alopecia. While it may appear in certain genetic syndromes, it is **less informative for disease identification** without additional clinical features.

**Rarity:**

Frontal balding is **very common**, particularly in males, making it **non-specific and minimally informative** for rare disease diagnosis.

**Demographics:**

Frontal balding predominantly affects **males** and typically begins in **adulthood**, with prevalence increasing with age. It is influenced by genetic predisposition and androgen sensitivity.

---

## Arteriovenous Fistula (HP:0004947)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Arteriovenous fistula is a **relatively specific vascular finding** indicating an abnormal connection between arteries and veins. This is **more informative** as it narrows the differential to vascular malformations and specific genetic vascular disorders.

**Rarity:**

Arteriovenous fistulas are **relatively rare**, making this finding **more informative** for disease identification.

**Demographics:**

Arteriovenous fistulas can present at any age depending on whether they are congenital or acquired. Congenital forms may be detected in childhood, while acquired forms can develop at any age following trauma or vascular disease.

---

## Cerebral Hemorrhage (HP:0001342)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Cerebral hemorrhage is a **moderately specific finding** indicating bleeding into brain tissue. While it narrows the differential to vascular and coagulation disorders, it can result from multiple etiologies including trauma, hypertension, coagulopathies, and vascular malformations. It is **more informative** than general neurological symptoms but requires additional investigation.

**Rarity:**

Cerebral hemorrhage is **relatively uncommon** in the general population, making it a **more informative finding** for disease identification.

**Demographics:**

Cerebral hemorrhage can occur at any age but shows **increased prevalence with advancing age** due to hypertension and cerebrovascular disease. Both males and females are affected, though some genetic causes may show different prevalence patterns.

---

## Preeclampsia (HP:0100602)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Preeclampsia is a **relatively specific obstetric finding** indicating pregnancy-induced hypertension with proteinuria. While it is **more informative** than general hypertension, it can result from various maternal and placental factors.

**Rarity:**

Preeclampsia is **relatively common** in pregnancy, occurring in approximately 3-5% of pregnancies, making it **less informative** for identifying rare genetic diseases.

**Demographics:**

Preeclampsia is **specific to pregnant women** and typically occurs in the **second and third trimesters**. Risk factors include primigravidity, maternal age extremes, and certain genetic predispositions.

---

## Splenomegaly (HP:0001744)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Splenomegaly is a **non-specific finding** that appears in numerous conditions including infections, hematologic disorders, metabolic diseases, and genetic syndromes. It is **less informative for disease identification** without additional clinical and laboratory findings.

**Rarity:**

Splenomegaly is **relatively common** in various disease states, making it **non-specific and less informative** for rare disease diagnosis.

**Demographics:**

Splenomegaly can occur at any age depending on the underlying cause. Both males and females are affected equally.

---

## Carotid Artery Occlusion (HP:0012474)

**Specificity and Informativeness:**

Carotid artery occlusion is a **relatively specific vascular finding** indicating complete obstruction of a carotid artery. This is **more informative** as it points toward specific vascular diseases, atherosclerosis, or genetic vascular disorders.

**Rarity:**

hpo_input.name: Babinski sign
hpo_input.definition: "Upturning of the big toe (and sometimes fanning of the other toes) in response to stimulation of the sole of the foot. If the Babinski sign is present it can indicate damage to the corticospinal tract." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Action tremor
hpo_input.definition: "A tremor present when the limbs are active, either when outstretched in a certain position or throughout a voluntary movement." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21418198]

hpo_input.name: Peripheral axonal neuropathy
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality characterized by disruption of the normal functioning of peripheral axons." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Motor stereotypy
hpo_input.definition: "Use of the same abnormal action in response to certain triggers or at random. They may be used as a way to regulate one's internal state but must otherwise have no apparent functional purpose." []

hpo_input.name: Abnormal left ventricular function
hpo_input.definition: "Inability of the left ventricle to perform its normal physiologic function. Failure is either due to an inability to contract the left ventricle or the inability to relax completely and fill with blood during diastole." [http://www.heart.org/HEARTORG/Conditions/HeartFailure/AboutHeartFailure/Types-of-Heart-Failure_UCM_306323_Article.jsp#.WmeKyJM-dL4, PMID:10956313]

hpo_input.name: Ectrodactyly

[https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Type II diabetes mellitus

hpo_input.name: Skin ulcer
