# Analysis of HPO Terms: Clinical Significance and Specificity

## Spastic Gait (HP:0002064)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Spastic gait is a relatively common finding across multiple neurological conditions, making it moderately informative but not highly specific for any single disease[1][3]. It appears frequently in cerebral palsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury, reducing its diagnostic specificity[1][3][5].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
This term is not rare and therefore has limited value as a rare disease indicator. However, when combined with other clinical features and demographic data, it can help narrow differential diagnoses.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Spastic gait can occur across all ages and genders. In children, it is commonly associated with cerebral palsy, which is present from birth or early childhood[3]. In adults, it frequently follows stroke or develops with progressive conditions like multiple sclerosis[1][5].

---

## Babinski Sign (HP:0003487)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
The Babinski sign is a relatively common neurological finding that indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, making it moderately informative but not disease-specific[2]. It can be present in multiple upper motor neuron syndromes.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
While not rare, the Babinski sign is highly informative because its presence specifically indicates corticospinal tract involvement, which narrows the differential diagnosis to conditions affecting the brain or spinal cord rather than peripheral causes.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
The Babinski sign can occur in any age group or gender, depending on the underlying cause (stroke, trauma, tumor, or degenerative disease).

---

## Action Tremor (HP:0002345)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Action tremor is a common motor symptom with limited specificity, as it appears in multiple neurological and systemic conditions including essential tremor, Parkinson's disease, cerebellar disorders, and metabolic disturbances[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Action tremor is not rare and therefore has low specificity for any particular disease. Its presence requires additional clinical context to establish a diagnosis.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Action tremor can affect individuals of any age and gender, though essential tremor and Parkinson's disease show increased prevalence with advancing age.

---

## Hypotonia (HP:0001252)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Hypotonia is a common finding in pediatric neurology and has moderate informativeness. It appears in numerous conditions affecting the central or peripheral nervous system, as well as in muscle disorders[2]. Its presence is important but requires additional clinical features for specific diagnosis.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Hypotonia is not rare and is relatively non-specific. However, when present in infants and young children, it warrants thorough investigation as it can indicate serious underlying conditions.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Hypotonia is predominantly recognized in infants and young children, where it presents as developmental delay or poor muscle tone. It is less commonly diagnosed in older individuals, though it can occur with acquired neurological or muscular disorders. No significant gender predilection is noted.

---

## Peripheral Axonal Neuropathy (HP:0003477)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Peripheral axonal neuropathy is relatively common, particularly in patients with diabetes, and has moderate informativeness. It indicates disruption of peripheral nerve function but does not specify the underlying cause[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
While not rare, peripheral axonal neuropathy is informative because it localizes the pathology to the peripheral nervous system rather than the central nervous system, helping to differentiate between central and peripheral causes of gait abnormality.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Peripheral axonal neuropathy increases in prevalence with age and is more common in individuals with diabetes or metabolic disorders. It can affect any gender, though diabetic neuropathy shows similar prevalence across genders when adjusted for diabetes prevalence.

---

## Motor Stereotypy (HP:0000733)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Motor stereotypy is relatively common in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions but has limited specificity. It appears in autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and other conditions[2].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Motor stereotypy is not rare and is non-specific for any particular disease. Its presence is more informative when combined with other developmental or behavioral features.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Motor stereotypy is predominantly recognized in children and individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders. It may show increased prevalence in males, particularly in autism spectrum disorder. It can persist into adulthood but is more clinically significant when identified in childhood.

---

## Abnormal Left Ventricular Function (HP:0005162)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Abnormal left ventricular function is relatively common in cardiology practice and has moderate informativeness. It indicates cardiac dysfunction but does not specify the underlying etiology, which can range from ischemic heart disease to cardiomyopathy to valvular disease.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
This finding is not rare and has limited specificity for any single disease. However, it is highly informative for identifying cardiac pathology requiring intervention.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Abnormal left ventricular function increases significantly with age and is more common in males, particularly in younger age groups with ischemic heart disease. In women, it becomes more prevalent after menopause. It can occur at any age with appropriate underlying conditions.

---

## Ectrodactyly (HP:0100257)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Ectrodactyly is a rare congenital malformation, making it highly informative and specific for certain genetic syndromes[2]. Its presence strongly suggests a genetic etiology.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Ectrodactyly is rare and highly informative. When present, it should prompt investigation for specific genetic syndromes such as ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting (EEC) syndrome or other rare genetic conditions.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Ectrodactyly is a congenital condition present from birth and affects both genders equally. It is identified in infancy or early childhood during physical examination.

---

## Type II Diabetes Mellitus (HP:0005978)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Type II diabetes mellitus is very common in the general population and has limited specificity for rare genetic diseases. However, it is highly informative for understanding metabolic complications and associated conditions like peripheral neuropathy[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Type II diabetes is not rare and is non-specific for rare disease diagnosis. Its presence is more useful for understanding disease complications and comorbidities.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Type II diabetes shows increased prevalence with advancing age and is more common in males in younger age groups, though prevalence becomes more equal with age. It can occur at any age but is predominantly diagnosed in adults over 45 years.

---

## Skin Ulcer (HP:0200042)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Skin ulcers are relatively common findings with multiple etiologies including vascular insufficiency, pressure injury, infection, and neuropathy[7]. They have limited specificity for any particular disease.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Skin ulcers are not rare and are non-specific. However, when occurring in the context of spastic gait and sensory loss, they indicate significant neurological impairment requiring preventive care[7].

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Skin ulcers can occur at any age and in any gender. They are more common in elderly individuals with mobility limitations and in patients with chronic neurological conditions affecting sensation.

---

## Epigastric Pain (HP:0410019)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Epigastric pain is very common with multiple gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal etiologies, making it non-specific and of limited value for rare disease diagnosis.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Epigastric pain is not rare and has minimal specificity for any particular disease. Its presence requires extensive differential diagnosis.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Epigastric pain can occur at any age and in any gender. It shows increased prevalence with certain conditions like peptic ulcer disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may vary by age and gender based on risk factor exposure.

The Babinski sign is a relatively common neurological finding that indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, making it moderately informative but not disease-specific[2]. It can be present in multiple upper motor neuron syndromes.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
While not rare, the Babinski sign is highly informative because its presence specifically indicates corticospinal tract involvement, which narrows the differential diagnosis to conditions affecting the brain or spinal cord rather than peripheral causes.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
The Babinski sign can occur in any age group or gender, depending on the underlying cause (stroke, trauma, tumor, or degenerative disease).

---

## Action Tremor (HP:0002345)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Action tremor is a common motor symptom with limited specificity, as it appears in multiple neurological and systemic conditions including essential tremor, Parkinson's disease, cerebellar disorders, and metabolic disturbances[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Action tremor is not rare and therefore has low specificity for any particular disease. Its presence requires additional clinical context to establish a diagnosis.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Action tremor can affect individuals of any age and gender, though essential tremor and Parkinson's disease show increased prevalence with advancing age.

---

## Hypotonia (HP:0001252)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Hypotonia is a common finding in pediatric neurology and has moderate informativeness. It appears in numerous conditions affecting the central or peripheral nervous system, as well as in muscle disorders[2]. Its presence is important but requires additional clinical features for specific diagnosis.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Hypotonia is not rare and is relatively non-specific. However, when present in infants and young children, it warrants thorough investigation as it can indicate serious underlying conditions.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Hypotonia is predominantly recognized in infants and young children, where it presents as developmental delay or poor muscle tone. It is less commonly diagnosed in older individuals, though it can occur with acquired neurological or muscular disorders. No significant gender predilection is noted.

---

## Peripheral Axonal Neuropathy (HP:0003477)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Peripheral axonal neuropathy is relatively common, particularly in patients with diabetes, and has moderate informativeness. It indicates disruption of peripheral nerve function but does not specify the underlying cause[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
While not rare, peripheral axonal neuropathy is informative because it localizes the pathology to the peripheral nervous system rather than the central nervous system, helping to differentiate between central and peripheral causes of gait abnormality.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Peripheral axonal neuropathy increases in prevalence with age and is more common in individuals with diabetes or metabolic disorders. It can affect any gender, though diabetic neuropathy shows similar prevalence across genders when adjusted for diabetes prevalence.

---

## Motor Stereotypy (HP:0000733)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Motor stereotypy is relatively common in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions but has limited specificity. It appears in autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and other conditions[2].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Motor stereotypy is not rare and is non-specific for any particular disease. Its presence is more informative when combined with other developmental or behavioral features.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Motor stereotypy is predominantly recognized in children and individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders. It may show increased prevalence in males, particularly in autism spectrum disorder. It can persist into adulthood but is more clinically significant when identified in childhood.

---

## Abnormal Left Ventricular Function (HP:0005162)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Abnormal left ventricular function is relatively common in cardiology practice and has moderate informativeness. It indicates cardiac dysfunction but does not specify the underlying etiology, which can range from ischemic heart disease to cardiomyopathy to valvular disease.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
This finding is not rare and has limited specificity for any single disease. However, it is highly informative for identifying cardiac pathology requiring intervention.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Abnormal left ventricular function increases significantly with age and is more common in males, particularly in younger age groups with ischemic heart disease. In women, it becomes more prevalent after menopause. It can occur at any age with appropriate underlying conditions.

---

## Ectrodactyly (HP:0100257)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Ectrodactyly is a rare congenital malformation, making it highly informative and specific for certain genetic syndromes[2]. Its presence strongly suggests a genetic etiology.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Ectrodactyly is rare and highly informative. When present, it should prompt investigation for specific genetic syndromes such as ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting (EEC) syndrome or other rare genetic conditions.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Ectrodactyly is a congenital condition present from birth and affects both genders equally. It is identified in infancy or early childhood during physical examination.

---

## Type II Diabetes Mellitus (HP:0005978)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Type II diabetes mellitus is very common in the general population and has limited specificity for rare genetic diseases. However, it is highly informative for understanding metabolic complications and associated conditions like peripheral neuropathy[4].

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Type II diabetes is not rare and is non-specific for rare disease diagnosis. Its presence is more useful for understanding disease complications and comorbidities.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Type II diabetes shows increased prevalence with advancing age and is more common in males in younger age groups, though prevalence becomes more equal with age. It can occur at any age but is predominantly diagnosed in adults over 45 years.

---

## Skin Ulcer (HP:0200042)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Skin ulcers are relatively common findings with multiple etiologies including vascular insufficiency, pressure injury, infection, and neuropathy[7]. They have limited specificity for any particular disease.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Skin ulcers are not rare and are non-specific. However, when occurring in the context of spastic gait and sensory loss, they indicate significant neurological impairment requiring preventive care[7].

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Skin ulcers can occur at any age and in any gender. They are more common in elderly individuals with mobility limitations and in patients with chronic neurological conditions affecting sensation.

---

## Epigastric Pain (HP:0410019)

**Commonality and Informativeness:**
Epigastric pain is very common with multiple gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal etiologies, making it non-specific and of limited value for rare disease diagnosis.

**Rarity and Disease Specificity:**
Epigastric pain is not rare and has minimal specificity for any particular disease. Its presence requires extensive differential diagnosis.

**Gender and Age Considerations:**
Epigastric pain can occur at any age and in any gender. It shows increased prevalence with certain conditions like peptic ulcer disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may vary by age and gender based on risk factor exposure.

Here is a detailed analysis of the provided HPO terms regarding their **commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and any gender or age predilections**, based on the definitions and relevant clinical information:

---

### 1. **HP:0000218 - High palate (High-arched palate)**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  High palate is a relatively common craniofacial feature seen in various genetic syndromes (e.g., Stickler syndrome, Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome) and can be a nonspecific finding. It is considered **less informative alone** because it occurs in many conditions and can also be seen in the general population without disease[1][5][9]. However, when combined with other features such as micrognathia or cleft palate, it becomes more informative.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  No specific gender predilection. It is typically identified in **children or infants** during clinical evaluation of craniofacial anomalies or developmental disorders[1][5].

---

### 2. **HP:0000347 - Micrognathia**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Micrognathia is a **common and clinically significant feature** in many congenital syndromes (e.g., Pierre Robin sequence, Stickler syndrome, Treacher Collins syndrome, Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome)[2][3][4][5][6][9][12][14][15]. It is **highly informative** for diagnosis when present with other craniofacial abnormalities and feeding or breathing difficulties. It can also occur as an isolated or idiopathic finding.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Primarily identified in **newborns and infants** due to feeding and respiratory issues. No strong gender bias reported[2][3][12][14].

---

### 3. **HP:0000368 - obsolete Low-set, posteriorly rotated ears**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  This term is marked obsolete, indicating it is no longer used in current HPO annotations. Low-set, posteriorly rotated ears are **common but nonspecific** dysmorphic features seen in many syndromes, thus less informative alone.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Typically noted in **infants or children** during dysmorphology assessments; no gender predilection.

---

### 4. **HP:0000954 - Single transverse palmar crease (Simian crease)**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  The single transverse palmar crease is **common in certain genetic conditions** such as Down syndrome but can also be seen in the general population. It is **moderately informative** when combined with other signs[5].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present from birth; no gender predilection.

---

### 5. **HP:0001007 - Hirsutism**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Hirsutism (male-pattern hair growth in females) is **common in endocrine disorders** (e.g., polycystic ovary syndrome) but nonspecific for genetic syndromes. It is **informative for hormonal or metabolic disorders** rather than congenital syndromes.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Primarily affects **post-pubertal females**.

---

### 6. **HP:0001162 - Postaxial hand polydactyly**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Postaxial polydactyly is a **relatively common congenital limb anomaly** and can be an isolated finding or part of syndromes. It is **informative when associated with other anomalies**[5].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present at birth; no strong gender bias.

---

### 7. **HP:0001249 - Intellectual disability**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Intellectual disability is a **common but nonspecific clinical feature** seen in many genetic and acquired conditions. It is **less informative alone** but critical when combined with other features.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Diagnosed in **children during developmental assessment**; no gender predilection.

---

### 8. **HP:0001508 - Failure to thrive**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Failure to thrive is a **common clinical sign** in pediatric medicine, nonspecific but **informative as an indicator of underlying systemic or genetic disorders**[3][6][14].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Occurs in **infants and young children**; no gender bias.

---

### 9. **HP:0001838 - Rocker bottom foot**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Rocker bottom foot is a **rare and highly informative congenital foot deformity** associated with specific syndromes (e.g., trisomy 18)[17]. It is **informative for specific diagnoses**.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present at birth; no gender predilection.

---

### 10. **HP:0002071 - Abnormality of extrapyramidal motor function**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  This neurological sign is **relatively rare and highly informative** for disorders affecting basal ganglia (e.g., Parkinsonism, certain metabolic or genetic disorders)[17].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in **adults but can occur in pediatric neurogenetic disorders**; no gender bias.

---

### 11. **HP:0002093 - Respiratory insufficiency**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Respiratory insufficiency is a **common clinical sign** in many acute and chronic conditions; nonspecific but **informative for severity of disease**.
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can occur at any age; no gender bias.

---

### 12. **HP:0002104 - Apnea**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Apnea is **common in neonates with airway obstruction or neurological disorders** and **informative for respiratory control issues**[3][6][14].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Primarily in **infants and neonates**; no gender bias.

---

### 13. **HP:0002352 - Leukoencephalopathy**
- **Commonality and Informativeness:**  
  Leukoencephalopathy is **rare and highly informative** for white matter diseases, including genetic leukodystrophies[17].
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can present in **infants, children, or adults** depending on etiology; no gender bias.

hpo_input.name: Cerebral cortical atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the cortex of the cerebrum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Optic atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the optic nerve. Optic atrophy results from the death of the retinal ganglion cell axons that comprise the optic nerve and manifesting as a pale optic nerve on fundoscopy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Tetraplegia
hpo_input.definition: "Paralysis of all four limbs, and trunk of the body below the level of an associated injury to the spinal cord. [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Respiratory failure
hpo_input.definition: "A severe form of respiratory insufficiency characterized by inadequate gas exchange such that the levels of oxygen or carbon dioxide cannot be maintained within normal limits." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Secondary microcephaly
hpo_input.definition: "Head circumference which falls below 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender because of insufficient head growth after birth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Development of small head that was not present at birth

hpo_input.name: Infantile muscular hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Muscular hypotonia (abnormally low muscle tone) manifesting in infancy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Feeding difficulties
hpo_input.definition: "Impaired ability to eat related to problems gathering food and getting ready to suck, chew, or swallow it." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6647-5493]

hpo_input.name: Polyhydramnios
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of excess amniotic fluid in the uterus during pregnancy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal sternum morphology

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. hpo_input.name: Positive Romberg sign
hpo_input.definition: "The patient stands with the feet placed together and balance and is asked to close his or her eyes. A loss of balance upon eye closure is a positive Romberg sign and is interpreted as indicating a deficit in proprioception." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Nystagmus
hpo_input.definition: "Rhythmic, involuntary oscillations of one or both eyes related to abnormality in fixation, conjugate gaze, or vestibular mechanisms." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dystonia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally increased muscular tone that causes fixed abnormal postures. There is a slow, intermittent twisting motion that leads to exaggerated turning and posture of the extremities and trunk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Recurrent pneumonia
hpo_input.definition: "An increased susceptibility to pneumonia as manifested by a history of recurrent episodes of pneumonia." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15750465]

hpo_input.name: Hypertelorism
hpo_input.definition: "Interpupillary distance more than 2 SD above the mean (alternatively, the appearance of an increased interpupillary distance or widely spaced eyes)." [PMID:19125427]

hpo_input.name: Urinary incontinence
hpo_input.definition: "Loss of the ability to control the urinary bladder leading to involuntary urination." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154, PMID:12559262]

hpo_input.name: Scoliosis
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Cobb angle greater than ten degrees

hpo_input.name: Pectus excavatum
hpo_input.definition: "A defect of the chest wall characterized by a depression of the sternum, giving the chest (\"pectus\") a caved-in (\"excavatum\") appearance." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Senile plaques
hpo_input.definition: "Senile plaques are extracellular deposits of amyloid in the gray matter of the brain." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Hyperactivity
hpo_input.definition: "Hyperactivity is a condition characterized by constant and unusually high levels of activity, even in situations where it is deemed inappropriate." []

hpo_input.name: Hyperkinetic movements
hpo_input.definition: "Motor hyperactivity with excessive movement of muscles of the body as a whole." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dysphagia
hpo_input.definition: "Difficulty in swallowing." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Rhabdomyolysis
hpo_input.definition: "Breakdown of muscle fibers that leads to the release of muscle fiber contents (myoglobin) into the bloodstream." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: EMG abnormality
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormal results of investigations using electromyography (EMG)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15961866, PMID:18751841]

hpo_input.name: Type IV atherosclerotic lesion
hpo_input.definition: "In type IV atherosclerotic lesions a dense accumulation of extracellular lipid occupies an extensive but well-defined region of the intima. This type of extracellular lipid accumulation is known as the lipid core. A fibrous tissue increase is not a feature, and complications such as defects of the lesion surface and thrombosis are not present. The type IV lesion is also known as atheroma. Type IV is the first lesion considered advanced in this classification because of the severe intimal disorganization caused by the lipid core. The characteristic core appears to develop from an increase and the consequent confluence of the small isolated pools of extracellular lipid that characterize type III lesions. The increase in lipid is believed to result from continued insudation from the plasma. Type IV lesions, when they first appear in younger people, are found in the same locations as adaptive intimal thickenings of the eccentric type. Thus, atheroma is, at least initially, an eccentric lesion." [PMID:7648691]

### 1. Which HPO terms are more common and less informative for a specific disease?

**More common and less specific (less informative) HPO terms** tend to be those that occur in many diseases or conditions and do not strongly point to a unique diagnosis:

- **Spasticity (HP:0001257):** Common in many neurological disorders involving upper motor neuron lesions; not specific to one disease.
- **Muscle weakness (HP:0001324):** Very common symptom across a wide range of neuromuscular and systemic diseases.
- **Feeding difficulties (HP:0011968):** Common in many pediatric and neurological conditions.
- **Respiratory failure (HP:0002878):** A common severe complication in many diseases.
- **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263):** Frequent in many genetic, metabolic, and neurological disorders in children under five.
- **Nystagmus (HP:0000639):** Occurs in various neurological and vestibular disorders.
- **Dystonia (HP:0001332):** Present in multiple movement disorders.
- **Urinary incontinence (HP:0000020):** Common in neurological and urological conditions.
- **Scoliosis (HP:0002650):** Common orthopedic finding in many syndromes and neuromuscular diseases.
- **Hyperactivity (HP:0000752) and Hyperkinetic movements (HP:0002487):** Seen in many neurodevelopmental disorders.
- **Dysphagia (HP:0002015):** Common in neurological and muscular diseases.
- **EMG abnormality (HP:0003457):** A diagnostic finding in many neuromuscular disorders, not disease-specific.
- **Recurrent pneumonia (HP:0006532):** Common in conditions with impaired airway clearance or immune deficiency.
- **Infantile muscular hypotonia (HP:0008947):** Common in various congenital and acquired neuromuscular disorders.
- **Polyhydramnios (HP:0001561):** A prenatal finding that can be associated with many fetal anomalies or maternal conditions.
- **Abnormal sternum morphology (HP:0000766), Pectus excavatum (HP:0000767):** Common skeletal abnormalities in various syndromes.
- **Tetraplegia (HP:0002445):** Occurs in spinal cord injuries or severe neurological diseases but is a broad clinical sign.
- **Secondary microcephaly (HP:0005484):** Occurs in many acquired brain injuries or developmental disorders.
- **Rhabdomyolysis (HP:0003201):** Can occur in various muscle diseases or systemic conditions.

hpo_input.name: Visual impairment
hpo_input.definition: "Visual impairment (or vision impairment) is vision loss (of a person) to such a degree as to qualify as an additional support need through a significant limitation of visual capability resulting from either disease, trauma, or congenital or degenerative conditions that cannot be corrected by conventional means, such as refractive correction, medication, or surgery." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8727-6592]

hpo_input.name: Intellectual disability
hpo_input.definition: "Intellectual disability, previously referred to as mental retardation, is characterized by subnormal intellectual functioning that occurs during the developmental period. It is defined by an IQ score below 70." []

hpo_input.name: 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria
hpo_input.definition: "An increased amount of 3-methylglutaconic acid in the urine." []

hpo_input.name: Chorea
hpo_input.definition: "Chorea (Greek for 'dance') refers to widespread arrhythmic involuntary movements of a forcible, jerky and restless fashion. It is a random-appearing sequence of one or more discrete involuntary movements or movement fragments. Movements appear random because of variability in timing, duration or location. Each movement may have a distinct start and end. However, movements may be strung together and thus may appear to flow randomly from one muscle group to another. Chorea can involve the trunk, neck, face, tongue, and extremities." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:20589866]

hpo_input.name: Ataxia
hpo_input.definition: "Cerebellar ataxia refers to ataxia due to dysfunction of the cerebellum. This causes a variety of elementary neurological deficits including asynergy (lack of coordination between muscles, limbs and joints), dysmetria (lack of ability to judge distances that can lead to under- or overshoot in grasping movements), and dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid movements requiring antagonizing muscle groups to be switched on and off repeatedly)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Ambiguous genitalia
hpo_input.definition: "A genital phenotype that is not clearly assignable to a single gender. Ambiguous genitalia can be evaluated using the Prader scale: Prader 0: Normal female external genitalia. Prader 1: Female external genitalia with clitoromegaly. Prader 2: Clitoromegaly with partial labial fusion forming a funnel-shaped urogenital sinus. Prader 3: Increased phallic enlargement. Complete labioscrotal fusion forming a urogenital sinus with a single opening. Prader 4: Complete scrotal fusion with urogenital opening at the base or on the shaft of the phallus. Prader 5: Normal male external genitalia. The diagnosis of ambiguous genitalia is made for Prader 1-4." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15102623]

hpo_input.name: Gait disturbance
hpo_input.definition: "The term gait disturbance can refer to any disruption of the ability to walk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:27770207]

hpo_input.name: Hepatic necrosis
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of cell death (necrosis) affecting the liver." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Delirium
hpo_input.definition: "A state of sudden and severe confusion." []

hpo_input.name: Anterior open-bite malocclusion
hpo_input.definition: "Anterior open bite is a malocclusion characterized by a gap between the anterior teeth (incisors), that is, by a deficiency in the normal vertical overlap between antagonist incisal edges when the posterior teeth are in occlusion." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9338-3017, PMID:27615261]
synonym: Absence of overlap of anterior upper and lower teeth
Anterior open bite between upper and lower teeth
Gap between upper and lower front teeth when biting

hpo_input.name: Barrett esophagus
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormal change (metaplasia) in the cells of the inferior portion of the esophagus. The normal squamous epithelium lining of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium. Columnar epithelium refers to a cell type that is typically found in more distal parts of the gastrointestinal system." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Petechiae
hpo_input.definition: "Petechiae are pinpoint-sized reddish/purple spots, resembling a rash, that appear just under the skin or a mucous membrane when capillaries have ruptured and some superficial bleeding into the skin has happened. This term refers to an abnormally increased susceptibility to developing petechiae." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:29493956]

hpo_input.name: Ingrown nail
hpo_input.definition: "Excessive growth of a nail laterally into the nail fold." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Bronchitis
hpo_input.definition: "Inflammation of the large airways in the lung including any part of the bronchi from the primary bronchi to the tertiary bronchi." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

  - Other terms generally show no strong gender predilection.

hpo_input.name: Cataract
hpo_input.definition: "A cataract is an opacity or clouding that develops in the crystalline lens of the eye or in its capsule." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Clouding of the lens of the eye

hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the dental enamel." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Brachydactyly
hpo_input.definition: "Digits that appear disproportionately short compared to the hand/foot. The word brachydactyly is used here to describe a series distinct patterns of shortened digits (brachydactyly types A-E). This is the sense used here." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21418198]

hpo_input.name: Global developmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "A delay in the achievement of motor or mental milestones in the domains of development of a child, including motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social and emotional skills. This term should only be used to describe children younger than five years of age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6410-0882, https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Scoliosis
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Cobb angle greater than ten degrees

hpo_input.name: Midline defect of the nose
hpo_input.definition: "This term groups together three conditions that presumably represent different degrees of severity of a midline defect of the nose or nasal tip." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Short stature
hpo_input.definition: "A height below that which is expected according to age and gender norms. Although there is no universally accepted definition of short stature, many refer to \"short stature\" as height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender (or below the 3rd percentile for age and gender dependent norms)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Depressed nasal bridge
hpo_input.definition: "Posterior positioning of the nasal root in relation to the overall facial profile for age." [PMID:19152422]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal epiphysis morphology
hpo_input.definition: "An anomaly of epiphysis, which is the expanded articular end of a long bone that developes from a secondary ossification center, and which during the period of growth is either entirely cartilaginous or is separated from the shaft by a cartilaginous disk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Abnormal shape of end part of bone

hpo_input.name: Abnormal dental morphology
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the morphology of the tooth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9338-3017]

hpo_input.name: Crumpled ear
hpo_input.definition: "Distortion of the course of the normal folds of the ear and the appearance of supernumerary crura and folds." [PMID:19152421]

hpo_input.name: Abnormally folded helix
hpo_input.definition: "Any structural anomaly of the border of the helix, which usually forms a rolled rim but is highly variable in shape." [PMID:19152421]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal morphology of the nasal alae
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the Ala of nose." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19152422]

synonym: Hole in heart wall separating two lower heart chambers

hpo_input.definition: "Rhythmic, involuntary oscillations of one or both eyes related to abnormality in fixation, conjugate gaze, or vestibular mechanisms." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.definition: "A misalignment of the eyes so that the visual axes deviate from bifoveal fixation. [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0986-4123, PMID:26319345]

hpo_input.definition: "Atypical behavior is an abnormality in a person's actions that can be controlled or modulated by the will of the individual. hpo_input.definition: "Inflammation of the urinary bladder." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity and Clinical Significance

## Overview of the HPO Terms

Based on the search results, I can provide analysis on several of these HPO terms, though not all have sufficient information in the provided sources. Here's what can be determined:

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**HP:0000286 - Epicanthus** is a relatively common finding that appears in multiple conditions. While it is a characteristic feature of blepharophimosis, ptosis, and epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES), epicanthus can occur alone or in association with various other conditions and ancestry patterns[1][3][9][17]. This makes it less specific for diagnosing a particular disease on its own.

**HP:0000486 - Strabismus** (crossed eyes) is noted as a frequent but non-specific finding. It appears as a minor feature in BPES but is also common in many other developmental and neurological conditions[1][5]. Similarly, **HP:0000639 - Nystagmus** represents involuntary eye movements that can result from multiple etiologies, making it a less informative standalone finding.

**HP:0004322 - Short stature** and **HP:0001263 - Global developmental delay** are broad developmental findings that occur across numerous genetic and non-genetic conditions, limiting their diagnostic specificity.

## Rare and Highly Informative Terms

**HP:0000286 - Epicanthus** combined with **HP:0000518 - Cataract** and other specific ocular findings becomes highly informative when appearing together. However, the most informative combination is:

**The tetrad of blepharophimosis features** (narrow eye openings, ptosis, epicanthus inversus, and telecanthus) is highly specific for BPES when all four are present together[1][5][11]. This combination is rare and strongly suggests mutations in the **FOXL2** gene[1][3][5].

**HP:0000682 - Abnormal dental enamel morphology** and **HP:0006482 - Abnormal dental morphology** are informative when they appear as part of specific syndromes. These terms become highly specific when associated with particular genetic conditions like amelogenesis imperfecta or other hereditary enamel defects[2][4][6][8][10].

**HP:0005280 - Depressed nasal bridge** is noted as a characteristic minor feature of BPES[1][5][7], and when combined with the major eyelid features, it adds diagnostic value.

## Gender and Age-Specific Patterns

**Gender-specific manifestations:**

**HP:0000286 - Epicanthus** in the context of BPES shows important gender differences. BPES Type I, which includes premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), affects only females[1][5][7]. Women with BPES Type I experience menopausal symptoms as early as 15 years old and develop infertility or subfertility before age 40[1][5][7][11].

**HP:0000682 - Abnormal dental enamel morphology** demonstrates marked gender differences in certain conditions. In X-linked amelogenesis imperfecta, males are affected more severely with generalized hypoplasia and hypomineralization, while carrier females typically present with vertical markings or striations on the enamel due to X chromosome inactivation[4].

**Age-specific manifestations:**

**HP:0001263 - Global developmental delay** is specifically defined for children younger than five years of age[1]. In BPES, infants and toddlers may experience delayed gross motor development due to the characteristic "chin-up" position (ocular torticollis) they adopt to see under their eyelids, which places stress on the neck and back[3].

**HP:0000518 - Cataract** and vision problems in BPES typically begin in childhood, with affected individuals at increased risk for refractive errors like myopia or hyperopia[5]. Severe ptosis in babies and young children can develop amblyopia (lazy eye) because the eyelids block their line of sight[11].

The eyelid malformations characteristic of BPES are **present at birth**[1][5], making them congenital findings that are immediately observable, whereas the ovarian insufficiency in BPES Type I manifests later during adolescence and early adulthood.

Here is an analysis of the given HPO terms based on their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and demographic associations, supported by the search results:

---

### 1. Azoospermia (HP:0000027) and Non-obstructive azoospermia (HP:0011961)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - *Azoospermia* is a relatively common clinical finding in male infertility, representing absence of sperm in semen. It is a broad term that can be caused by many conditions, making it somewhat less specific for a particular disease but highly relevant in reproductive medicine[1][2][3][4].
  - *Non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA)* is a subtype caused by impaired sperm production (testicular failure), which is more specific and informative for underlying testicular or hormonal pathologies such as genetic abnormalities (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome), chemotherapy effects, or pituitary dysfunction[1][2][3][5][6].
  - NOA is more informative for diagnosing specific causes of male infertility than azoospermia alone.

- **Demographics:**
  - These conditions affect *males*, typically in reproductive age groups (young to middle-aged adults). NOA is often related to genetic or acquired testicular dysfunction, which can manifest at puberty or later[1][2][3][5].
  - Some causes like chemotherapy-induced azoospermia can affect males of any age undergoing treatment[3][5].

---

### 2. Increased circulating gonadotropin level (HP:0000837)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Elevated gonadotropins (FSH, LH) are a common endocrine finding in various conditions involving gonadal failure or pituitary feedback dysregulation. It is a *less specific* but important biomarker indicating primary gonadal failure or pituitary overactivity[1][3][5].
  - It is informative in distinguishing types of azoospermia (e.g., high FSH in NOA due to testicular failure) and other endocrine disorders.

- **Demographics:**
  - Primarily observed in *males* with testicular dysfunction or *both genders* in various endocrine disorders.
  - Can occur at any age but often noted in adults with reproductive or pituitary disorders[1][3].

---

### 3. Abnormal spermatogenesis (HP:0008669)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Abnormal spermatogenesis is a *rare and highly informative* term indicating defective sperm development, often underlying NOA or other testicular pathologies[1][2][3][6].
  - It is a specific pathological process rather than a common symptom, useful for diagnosis and treatment planning.

- **Demographics:**
  - Affects *males* in reproductive age.
  - May be congenital (genetic syndromes) or acquired (toxins, infections)[2][3][6].

---

### 4. Decreased testicular size (HP:0008734)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Small or hypoplastic testes are a *relatively uncommon but informative* sign indicating testicular atrophy or developmental defects, often associated with infertility, Klinefelter syndrome, or hormonal deficiencies[1][2][3].
  - It is a useful clinical sign to differentiate causes of azoospermia and testicular failure.

- **Demographics:**
  - Found in *males*, often in adolescence or adulthood when testicular development or function is impaired[1][2].

---

### 5. Pain (HP:0012531)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Pain is a *very common and non-specific* symptom associated with numerous conditions, making it less informative for specific diseases without context[7].
  - It can accompany infections, tumors, or trauma but is not diagnostic on its own.

- **Demographics:**
  - Occurs in *all genders and ages* depending on the underlying cause.

---

### 6. Brain neoplasm (HP:0030692)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Brain tumors are *rare but highly informative* for neurological diseases and cancers.
  - The term encompasses benign and malignant tumors, critical for diagnosis and treatment.

- **Demographics:**
  - Can occur at any age but some types have age predilections (e.g., gliomas more common in adults, medulloblastomas in children).

---

### 7. Stroke (HP:0001297)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Stroke is a *common and highly informative* clinical event indicating acute cerebrovascular disease.
  - It is a key diagnostic term for neurological emergencies.

- **Demographics:**
  - More common in *older adults* but can occur at any age depending on risk factors.

---

### 8. Neurofibrillary tangles (HP:0002185)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Neurofibrillary tangles are *rare and highly specific* pathological features of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.
  - They are informative biomarkers for diagnosis and research.

- **Demographics:**
  - Typically found in *older adults* with dementia.

---

### 9. Lewy bodies (HP:0100315)

- **Commonality and Informativeness:**
  - Lewy bodies are *rare and highly informative* pathological inclusions in diseases like Parkinson’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
  - They are diagnostic for specific neurodegenerative disorders.

- **Demographics:**
  - Primarily affect *older adults*.

---

# Analysis of HPO Terms in Relation to Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia

Based on the search results provided, I can analyze these HPO terms in the context of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), which is the primary condition described in the medical literature.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Progressive spastic paraplegia (HP:0007020)** is the **hallmark and defining feature** of HSP itself[1][2][3]. While this term is highly relevant to HSP diagnosis, it is not specific to HSP alone, as spastic paraplegia can result from multiple neurological conditions. This makes it common but less informative for differential diagnosis.

**Muscle spasm (HP:0003394)** is a general symptom that can occur in many neurological and muscular conditions. While spasticity and muscle tightness are central to HSP[3], muscle spasms as a standalone finding lack specificity for HSP.

**Cough (HP:0012735)** is a non-specific symptom that appears in countless medical conditions and is not mentioned in the HSP literature provided. This term is neither common nor particularly informative for HSP diagnosis.

## Rare and Informative Terms

**EMG: neuropathic changes (HP:0003445)** represents a more specific diagnostic finding. Electromyography can reveal denervation patterns characteristic of the nerve degeneration seen in HSP, making this a more informative diagnostic marker.

**Decreased activity of mitochondrial respiratory chain (HP:0008972)** is particularly informative for specific genetic subtypes of HSP. Research indicates that alterations in fatty-acid-metabolizing enzymes affect mitochondrial form and function in hereditary spastic paraplegia[5], making this finding relevant to certain complicated forms of HSP with metabolic components.

**Pes cavus (HP:0001761)** (high-arched foot) is a recognized skeletal manifestation that can occur in certain forms of HSP, particularly complicated types. This is more specific than general spasticity and can help differentiate HSP from other conditions.

## Terms Not Relevant to HSP

The following HPO terms appear **unrelated to hereditary spastic paraplegia** based on the provided medical literature:

- **Optic atrophy (HP:0000648)** — not mentioned as an HSP feature
- **Jejunal atresia (HP:0005235)** — a gastrointestinal developmental defect unrelated to HSP
- **Atypical nevus (HP:0001062)** — a dermatological finding unrelated to HSP
- **Conductive hearing impairment (HP:0000405)** — not associated with HSP
- **Hemoptysis (HP:0002105)** — a pulmonary symptom unrelated to HSP
- **Atrial flutter (HP:0004749)** — a cardiac arrhythmia unrelated to HSP
- **Epiretinal membrane (HP:0100014)** — an ophthalmological finding unrelated to HSP
- **Autoimmune antibody positivity (HP:0030057)** — not mentioned as an HSP feature

## Gender and Age Considerations

**Gender**: HSP affects both sexes equally[2]. There is no gender predisposition mentioned in the medical literature for any of these HPO terms in the context of HSP.

**Age of Onset**: HSP can present at any age, from infancy to old age, depending on the specific genetic form[2]. Therefore, age-specific patterns cannot be definitively established for these HPO terms without more detailed genetic subtype information. The progressive nature of HSP means that symptoms worsen over time regardless of initial age of onset[3].

**Inheritance Patterns**: While HSP itself shows various inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked), the search results do not indicate that specific HPO terms are more common in particular demographic groups.

hpo_input.name: Hyperactivity

hpo_input.name: Hyperkinetic movements

hpo_input.name: Tremor

hpo_input.name: Cardiomegaly

hpo_input.name: Chronic pain

hpo_input.name: Micrognathia
hpo_input.definition: "Developmental hypoplasia of the mandible." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Obesity
hpo_input.definition: "Accumulation of substantial excess body fat." []

hpo_input.name: Epicanthus
hpo_input.definition: "A fold of skin starting above the medial aspect of the upper eyelid and arching downward to cover, pass in front of and lateral to the medial canthus." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Deeply set eye
hpo_input.definition: "An eye that is more deeply recessed into the plane of the face than is typical." [PMID:19125427]

hpo_input.name: Laryngeal stenosis
hpo_input.definition: "Stricture or narrowing of the larynx that may be associated with symptoms of respiratory difficulty depending on the degree of laryngeal narrowing." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Epidermoid cyst

hpo_input.name: Liver abscess

hpo_input.name: Chylous ascites
hpo_input.definition: "Extravasation of chyle into the peritoneal cavity." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

Answer the following three questions for each hpo term:
1. Which of these hpo terms are more common and less informative for a specific disease?
2. Which of these hpo terms are rare and informative for a specific disease?
3. Is there a spesific gender or age group that is more likely to have these hpo terms?

Here is a detailed analysis of the provided HPO terms regarding their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and any gender or age group predilections based on the search results and known clinical context:

---

### 1. Protruding ear (HP:0000411)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Protruding ears are relatively common and usually benign, often present at birth without medical problems. They are typically caused by underdevelopment of the antihelical fold and do not affect hearing[3][5][7]. As such, **protruding ears are common and less informative for specific diseases** unless seen with other syndromic features. However, they can be a feature in genetic syndromes such as Fragile X syndrome, where large or protruding ears are characteristic[9].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present from birth, affecting both genders equally. No specific gender predilection noted.  
- **Summary:** Common, usually isolated and benign; informative if part of syndromic presentation (e.g., Fragile X syndrome).

---

### 2. Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum (HP:0002079)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum is a rare and **informative feature for specific neurological and developmental disorders**, including agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC)[2][6][8][14]. It is associated with developmental delay, seizures, intellectual disability, and other brain anomalies[4][12][14].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Diagnosed mostly in infancy or early childhood, sometimes prenatally. No specific gender predilection reported.  
- **Summary:** Rare, highly informative for neurodevelopmental disorders and brain malformations.

---

### 3. Delayed gross motor development (HP:0002194)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Delayed gross motor development is a **common but nonspecific feature** seen in many developmental disorders and is less informative by itself without additional context[4][12]. It signals a delay in large muscle control milestones like sitting and walking.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Observed in infancy and early childhood during milestone assessment. No gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific; useful as a general developmental delay marker.

---

### 4. Abnormal sacral segmentation (HP:0008468)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and informative structural anomaly** related to vertebral development defects. It is less common and can be diagnostic in specific syndromes involving vertebral segmentation defects.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital, identified in infancy or childhood. No known gender predilection.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative for skeletal/vertebral syndromes.

---

### 5. Prominent protruding coccyx (HP:0008472)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a rare and **informative feature** when present, often noted as a large or prominent tailbone. It can be part of skeletal dysplasias or syndromes affecting the spine.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital or developmental, no specific gender predilection.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative for skeletal anomalies.

---

### 6. Postnatal growth retardation (HP:0008897)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Postnatal growth retardation is **common but nonspecific**, seen in many genetic, metabolic, or chronic conditions[14]. Alone, it is less informative but important as a general clinical feature.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Occurs after birth, in infancy and childhood. No gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific marker of growth failure.

---

### 7. Hearing impairment (HP:0000365)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Hearing impairment is **common and nonspecific**, occurring in many conditions from congenital to acquired causes[4]. It is less informative alone but critical in syndromic diagnosis when combined with other features.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can present at any age, congenital or acquired. No gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific; important in syndromic context.

---

### 8. Autistic behavior (HP:0000729)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Autistic behavior is **common in neurodevelopmental disorders** and highly informative for autism spectrum disorders (ASD)[7]. It is a key diagnostic feature for ASD.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Diagnosed in early childhood, with a higher prevalence in males.  
- **Summary:** Common in ASD, highly informative; male predominance.

---

### 9. Joint hypermobility (HP:0001382)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Joint hypermobility is relatively common in the general population and can be benign or part of connective tissue disorders like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, making it **informative when associated with other features**[9].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in females and children; may decrease with age.  
- **Summary:** Common, sometimes informative in syndromic context; female and pediatric predominance.

---

### 10. Seizure (HP:0001250)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Seizures are common neurological events but **informative for many specific neurological diseases**, including agenesis of the corpus callosum and epilepsy syndromes[4][12][14].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can occur at any age; some epilepsy syndromes have age and gender predilections.  
- **Summary:** Common symptom, highly informative for neurological disorders.

---

### 11. Lower limb hyperreflexia (HP:0002395)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and informative neurological sign** indicating upper motor neuron involvement, useful in diagnosing specific neurological diseases.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  No specific gender or age predilection; depends on underlying disease.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative neurological sign.

---

### 12. Lipoma (HP:0012032)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Lipomas are common benign fatty tumors and generally **less informative for specific diseases** unless multiple or syndromic (e.g., lipomatosis).  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Occur in adults more commonly; no strong gender predilection.  
- **Summary:** Common benign tumor, less informative alone.

---

### 13. Neurodevelopmental delay (HP:0012758)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Neurodevelopmental delay is common in many pediatric neurological disorders and **informative as a general developmental marker**[12][14].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Diagnosed in infancy and early childhood; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific but informative developmental marker.

---

### 14. Abnormal palate morphology (HP:0000174)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Abnormal palate morphology is **less common and informative** in syndromes such as cleft palate syndromes and other craniofacial disorders.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital, diagnosed at birth or early childhood. No gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative for craniofacial syndromes.

---

### 15. Abnormal conjugate eye movement (HP:0000549)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and informative neurological sign** indicating brainstem or cranial nerve dysfunction.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  No specific gender or age predilection; depends on underlying cause.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative neurological sign.

---

### 16. Slanting of the palpebral fissure (HP:0200006)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Slanting palpebral fissures are **common and informative** in many genetic syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome).  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present from birth; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, informative for genetic syndromes.

---

- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and informative craniofacial feature** seen in some syndromes.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative for syndromic diagnosis.

---

### 18. Abnormal nasal tip morphology (HP:0000436)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is **less common and informative** in craniofacial syndromes.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative craniofacial feature.

---

### 19. Abnormal eyebrow morphology (HP:0000534)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is **less common and informative** in syndromes with facial dysmorphism.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative facial feature.

---

### 20. Dystonia (HP:0001332)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Dystonia is a **rare and highly informative neurological sign** indicating basal ganglia or motor pathway dysfunction.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can occur at any age; some forms have age and gender predilections.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative neurological sign.

---

### 21. Carotid artery occlusion (HP:0012474)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and highly informative vascular finding** indicating serious cerebrovascular disease.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in adults; no specific gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, highly informative vascular pathology.

---

### 22. Hyperactivity (HP:0000752)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Hyperactivity is **common and nonspecific**, seen in ADHD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in children, especially males.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific behavioral feature.

---

### 23. Hyperkinetic movements (HP:0002487)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  These are **rare and informative neurological signs** indicating movement disorders.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  No specific gender or age predilection.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative neurological sign.

---

### 24. Tremor (HP:0001337)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Tremor is **common and informative** for various neurological disorders.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common with aging; no strong gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, informative neurological sign.

---

### 25. Cardiomegaly (HP:0001640)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Cardiomegaly is **common and nonspecific**, seen in many cardiac conditions.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in adults; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific cardiac sign.

---

### 26. Chronic pain (HP:0012532)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Chronic pain is **common and nonspecific**, seen in many conditions.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in adults; some gender differences reported.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific symptom.

---

### 27. Micrognathia (HP:0000347)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Micrognathia is a **rare and informative craniofacial anomaly** seen in syndromes like Pierre Robin sequence and others[1][9].  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative craniofacial feature.

---

### 28. Obesity (HP:0001513)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Obesity is **common and nonspecific**, but can be informative in syndromic obesity.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  More common in adults but increasingly seen in children; no strong gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, nonspecific.

---

### 29. Epicanthus (HP:0000286)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Epicanthal folds are **common and informative** in many genetic syndromes and ethnic groups.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Present from birth; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common, informative facial feature.

---

### 30. Deeply set eye (HP:0000490)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Deeply set eyes are **less common and informative** in syndromic diagnoses.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Congenital; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative facial feature.

---

### 31. Laryngeal stenosis (HP:0001602)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Laryngeal stenosis is **rare and informative** for airway and congenital anomalies.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Can be congenital or acquired; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative airway anomaly.

---

- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Epidermoid cysts are **common benign skin lesions**, less informative unless multiple or syndromic.  
- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Usually appear around puberty; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Common benign lesion, less informative.

### 33. Liver abscess (HP:0100523)
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Liver abscess is **rare and highly informative** for infectious or inflammatory diseases.

  More common in adults; no gender bias.  
- **Summary:** Rare, informative infectious pathology.

- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Chylous ascites is **rare and informative** for lymphatic or congenital disorders.

hpo_input.name: EEG abnormality
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormality observed by electroencephalogram (EEG), which is used to record of the brain's spontaneous electrical activity from multiple electrodes placed on the scalp." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypertelorism
hpo_input.definition: "Interpupillary distance more than 2 SD above the mean (alternatively, the appearance of an increased interpupillary distance or widely spaced eyes)." [PMID:19125427]

hpo_input.name: Narrow forehead
hpo_input.definition: "Width of the forehead or distance between the frontotemporales is more than two standard deviations below the mean (objective); or apparently narrow intertemporal region (subjective)." [PMID:19125436]

hpo_input.name: Oculomotor apraxia
hpo_input.definition: "Ocular motor apraxia is a deficiency in voluntary, horizontal, lateral, fast eye movements (saccades) with retention of slow pursuit movements. The inability to follow objects visually is often compensated by head movements. There may be decreased smooth pursuit, and cancelation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:20615230]
synonym: Defective or absent horizontal voluntary eye movements

hpo_input.name: Delayed speech and language development
hpo_input.definition: "A degree of language development that is significantly below the norm for a child of a specified age." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Osteopenia
hpo_input.definition: "Osteopenia is a term to define bone density that is not normal but also not as low as osteoporosis. By definition from the World Health Organization osteopenia is defined by bone densitometry as a T score -1 to -2.5." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21234807]

hpo_input.name: Osteoporosis
hpo_input.definition: "Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone density and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue with a consequent increase in bone fragility. According to the WHO criteria, osteoporosis is defined as a BMD that lies 2.5 standard deviations or more below the average value for young healthy adults (a T-score below -2.5 SD)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:28293453]

hpo_input.name: Cerebellar atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Cerebellar atrophy is defined as a cerebellum with initially normal structures, in a posterior fossa with normal size, which displays enlarged fissures (interfolial spaces) in comparison to the foliae secondary to loss of tissue. Cerebellar atrophy implies irreversible loss of tissue and result from an ongoing progressive disease until a final stage is reached or a single injury, e.g. an intoxication or infectious event." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:12169461, PMID:26331051]

hpo_input.name: Generalized hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Generalized muscular hypotonia (abnormally low muscle tone)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Cerebellar hypoplasia
hpo_input.definition: "Cerebellar hypoplasia is a descriptive term implying a cerebellum with a reduced volume, but a normal shape and is stable over time." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:26331051, PMID:27160001]

hpo_input.name: Tremor
hpo_input.definition: "An unintentional, oscillating to-and-fro muscle movement about a joint axis." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:16344298, PMID:20589866]

hpo_input.name: Hyperreflexia
hpo_input.definition: "Hyperreflexia is the presence of hyperactive stretch reflexes of the muscles." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Neurodevelopmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "Neurodevelopmental delay (NDD) refers to delays in the maturation of the brain and central nervous system; infants and young children with NDD may experience delays in the development of one or more skills including gross motor abilities, fine-motor coordination, language abilities and ability to solve increasingly complex problems." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6670-9157, PMID:31783983]

hpo_input.name: Anteverted nares
hpo_input.definition: "Anteriorly-facing nostrils viewed with the head in the Frankfurt horizontal and the eyes of the observer level with the eyes of the subject. This gives the appearance of an upturned nose (upturned nasal tip)." [PMID:19152422]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal involuntary eye movements
hpo_input.definition: "Anomalous movements of the eyes that occur without the subject wanting them to happen." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal speech pattern
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality in the sound (volume) or cadence (rate) of speech." []

hpo_input.name: Ureteral obstruction
hpo_input.definition: "Obstruction of the flow of urine through the ureter." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Constipation
hpo_input.definition: "Infrequent or difficult evacuation of feces." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Optic atrophy
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the optic nerve. Optic atrophy results from the death of the retinal ganglion cell axons that comprise the optic nerve and manifesting as a pale optic nerve on fundoscopy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21418198]

hpo_input.name: Visual impairment
hpo_input.definition: "Visual impairment (or vision impairment) is vision loss (of a person) to such a degree as to qualify as an additional support need through a significant limitation of visual capability resulting from either disease, trauma, or congenital or degenerative conditions that cannot be corrected by conventional means, such as refractive correction, medication, or surgery." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8727-6592]

hpo_input.name: Exostoses
hpo_input.definition: "An exostosis is a benign growth the projects outward from the bone surface. It is capped by cartilage, and arises from a bone that develops from cartilage." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Formation of new noncancerous bone on top of existing bone

hpo_input.name: Mydriasis
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormal dilatation of the iris." [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:DDD_ncarter]

hpo_input.name: Sciatica
hpo_input.definition: "Pain in the lower back and hip radiating in the distribution of the sciatic nerve." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:17872935]

hpo_input.name: Myeloproliferative disorder
hpo_input.definition: "Proliferation (excess production) of hemopoietically active tissue or of tissue which has embryonic hemopoietic potential." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Supernumerary testes
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of more than two testes." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Pectus carinatum
hpo_input.definition: "A deformity of the chest caused by overgrowth of the ribs and characterized by protrusion of the sternum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
