hpo_input.name: Hydronephrosis
hpo_input.definition: "Severe distention of the kidney with dilation of the renal pelvis and calices." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Gastroesophageal reflux
hpo_input.definition: "A condition in which the stomach contents leak backwards from the stomach into the esophagus through the lower esophageal sphincter." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Stomach cancer
hpo_input.definition: "A cancer arising in any part of the stomach." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Urinary incontinence
hpo_input.definition: "Loss of the ability to control the urinary bladder leading to involuntary urination." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154, PMID:12559262]

| **Microcephaly (HP:0000252)**     | Common in many neurodevelopmental disorders; less specific alone | Highly informative when combined with other neurological signs; seen in genetic syndromes and congenital infections[PMID:15806441,19125436] | Present from birth or early childhood; no strong gender bias noted |
| **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)** | Common in pediatric neurology; broad and less specific | Informative in early childhood (<5 years) for diagnosing neurodevelopmental disorders[HPO definition] | Specifically used for children under 5 years old |
| **Neonatal hypotonia (HP:0001319)** | Common in neonatal intensive care; less specific | Informative for congenital neuromuscular disorders and genetic syndromes presenting at birth[HPO definition] | Occurs in neonates (newborn period) by definition |
| **Abnormal facial shape (HP:0001999)** | Very broad and common descriptor; low specificity | Informative when combined with specific facial dysmorphisms in syndromic diagnoses[HPO definition] | No specific gender or age predilection |
| **Poor speech (HP:0002465)**      | Common symptom in many neurodevelopmental and neurological conditions | Informative when associated with developmental delay or syndromes affecting speech[4] | More relevant in children and developmental age groups |
| **Epicanthus (HP:0000286)**        | Common in many populations, especially in infants and certain ethnic groups; less specific | Informative if combined with other dysmorphic features in syndromes[HPO definition] | More common in infants and certain ethnicities; no gender bias |
| **Low-set, posteriorly rotated ears (HP:0000368)** (obsolete) | Common dysmorphic feature in many syndromes; less specific | Informative in syndromic contexts but now considered obsolete term | No specific gender or age predilection |
| **Downturned corners of mouth (HP:0002714)** | Occurs in various syndromes; moderately informative | More informative when part of a facial gestalt in genetic syndromes[HPO definition] | No specific gender or age predilection |
| **Feeding difficulties (HP:0011968)** | Common in infants and children with various conditions; less specific | Informative in congenital syndromes affecting oral-motor function or neurological status[HPO definition] | Mainly infants and young children |
| **Dystonia (HP:0001332)**          | Less common; more specific for neurological movement disorders | Highly informative for specific movement disorder syndromes and genetic conditions[HPO definition] | Can occur at any age depending on etiology |
| **Abnormal forehead morphology (HP:0000290)** | Broad and less specific | Informative when combined with other craniofacial anomalies in syndromes[HPO definition] | No specific gender or age predilection |
| **Anteverted nares (HP:0000463)**  | Common in many populations; less specific | Informative in syndromic contexts with other facial features[5][HPO definition] | No specific gender or age predilection |
| **Cleft palate (HP:0000175)**      | Relatively common congenital anomaly; less specific alone | Highly informative for syndromes with craniofacial malformations[HPO definition] | Present from birth; no gender bias |
| **Optic atrophy (HP:0000648)**     | Less common; more specific | Informative for neuro-ophthalmologic and genetic disorders[HPO definition] | Can present at any age depending on cause |
| **Hydronephrosis (HP:0000126)**    | Common in prenatal and pediatric urology; less specific | Informative for congenital urinary tract anomalies and syndromes[HPO definition] | More common in infants and children |
| **Gastroesophageal reflux (HP:0002020)** | Common in infants and adults; less specific | Informative when severe or part of syndromic gastrointestinal involvement[HPO definition] | More common in infants and elderly |
| **Stomach cancer (HP:0012126)**    | Rare in children; more common in adults | Informative for adult-onset malignancies; less relevant for pediatric syndromes[HPO definition] | More common in adults, no gender specificity |
| **Urinary incontinence (HP:0000020)** | Common symptom in many conditions; less specific | Informative in neurological or congenital urinary tract disorders[HPO definition] | More common in elderly and children with developmental issues |

### Summary Highlights:

- **More common and less informative terms** tend to be broad, frequently observed features or symptoms such as *global developmental delay*, *feeding difficulties*, *epicanthus*, *abnormal facial shape*, *gastroesophageal reflux*, and *urinary incontinence*. These occur in many conditions and are less specific for a particular diagnosis.

- **Rare and more informative terms** include *thin upper lip vermilion* (especially in rare syndromes like FHEIG), *dystonia*, *optic atrophy*, *cleft palate*, and *neonatal hypotonia*. These features, especially when combined with other signs, can help pinpoint specific genetic or congenital disorders.

- **Age and gender predilections** are mostly related to the developmental stage or congenital onset. For example, *neonatal hypotonia* and *feeding difficulties* are neonatal/infant features; *global developmental delay* is defined for children under 5 years; *stomach cancer* is adult-onset; *epicanthus* is more common in infants and certain ethnic groups but not gender-specific. No strong gender biases are noted for most terms.

This synthesis is based on HPO definitions and clinical relevance as reported in Orphanet, Monarch Initiative, FDNA, and related genetic syndrome literature[1][2][3][4][5].

# Analysis of HPO Terms for Clinical Significance

## Global Developmental Delay (HP:0001263)

**Common and Less Informative**

Global developmental delay is a highly common condition affecting approximately 1-3% of preschool-aged children worldwide[1][2]. This term is relatively non-specific as it describes delays across multiple developmental domains rather than pinpointing a particular etiology. It serves as a broad diagnostic umbrella encompassing motor skills, speech and language, cognitive skills, and social-emotional development[1][5]. The condition has diverse causes ranging from genetic abnormalities to environmental factors, making it less informative for identifying a specific underlying disease without further investigation[2].

**Rare and Informative**

This term is not rare; rather, it is a common presentation that requires further diagnostic workup to identify specific conditions. However, when global developmental delay persists beyond age 5, it becomes more informative as it may indicate an underlying intellectual disability or specific learning disorder[4].

**Age and Gender Considerations**

Global developmental delay is defined specifically for children younger than five years of age[1]. There is no significant gender predilection noted in the search results, suggesting equal prevalence across males and females during early childhood[1][2].

## Motor Delay (HP:0001270)

**Common and Less Informative**

Motor delay is a common component of developmental delays, representing delays in acquiring motor skills such as rolling over, sitting up, crawling, and walking[1][3]. This term is relatively non-specific as motor delays can result from numerous causes including genetic conditions, premature birth, brain trauma, or environmental factors[1][5]. Without additional clinical context, motor delay alone does not indicate a specific disease.

**Rare and Informative**

Motor delay becomes more informative when associated with specific patterns or additional neurological findings. For example, motor delay combined with hyperreflexia or spasticity may suggest upper motor neuron involvement or conditions like cerebral palsy[7].

**Age and Gender Considerations**

Motor delays are typically identified in infants and young children, with most developmental screening occurring between birth and five years of age[1]. No gender-specific predilection is documented in the available literature.

## Hyperreflexia (HP:0001347)

**Common and Less Informative**

Hyperreflexia, or increased deep tendon reflexes, is a relatively common neurological finding that can occur in various conditions. Without additional clinical context, it is not highly specific for any particular disease.

**Rare and Informative**

Hyperreflexia becomes more informative when present alongside other neurological signs. It may indicate upper motor neuron lesions, spasticity, or conditions affecting the corticospinal tract[3]. # Analysis of HPO Terms for Clinical Significance

## Overview

The HPO terms provided represent a mix of clinical features with varying degrees of specificity and diagnostic utility. Below is an analysis of their relevance to disease diagnosis and their demographic patterns.

## 1. Common and Less Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are relatively common in the general population or across multiple conditions, making them less specific for diagnosis:

**Abnormal skull morphology (HP:0000929)** is a broad, non-specific descriptor that encompasses many skull variations. It serves as an umbrella term for more specific conditions like brachycephaly but lacks diagnostic precision on its own.[1]

**Short stature (HP:0004322)** is a common finding in numerous genetic and metabolic disorders, endocrine conditions, and nutritional deficiencies. Its presence alone does not point to a specific disease.[1][2]

**Abnormal foot morphology (HP:0001760)** appears in diverse conditions ranging from skeletal dysplasias to neuromuscular disorders, making it relatively non-specific for diagnosis.

**Abnormal oral cavity morphology (HP:0000163)** is a general term that could apply to many conditions affecting oral structures and is therefore less informative without additional specificity.

**Diarrhea (HP:0002014)** is an extremely common symptom with hundreds of potential etiologies, from infectious to genetic causes, making it minimally informative for specific disease identification.

**Generalized hirsutism (HP:0002230)** occurs in various endocrine disorders, metabolic conditions, and as a normal variant, limiting its diagnostic specificity.

## 2. Rare and Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are more specific and informative for particular genetic or developmental conditions:

**Brachycephaly (HP:0000248)** is a distinctive skull morphology characterized by a decreased anterior-posterior diameter with a cephalic index greater than 81%.[1][4] When present, particularly in its synostotic form resulting from bicoronal suture fusion, it strongly suggests specific genetic syndromes or developmental abnormalities.[4] This term is particularly informative when combined with other skeletal or facial features.

**Oligodontia (HP:0000677)** — the absence of six or more teeth — is a relatively rare finding that indicates specific genetic syndromes affecting tooth development, such as KBG syndrome or ectodermal dysplasias.[2]

**Short distal phalanx of finger (HP:0009882)** is a specific skeletal finding that appears in particular genetic syndromes. When present with other features like brachycephaly and oligodontia, it becomes highly informative for conditions like KBG syndrome.[2]

**Underdeveloped supraorbital ridges (HP:0009891)** is a distinctive facial feature that, when combined with other craniofacial abnormalities, can help identify specific syndromes associated with craniosynostosis or other genetic conditions.[3]

**Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the nasal bone (HP:0010940)** is a relatively rare skeletal finding that appears in specific genetic syndromes and can be highly informative when present with other characteristic features.

**Hypoplasia of the maxilla (HP:0000327)** is a specific craniofacial finding that appears in syndromes associated with craniosynostosis, such as Apert syndrome and Crouzon syndrome.[3]

**Low anterior hairline (HP:0000294)** is a distinctive feature that appears in specific genetic syndromes and can be informative when combined with other craniofacial abnormalities.

**Hypertelorism (HP:0000316)** — widely spaced eyes — is a characteristic feature of several genetic syndromes, particularly those involving craniosynostosis such as Crouzon and Apert syndromes.[3]

**Nystagmus (HP:0000639)** indicates neurological involvement and appears in specific genetic conditions affecting the nervous system, making it informative when present with other features.

**Intellectual disability, mild (HP:0001256)** becomes informative when combined with specific physical features, as it suggests genetic syndromes affecting neurodevelopment, such as KBG syndrome where developmental delay is common.[2]

**Patent ductus arteriosus (HP:0001643)** is a specific cardiac finding that, when present with other features, can indicate particular genetic syndromes.

## 3. Gender and Age-Related Patterns

**Age-Related Patterns:**

Most of these HPO terms manifest in **infancy and early childhood**. Brachycephaly typically develops within the first three months of life in positional cases, though synostotic forms are present from birth.[4] Craniofacial abnormalities like hypertelorism, maxillary hypoplasia, and supraorbital ridge underdevelopment are congenital and evident from birth or early infancy.[3]

Dental abnormalities like oligodontia become apparent as teeth begin to erupt, typically between 6 months and 3 years of age.[2]

Intellectual disability manifestations become more apparent as developmental milestones are assessed during infancy and early childhood, though formal diagnosis may occur later.

**Gender Patterns:**

The HPO terms listed show **no significant gender predilection** for most features. Genetic syndromes causing these abnormalities typically follow Mendelian inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant for KBG syndrome and many craniosynostosis syndromes) that affect males and females equally.[2][3]

However, some conditions may show subtle differences:
- **Brachycephaly** from positional causes affects approximately 1 in 5 babies regardless of gender, though some studies suggest slightly higher rates in preterm infants of both sexes.[5]
- **Cardiac conditions** like patent ductus arteriosus may show slightly higher prevalence in females in some populations, though this is not specific to the genetic syndromes discussed here.

The combination of multiple rare features (such as brachycephaly + oligodontia + short distal phalanges + hypertelorism) is highly suggestive of specific genetic syndromes like KBG syndrome, which affects both genders equally and typically manifests in infancy with developmental delays becoming apparent in early childhood.[2]

hpo_input.definition: "Spasticity and weakness of the leg and hip muscles." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A seizure is an intermittent abnormality of nervous system physiology characterized by a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15816939]

hpo_input.name: Neurodevelopmental delay
hpo_input.definition: "Neurodevelopmental delay (NDD) refers to delays in the maturation of the brain and central nervous system; infants and young children with NDD may experience delays in the development of one or more skills including gross motor abilities, fine-motor coordination, language abilities and ability to solve increasingly complex problems." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6670-9157, PMID:31783983]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal reflex
hpo_input.definition: "Any anomaly of a reflex, i.e., of an automatic response mediated by the nervous system (a reflex does not need the intervention of conscious thought to occur)." []

hpo_input.name: Hypoplasia of the corpus callosum
hpo_input.definition: "Underdevelopment of the corpus callosum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21263138]
synonym: Underdevelopment of part of brain called corpus callosum

hpo_input.name: Crohn's disease
hpo_input.definition: "A chronic granulomatous inflammatory disease of the intestines that may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus, causing a wide variety of symptoms. It primarily causes abdominal pain, diarrhea which may be bloody, vomiting, or weight loss, but may also cause complications outside of the gastrointestinal tract such as skin rashes, arthritis, inflammation of the eye, tiredness, and lack of concentration. Crohn's disease is thought to be an autoimmune disease, in which the body's immune system attacks the gastrointestinal tract, causing inflammation." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Drooling
hpo_input.definition: "Habitual flow of saliva out of the mouth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15202698]

hpo_input.name: Hyperchloremia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally increased chloride concentration in the blood." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dermoid cyst
hpo_input.definition: "A congenital subcutaneous cyst that arises from entrapment of skin along the lines of embryonic fusion. In contrast to epidermal cysts, dermoid cysts tend to contain various adnexal structures such as hair, sebaceous, eccrine or apocrine glands. Dermoid cysts are present at birth, and are indolent, firm, deep, subcutaneous nodules. They are often located on the head and neck, and rarely in the anogenital area. Dermoid cysts are slowly progressive and can grow to a size of 1 to 4 cm." []

hpo_input.name: Hyperacusis
hpo_input.definition: "Over-sensitivity to certain frequency ranges of sound." [PMID:14645606, PMID:14647932, PMID:31669363]

hpo_input.name: Pancytopenia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormal reduction in numbers of all blood cell types (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Resting tremor
hpo_input.definition: "A resting tremor occurs when muscles are at rest and becomes less noticeable or disappears when the affected muscles are moved. Resting tremors are often slow and coarse." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:22675666]

hpo_input.name: Chronic constipation
hpo_input.definition: "Constipation for longer than three months with fewer than 3 bowel movements per week, straining, lumpy or hard stools, and a sensation of anorectal obstruction or incomplete defecation." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5208-3432]

hpo_input.name: Depression
hpo_input.definition: "Frequently experiencing feelings of being down, miserable, and/or hopeless; struggling to recover from these moods; having a pessimistic outlook on the future; feeling a pervasive sense of shame; having a low self-worth; experiencing thoughts of suicide and engaging in suicidal behavior." []

hpo_input.name: Low frustration tolerance
hpo_input.definition: "The feeling of frustration can be defined as an emotional reaction that occurs when a desired goal is not achieved. Frustration intolerance is defined as an age-inappropriate response to frustration, characterized by crying or temper tantrums in children, or aggressive or other undesirable behaviors." []

hpo_input.name: Mental deterioration
hpo_input.definition: "Loss of previously present mental abilities, generally in adults." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Rigidity
hpo_input.definition: "Continuous involuntary sustained muscle contraction. When an affected muscle is passively stretched, the degree of resistance remains constant regardless of the rate at which the muscle is stretched. This feature helps to distinguish rigidity from muscle spasticity." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Sleep abnormality
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormal pattern in the quality, quantity, or characteristics of sleep." [PMID:32809555]

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of binocular vision
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of binocular vision, that is of the ability to synthesize the visual inputs from both eyes to a single image with perception of depth." [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:DDD_ncarter]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal diminished volition
hpo_input.definition: "A reduction in willful and motivated goal-directed behavior that is considered the determinant of behavior and adaptation that allows individuals to get started, be energized to perform a sustained and directed action." []

hpo_input.name: Disinhibition
hpo_input.definition: "Reduced ability to control, or a failure to resist a temptation, urge, or impulse. Examples include disregard for social conventions, general impulsivity, and poor risk assessment." []

hpo_input.name: Dystonia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally increased muscular tone that causes fixed abnormal postures. There is a slow, intermittent twisting motion that leads to exaggerated turning and posture of the extremities and trunk." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Postural instability
hpo_input.definition: "A tendency to fall or the inability to keep oneself from falling; imbalance. The retropulsion test is widely regarded as the gold standard to evaluate postural instability, Use of the retropulsion test includes a rapid balance perturbation in the backward direction, and the number of balance correcting steps (or total absence thereof) is used to rate the degree of postural instability. Healthy subjects correct such perturbations with either one or two large steps, or without taking any steps, hinging rapidly at the hips while swinging the arms forward as a counterweight. In patients with balance impairment, balance correcting steps are often too small, forcing patients to take more than two steps. Taking three or more steps is generally considered to be abnormal, and taking more than five steps is regarded as being clearly abnormal. Markedly affected patients continue to step backward without ever regaining their balance and must be caught by the examiner (this would be called true retropulsion). Even more severely affected patients fail to correct entirely, and fall backward like a pushed toy soldier, without taking any corrective steps." [PMID:25613349]

hpo_input.name: Telangiectasia
hpo_input.definition: "Telangiectasias refer to small dilated blood vessels located near the surface of the skin or mucous membranes, measuring between 0.5 and 1 millimeter in diameter. Telangiectasia are located especially on the tongue, lips, palate, fingers, face, conjunctiva, trunk, nail beds, and fingertips." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Apathy
hpo_input.definition: "Apathy is a quantitative reduction of interest, motivation and the initiation and persistence of goal-directed behavior, where often the accompanying emotions, thoughts, and social interactions are also diminished. The individual is typically non-reactive to provocations, positive or negative, and appears to not care. Distinguished from lethargy which involves lack of physical or mental energy." []
synonym: Lack of feeling, emotion, interest, motivation, initiation

hpo_input.name: Dementia
hpo_input.definition: "A loss of global cognitive ability of sufficient amount to interfere with normal social or occupational function. Dementia represents a loss of previously present cognitive abilities, generally in adults, and can affect memory, thinking, language, judgment, and behavior." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Tractional retinal detachment
hpo_input.definition: "A type of retinal detachment arising due to a combination of contracting retinal membranes, abnormal vitreoretinal adhesions, and vitreous changes. It is usually seen in the context of diseases that induce a fibrovascular response, e.g. diabetes." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, ISBN-13:978-0199679980]

hpo_input.name: Acute hepatitis
hpo_input.definition: "Acute hepatic injury resulting from inflammation typically accompanied by increased serum alanine transaminase activity. Etiologies include viral hepatitis, drugs, toxins, and autoimmune disorders." []

### 1. Abnormality of the dentition (HP:0000164)

- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a broad and common term encompassing many dental abnormalities such as discoloration, weak teeth, malformation, and missing teeth. It is less informative by itself for a specific disease because it covers a wide range of dental issues seen in many conditions. However, specific abnormalities within this category (e.g., dentinogenesis imperfecta, amelogenesis imperfecta) are rare and informative for particular genetic disorders[1][2][4][7].

- **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  These abnormalities can present at any age, often noticeable in childhood when primary teeth erupt or in early adulthood with permanent teeth. There is no specific gender predilection reported.

  Brachycephaly (shortened anterior-posterior skull dimension) is relatively common as a nonspecific cranial shape variant and is less informative alone for a specific disease. - **Gender/Age Predilection:**  
  Typically identified in infancy or early childhood during skull growth. No strong gender bias is noted.

hpo_input.name: EMG: myopathic abnormalities
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of abnormal electromyographic patterns indicative of myopathy, such as small-short polyphasic motor unit potentials." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles
Progressive distal muscle weakness
hpo_input.definition: "Progressively reduced strength of the distal musculature." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Amyotrophy of ankle musculature
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the muscles of the ankle." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Somatic sensory dysfunction
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the primary sensation that is mediated by peripheral nerves (pain, temperature, touch, vibration, joint position). The word hypoesthesia (or hypesthesia) refers to a reduction in cutaneous sensation to a specific type of testing." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Impaired vibratory sensation
hpo_input.definition: "A decrease in the ability to perceive vibration. Clinically, this is usually tested with a tuning fork which vibrates at 128 Hz and is applied to bony prominences such as the malleoli at the ankles or the metacarpal-phalangeal joints. There is a slow decay of vibration from the tuning fork. The degree of vibratory sense loss can be crudely estimated by counting the number of seconds that the examiner can perceive the vibration longer than the patient." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal circulating enzyme concentration
hpo_input.definition: "The concentration or activity of an enzyme in the blood circulation is outside of the limits of the normal range." []

hpo_input.name: Peripheral axonal neuropathy
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality characterized by disruption of the normal functioning of peripheral axons." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Ureteral obstruction
hpo_input.definition: "Obstruction of the flow of urine through the ureter." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Fever
hpo_input.definition: "Body temperature elevated above the normal range." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154, PMID:9759682]

hpo_input.name: Glucose intolerance
hpo_input.definition: "Glucose intolerance (GI) can be defined as dysglycemia that comprises both prediabetes and diabetes. It includes the conditions of impaired fasting glucose (IFG) and impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and diabetes mellitus (DM)." [PMID:29763085]

hpo_input.name: Atypical behavior
hpo_input.definition: "Atypical behavior is an abnormality in a person's actions that can be controlled or modulated by the will of the individual. While abnormal behaviors can be difficult to control, they are distinct from other abnormal actions that cannot be affected by the individual's will." []

hpo_input.name: Ectopia lentis
hpo_input.definition: "Dislocation or malposition of the crystalline lens of the eye. A partial displacement (or dislocation) of the lens is described as a subluxation of the lens, while a complete displacement is termed luxation of the lens. A complete displacement occurs if the lens is completely outside the patellar fossa of the lens, either in the anterior chamber, in the vitreous, or directly on the retina. If the lens is partially displaced but still contained within the lens space, then it is termed subluxation." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Phthisis bulbi
hpo_input.definition: "Atrophy of the eyeball with blindness and decreased intraocular pressure due to end-stage intraocular disease." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Ascites
hpo_input.definition: "Accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity (between the layers of the peritoneum that lines the abdomen)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Accumulation of fluid in the abdomen

hpo_input.name: Elevated urinary catecholamine level
hpo_input.definition: "The concentration of a catecholamine in the urine, normalized for urine concentration, is above the upper limit of normal." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
hpo_input.definition: "Hemorrhage occurring between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater." [https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4530-3154]

hpo_input.name: Myoglobinuria
hpo_input.definition: "Presence of myoglobin in the urine." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

Here is a detailed analysis of the provided Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms with respect to their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and any known gender or age group associations:

| HPO Term ID | Name | Commonality & Informativeness | Gender/Age Group Association |
|-------------|------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **HP:0003458** | EMG: myopathic abnormalities | **Common but less specific:** This term describes abnormal electromyographic patterns indicative of myopathy, such as small-short polyphasic motor unit potentials. It is a common finding in many myopathies (e.g., inflammatory, toxic, metabolic, congenital) and thus less informative for pinpointing a specific disease[1][3][13]. | No specific gender or age predilection; occurs in various myopathies across ages[1][7]. |
| **HP:0006466** | Ankle flexion contracture | No direct definition or data found; contractures are common secondary features in chronic neuromuscular diseases but are nonspecific. Likely **common and less informative** unless combined with other signs. | Contractures often develop over time; more common in chronic or progressive neuromuscular disorders, affecting all ages depending on disease. |
| **HP:0009005** | Weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles | No direct definition; weakness of intrinsic hand muscles is often seen in distal myopathies and neuropathies. It can be **informative** when combined with distal muscle involvement[4][6]. | Often presents in adults with distal myopathies; no strong gender bias reported. |
| **HP:0009063** | Progressive distal muscle weakness | **Rare and informative:** Progressive distal muscle weakness is characteristic of distal myopathies such as Nonaka myopathy, inclusion body myositis, and others[2][4][6]. It helps differentiate distal myopathies from neuropathies. | Typically adult onset (often >30 years), but some forms start in childhood or adolescence. No clear gender predominance[2][4][6][10]. |
| **HP:0002355** | obsolete Difficulty walking | Term marked obsolete; difficulty walking is a **common but nonspecific symptom** in many neuromuscular and neurological disorders. | Affects all ages and genders depending on underlying cause. |
| **HP:0009031** | Amyotrophy of ankle musculature | **Rare and informative:** Atrophy localized to ankle muscles is typical in distal myopathies and some neuropathies[4][6]. It can help localize disease. | Usually adult onset in distal myopathies; no strong gender bias reported. |
| **HP:0003474** | Somatic sensory dysfunction | **Common but less specific:** Sensory abnormalities (pain, temperature, touch, vibration) occur in peripheral neuropathies and some myopathies with neuropathic features[7]. | Can occur at any age; some neuropathies have genetic predispositions; no strong gender bias. |
| **HP:0002495** | Impaired vibratory sensation | **Common in neuropathies:** Decreased vibration sense is typical in large-fiber sensory neuropathies, less so in pure myopathies[7]. | More common in older adults and in diseases affecting peripheral nerves; no clear gender bias. |
| **HP:0011021** | Abnormal circulating enzyme concentration | **Common but nonspecific:** Elevated enzymes like creatine kinase (CK) are frequent in muscle diseases but not disease-specific[3][7]. | Can occur at any age depending on disease; some enzyme elevations more common in males due to muscle mass differences. |
| **HP:0003477** | Peripheral axonal neuropathy | **Common but less specific:** Axonal neuropathy is a frequent feature in many peripheral nerve disorders and some myopathies with neuropathic involvement[7]. | Can affect all ages; some hereditary forms present in childhood, acquired forms in adults; no strong gender bias. |
| **HP:0006000** | Ureteral obstruction | **Rare and disease-specific:** Obstruction of urine flow through ureters is uncommon in neuromuscular diseases but may be relevant in syndromic conditions. | No specific gender or age predilection; depends on underlying cause. |
| **HP:0001945** | Fever | **Common but nonspecific:** Elevated body temperature occurs in infections, inflammatory diseases, and some metabolic conditions[14]. | Affects all ages and genders. |
| **HP:0001952** | Glucose intolerance | **Common but nonspecific:** Seen in metabolic disorders and diabetes; may be secondary in some neuromuscular diseases[7]. | More common in adults, especially middle-aged and older; no strong gender bias. |
| **HP:0000708** | Atypical behavior | **Common but nonspecific:** Behavioral abnormalities occur in many neurological and psychiatric disorders[7]. | Can affect all ages; some conditions have age or gender predilections. |
| **HP:0001083** | Ectopia lentis | **Rare and informative:** Lens dislocation is a hallmark of connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria[7]. | Often presents in childhood or adolescence; no strong gender bias. |
| **HP:0000667** | Phthisis bulbi | **Rare and disease-specific:** End-stage eyeball atrophy with blindness is uncommon and usually secondary to severe ocular disease[7]. | No specific gender or age predilection; depends on ocular disease history. |
| **HP:0001541** | Ascites | **Common but nonspecific:** Fluid accumulation in the abdomen occurs in liver disease, heart failure, and malignancies[7]. | More common in adults with chronic systemic diseases; no gender bias. |
| **HP:0011976** | Elevated urinary catecholamine level | **Rare and informative:** Elevated catecholamines suggest pheochromocytoma or neuroblastoma[7]. | More common in children (neuroblastoma) or adults (pheochromocytoma); no strong gender bias. |
| **HP:0002138** | Subarachnoid hemorrhage | **Rare and disease-specific:** Bleeding between arachnoid and pia mater is an acute neurological emergency[7]. | More common in adults; some risk factors vary by gender (e.g., aneurysm prevalence). |
| **HP:0002913** | Myoglobinuria | **Rare and informative:** Presence of myoglobin in urine indicates muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis)[7]. | Can occur at any age; triggered by trauma, metabolic, or genetic muscle diseases. |
| **HP:0005191** | Congenital knee dislocation | **Rare and informative:** Present at birth, often associated with syndromes or connective tissue disorders[7]. | Present in neonates; no strong gender bias. |

### Summary of Key Points

- **More common and less informative terms:**  
  - EMG: myopathic abnormalities (HP:0003458)  
  - Abnormal circulating enzyme concentration (HP:0011021)  
  - Somatic sensory dysfunction (HP:0003474)  
  - Impaired vibratory sensation (HP:0002495)  
  - Peripheral axonal neuropathy (HP:0003477)  
  - Fever (HP:0001945)  
  - Glucose intolerance (HP:0001952)  
  - Atypical behavior (HP:0000708)  
  - Ascites (HP:0001541)  

- **Rare and informative terms for specific diseases:**  
  - Progressive distal muscle weakness (HP:0009063) — characteristic of distal myopathies[2][4][6]  
  - Amyotrophy of ankle musculature (HP:0009031) — helps localize distal muscle involvement[4][6]  
  - Ectopia lentis (HP:0001083) — indicative of connective tissue disorders[7]  
  - Elevated urinary catecholamine level (HP:0011976) — suggests neuroendocrine tumors[7]  
  - Subarachnoid hemorrhage (HP:0002138) — acute neurological event[7]  
  - Myoglobinuria (HP:0002913) — indicates muscle breakdown[7]  
  - Congenital knee dislocation (HP:0005191) — congenital musculoskeletal anomaly[7]  

- **Gender and age associations:**  
  - Many neuromuscular terms (e.g., distal muscle weakness, amyotrophy) typically present in adults, often middle-aged or older, with no strong gender bias[2][4][6].  
  - Some conditions like Laing distal myopathy begin in childhood or adolescence[10].  
  - Certain enzyme elevations or symptoms may be more common in males due to muscle mass differences but generally affect both genders.  
  - Rare terms like ectopia lentis and congenital knee dislocation present early in life.  
  - Terms related to systemic or acute conditions (fever, subarachnoid hemorrhage) affect all ages and genders variably.

This synthesis integrates definitions and clinical context from multiple sources to classify the HPO terms by their diagnostic utility and demographic associations.

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of the dentition
hpo_input.definition: "Any abnormality of the teeth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9338-3017]

hpo_input.name: Brachycephaly
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of skull shape characterized by a decreased anterior-posterior diameter. That is, a cephalic index greater than 81%. Alternatively, an apparently shortened anteroposterior dimension (length) of the head compared to width." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19125436]

hpo_input.name: Hypertelorism
hpo_input.definition: "Interpupillary distance more than 2 SD above the mean (alternatively, the appearance of an increased interpupillary distance or widely spaced eyes)." [PMID:19125427]

hpo_input.name: Hypoplasia of the maxilla
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormally small dimension of the Maxilla. Usually creating a malocclusion or malalignment between the upper and lower teeth or resulting in a deficient amount of projection of the base of the nose and lower midface region." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Astigmatism
hpo_input.definition: "A type of refraction error associated with abnormal curvatures on the anterior and/or posterior surface of the cornea." [HPO_CONTRIBUTOR:DDD_ncarter, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0986-4123]
synonym: Abnormal curving of the cornea or lens of the eye

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of vision
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormality of eyesight (visual perception)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Nystagmus
hpo_input.definition: "Rhythmic, involuntary oscillations of one or both eyes related to abnormality in fixation, conjugate gaze, or vestibular mechanisms." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Sclerocornea
hpo_input.definition: "A congenital anomaly in which a part or the whole of the cornea acquires the characteristics of sclera, resulting in clouding of the cornea." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Hardening of skin and connective tissue

hpo_input.name: Abnormal skull morphology
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the skull, the bony framework of the head which is comprised of the neurocranium (with eight cranial bones) and the viscerocranium (facial skeleton) that comprises fourteen facial bones with the mandible as its largest bone." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Umbilical hernia
hpo_input.definition: "Protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the abdominal wall musculature around the umbilicus. Skin and subcutaneous tissue overlie the defect." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormal foot morphology
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of the skeleton of foot." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Generalized hirsutism
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormally increased hair growth over much of the entire body." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Short stature
hpo_input.definition: "A height below that which is expected according to age and gender norms. Although there is no universally accepted definition of short stature, many refer to \"short stature\" as height more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender (or below the 3rd percentile for age and gender dependent norms)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Coronal craniosynostosis
hpo_input.definition: "Premature closure of the coronal suture of skull." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Short distal phalanx of finger
hpo_input.definition: "Short distance from the end of the finger to the most distal interphalangeal crease or the distal interphalangeal joint flexion point. That is, hypoplasia of one or more of the distal phalanx of finger." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19125433]
synonym: Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges of the hand

hpo_input.name: Underdeveloped supraorbital ridges
hpo_input.definition: "Flatness of the supraorbital portion of the frontal bones." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19125436]

hpo_input.name: Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the nasal bone
hpo_input.definition: "Absence or underdevelopment of the nasal bone." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Craniofacial dysostosis
hpo_input.definition: "A characteristic appearance resulting from defective ossification of craniofacial bones." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Overweight
hpo_input.definition: "Increased body weight with a body mass index of 25-29.9 kg per square meter." []

hpo_input.name: Seizure
hpo_input.definition: "A seizure is an intermittent abnormality of nervous system physiology characterized by a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:15816939]

hpo_input.name: Cachexia
hpo_input.definition: "Severe weight loss, wasting of muscle, loss of appetite, and general debility related to a chronic disease." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypocalcemia
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormally decreased calcium concentration in the blood." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Pain
hpo_input.definition: "An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage." [https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5208-3432]

hpo_input.name: Intellectual disability, mild
hpo_input.definition: "Mild intellectual disability is defined as an intelligence quotient (IQ) in the range of 50-69." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hyperkinetic movements
hpo_input.definition: "Motor hyperactivity with excessive movement of muscles of the body as a whole." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Chest pain
hpo_input.definition: "An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the chest." []

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of the adrenal glands
hpo_input.definition: "Abnormality of the adrenal glands, i.e., of the endocrine glands located at the top of the kindneys." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Abnormality of thrombocytes
hpo_input.definition: "An abnormality of platelets." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Acute hepatitis
hpo_input.definition: "Acute hepatic injury resulting from inflammation typically accompanied by increased serum alanine transaminase activity. Etiologies include viral hepatitis, drugs, toxins, and autoimmune disorders." []

hpo_input.name: Schmorl's node
hpo_input.definition: "A Schmorl's node is the herniation of nucleus pulposus through the cartilaginous and bony end plate into the body of the adjacent vertebra." [PMID:22544358]

hpo_input.name: Increased circulating prolactin concentration
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of abnormally increased levels of prolactin in the blood. Prolactin is a peptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland that plays a role in breast development and lactation during pregnancy." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0538-4547, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Dyssynergia
hpo_input.definition: "A type of ataxia characterized by the impairment of the ability to smoothly perform the elements of a voluntary movement in the appropriate order and speed. hpo_input.name: Visual agnosia

hpo_input.name: Typical atrial flutter
hpo_input.definition: "Typical atrial flutter is an organized atrial tachycardia. It can also be defined as a macroreentrant tachycardia confined to the right atrium. This arrhythmia has a 200-260 ms cycle length, although it may fluctuate depending on patient's previous treatment or ablation, congenital heart disease, etc. Ventricular rate response will be limited by the atrioventricular node conductions, usually presenting a 2:1 or 3:1 response, during atrial flutter. Typical (counter clockwise) flutter is associated with the common flutter pattern: a regular continuous undulation with dominant negative deflections in inferior leads II, III and aVF, often described also as a saw tooth pattern, and flat atrial deflections in leads I and aVL. Atrial deflections in V1 can be positive, biphasic or negative." [PMID:28835836]

hpo_input.name: Limb pain
hpo_input.definition: "Chronic pain in the limbs with no clear focal etiology." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Psoriasiform dermatitis
hpo_input.definition: "A skin abnormality characterized by redness and irritation, with thick, red skin that displays flaky, silver-white patches (scales)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

Here is a detailed analysis of the provided Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms focusing on their commonality, informativeness for specific diseases, and age or gender predilections where applicable:

---

### 1. **Global developmental delay (HP:0001263)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a relatively **common phenotype**, affecting approximately 1–3% of preschool-aged children worldwide[1][2]. It is a broad, less specific term describing delays in multiple developmental domains (motor, speech, cognitive, social). Because it is nonspecific and can result from many causes (genetic, environmental, perinatal insults), it is **less informative for pinpointing a specific disease** but very useful as an initial clinical descriptor[1][2][5].  
- **Rare & Informative?** No, it is common and nonspecific.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  This term is specifically used for **children younger than five years old**[1]. It applies equally across genders but is age-specific to early childhood[1][2][5].

---

### 2. **Intellectual disability, moderate (HP:0002342)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Moderate intellectual disability (IQ 35-49) is a **more specific phenotype** than global developmental delay and can be informative in the context of syndromes or genetic conditions that cause cognitive impairment[5]. It is less common than mild intellectual disability but still seen in various genetic and acquired conditions.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Moderately rare and more informative than broad developmental delay.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Typically diagnosed in **children and adolescents** as IQ testing is age-dependent. No specific gender bias, though some genetic causes may have gender predilections.

---

### 3. **Abnormal cortical gyration (HP:0002536)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and highly informative phenotype** indicating structural brain abnormalities, often linked to specific neurodevelopmental disorders or malformations of cortical development[5]. It is very useful for diagnosis in neurogenetic or neuroimaging contexts.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Yes, rare and highly informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Typically identified in **infants or children** undergoing neuroimaging for developmental delay or seizures. No specific gender predilection.

---

### 4. **Depigmentation/hyperpigmentation of skin (HP:0007483)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **common but nonspecific finding** seen in many dermatological or systemic conditions. Without further specification, it is **less informative** for a specific disease.  
- **Rare & Informative?** No, common and nonspecific.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Can occur at any age and in both genders depending on underlying cause.

---

### 5. **Infantile muscular hypotonia (HP:0008947)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Muscular hypotonia in infancy is **relatively common in various neuromuscular and genetic disorders** and is an important clinical sign. While common, it is **informative for neuromuscular or central nervous system pathology**.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Common but moderately informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Specific to **infants**; no gender bias.

---

### 6. **Dilated fourth ventricle (HP:0002198)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and specific neuroimaging finding** indicating abnormal cerebrospinal fluid dynamics or brain malformations. It is **informative for specific neurological diseases**.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Yes, rare and informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Detected in **infants or children** during brain imaging; no gender bias.

---

### 7. **Curly hair (HP:0002212)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Curly hair is a **common normal variant** and generally **not informative** for disease unless part of a syndrome.  
- **Rare & Informative?** No, common and nonspecific.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Present from birth, no gender bias.

---

### 8. **Curved fingers (HP:0004095)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This can be a **common physical trait or part of syndromes** (e.g., arthrogryposis, connective tissue disorders). It is **moderately informative** when combined with other features.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Moderately informative depending on context.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Present from birth, no gender bias.

---

### 9. **5-minute APGAR score of 5 (HP:0030925)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  A low APGAR score at 5 minutes is a **common clinical measure** indicating neonatal distress but is **nonspecific** for any particular disease.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Common but nonspecific.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Specific to **newborns**; no gender bias.

---

### 10. **Abnormal cerebral ventricle morphology (HP:0002118)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and informative neuroimaging finding** that can indicate hydrocephalus, brain malformations, or other CNS disorders.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Yes, rare and informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Detected in **infants or children**; no gender bias.

---

### 11. **Patent ductus arteriosus (HP:0001643)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  PDA is **common in preterm infants** but less common in full-term infants. It is a **clinically important and informative cardiac finding**.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Common in preterm infants, informative for neonatal cardiac disease.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Primarily affects **newborns, especially preterm**; no strong gender bias.

### 12. **Pes planus (HP:0001763)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Flat feet are **common in children and adults** and often benign but can be informative in connective tissue disorders. Generally **less informative alone**.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Common and less informative unless syndromic.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Common in **children and adults**; no gender bias.

- **Rare & Informative?** Common but can be informative in specific diseases.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Commonly diagnosed in **adolescents**, more frequent in females.

  Can occur at any age; some seizure types have age or gender predilections.

- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **rare and highly specific sign** of Wilson disease (a disorder of copper metabolism). It is **very informative for diagnosis**.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and highly informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Typically appears in **adolescents and young adults**; no strong gender bias.

---

### 16. **Spondylolisthesis (HP:0003302)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  This is a **relatively uncommon but specific spinal abnormality** that can be informative in musculoskeletal or traumatic contexts.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  More common in **adolescents and adults**, especially athletes; no strong gender bias.

---

### 17. **Carcinoid tumor (HP:0100570)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Carcinoid tumors are **rare neuroendocrine tumors** and **highly informative** when present.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and highly informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Typically diagnosed in **adults**; no strong gender bias.

### 18. **Myelodysplasia (HP:0002863)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndrome) is a **rare hematologic disorder** and highly informative.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and highly informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  More common in **older adults**; no strong gender bias.

---

### 19. **Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HP:0005575)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  HUS is a **rare but serious thrombotic microangiopathy**, very informative for specific renal and hematologic pathology.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and highly informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  More common in **children**, especially after certain infections; no strong gender bias.

---

### 20. **Benign prostatic hyperplasia (HP:0008711)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  Very **common in older men**, highly informative for male urinary symptoms.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Common and informative for male-specific disease.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Occurs in **older males** only.

---

### 21. **Ureteral duplication (HP:0000073)**  
- **Commonality & Informativeness:**  
  A **rare congenital anomaly** that is informative in urologic disease contexts.  
- **Rare & Informative?** Rare and informative.  
- **Age/Gender Predilection:**  
  Present from birth; no strong gender bias.

# Analysis of HPO Terms: Specificity, Rarity, and Demographics

## Overview of the HPO Terms

The provided list contains 34 Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms spanning various clinical features from facial characteristics to neurological and systemic manifestations. These terms vary significantly in their diagnostic specificity and clinical utility.

## 1. Common and Less Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are relatively common in the general population or across multiple conditions, making them less specific for diagnosis:

**Seizure (HP:0001250)** represents a common neurological manifestation occurring across numerous genetic syndromes, metabolic disorders, and acquired conditions. Its presence alone provides limited diagnostic specificity.

**Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)** is a broad phenotypic feature associated with hundreds of genetic conditions and acquired disorders. While clinically significant, it lacks specificity for particular diseases.

**Short stature (HP:0004322)** appears in many growth disorders, endocrine conditions, and genetic syndromes. This term is frequently observed across diverse etiologies.

**Failure to thrive (HP:0001508)** is a nonspecific indicator of poor growth or development that can result from nutritional, metabolic, genetic, or environmental factors.

**Cataract (HP:0000518)** occurs in numerous conditions including metabolic disorders, genetic syndromes, and age-related changes, limiting its diagnostic value as a standalone feature.

**Abnormal nail morphology (HP:0001597)** and **Abnormal hair morphology (HP:0001595)** are relatively common findings in various dermatological and systemic conditions.

**Dementia (HP:0000726)** and **Old-aged sensorineural hearing impairment (HP:0040113)** are primarily age-related features with limited specificity for genetic disease diagnosis in younger populations.

## 2. Rare and Highly Informative HPO Terms

The following terms are more specific and informative for particular genetic syndromes:

**Everted lower lip vermilion (HP:0000232)** is a distinctive facial feature that, when combined with other findings, can point toward specific genetic syndromes.[1] This term appears in conditions such as Neu-Laxova Syndrome and other rare genetic disorders.[6]

**Cutis laxa (HP:0000973)** represents wrinkled, redundant, inelastic skin characteristic of specific genetic conditions affecting connective tissue and elastin production. This finding is relatively rare and highly suggestive of particular genetic etiologies.

**Wide anterior fontanel (HP:0000260)** is informative when present beyond expected developmental timeframes, suggesting skeletal dysplasias, metabolic bone disease, or specific genetic syndromes affecting bone ossification.

**Decreased skull ossification (HP:0004331)** is a specific radiological finding associated with particular genetic conditions affecting bone development and mineralization.

**Reduced subcutaneous adipose tissue (HP:0003758)** and **Lipoatrophy (HP:0100578)** are relatively uncommon findings that, when present, suggest specific metabolic or genetic disorders affecting fat tissue distribution and metabolism.

**Intrauterine growth retardation (HP:0001511)** combined with other features can be informative for prenatal-onset genetic conditions.

**Abnormal dermatoglyphics (HP:0007477)** represents a specific finding related to abnormal fingerprint patterns, which can be associated with particular genetic syndromes and chromosomal abnormalities.

**Long eyelashes in irregular rows (HP:0007740)** is a distinctive feature appearing in specific genetic conditions.

**Ectodermal dysplasia (HP:0000968)** represents a group of conditions with abnormal development of skin, hair, nails, teeth, or sweat glands, making it informative when identified.

**Thick eyebrow (HP:0000574)** can be informative when part of a characteristic facial gestalt in specific syndromes.

## 3. Gender and Age-Related Patterns

**Actinic cheilitis and everted lower lip considerations:** Research indicates that **three times more men than women develop actinic cheilitis**, a condition that can be associated with or exacerbated by everted lower lip morphology.[3]

**Allergic contact cheilitis:** This condition affects females more commonly than males in a ratio of approximately 9:1.[2]

**Age-related features:** Terms such as **Dementia (HP:0000726)**, **Old-aged sensorineural hearing impairment (HP:0040113)**, **Age-related nuclear cataract (HP:0011142)**, and **Corneal arcus (HP:0001084)** are predominantly observed in elderly populations, with limited relevance to pediatric genetic disease diagnosis.

**Prenatal and early childhood features:** Terms including **Intrauterine growth retardation (HP:0001511)**, **Wide anterior fontanel (HP:0000260)**, **Decreased skull ossification (HP:0004331)**, **Failure to thrive (HP:0001508)**, and **Short stature (HP:0004322)** are more informative when identified in infants and young children, as they reflect developmental abnormalities.

**Neurological features in children:** **Seizure (HP:0001250)** and **Intellectual disability (HP:0001249)** can occur at any age but are particularly relevant for pediatric genetic syndrome diagnosis when present in early childhood.

**Reproductive features:** **Oligozoospermia (HP:0000798)** is specific to males and relevant only in the context of male infertility evaluation.

The combination of multiple rare and specific HPO terms, particularly those affecting facial features (everted lower lip vermilion), connective tissue (cutis laxa), skeletal development (decreased skull ossification, wide anterior fontanel), and dermatological findings (abnormal dermatoglyphics), provides substantially greater diagnostic utility than individual common terms alone.

# Analysis of HPO Terms in Relation to Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)

Based on the search results, I can provide a comprehensive analysis of these HPO terms in the context of FAP, which is the primary condition discussed in the provided information.

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**Adenomatous colonic polyposis (HP:0005227)** and **Colorectal polyposis (HP:0200063)** are the defining features of FAP but are common across multiple polyposis syndromes. While these terms are central to FAP diagnosis, they are less specific because they also occur in other conditions such as MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.[9] These terms describe the primary manifestation but do not distinguish FAP from other inherited polyposis conditions.

**Neoplasm of the stomach (HP:0006753)** is relatively common in FAP patients, with gastric fundic polyps being a recognized extracolonic manifestation.[3] However, this term is also nonspecific, as stomach tumors occur in many conditions unrelated to FAP.

**Renal cyst (HP:0000107)**, **Addictive behavior (HP:0030858)**, **Pollakisuria (HP:0100515)**, **Atelectasis (HP:0100750)**, **Abnormal erythrocyte morphology (HP:0001877)**, and **Hypervolemia (HP:0011105)** are not mentioned in the FAP literature provided and appear to be unrelated to this condition. These terms are either general medical findings or unrelated to FAP pathology.

## Rare and Informative Terms

**Thyroid adenoma (HP:0000854)** is a rare but informative finding in FAP. The search results indicate that thyroid cancer represents an increased risk in FAP patients, though it typically occurs in less than 10% of affected individuals.[1] This extracolonic manifestation, while uncommon, is characteristic of FAP and helps distinguish it from other polyposis syndromes.

**Neoplasm of the skin (HP:0008069)** is highly informative for FAP diagnosis. The condition is associated with soft tissue tumors including epidermoid cysts and fibromas.[1] When colonic polyposis is accompanied by clinically obvious osteomas and soft tissue tumors, the term **Gardner syndrome** is used, making skin neoplasms a distinctive feature.[1] This combination of findings is relatively rare and highly specific to FAP variants.

**Hamartomatous polyposis (HP:0004390)** is notably absent from FAP presentations. This term describes polyps composed of normal cellular elements with distorted architecture, which is characteristic of conditions like Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, not FAP. The adenomatous polyps in FAP are fundamentally different from hamartomatous polyps, making this term informative by its absence in FAP cases.

## Age and Gender Patterns

**Age groups most affected:**

FAP shows a clear age-related pattern. Polyps typically appear by the mid-teens, with an average age of 16 years for classic FAP.[1] Without intervention, colorectal cancer develops by the third or fourth decade of life, usually before age 40.[1][3][8] Screening with sigmoidoscopy is recommended beginning at ages 10 to 12 years.[2] Surgery is typically performed between the late teens and late 30s.[1][2]

For extracolonic manifestations, infants and young children with FAP are at risk for hepatoblastoma (a rare liver tumor) and should be screened frequently until age 5.[6] Thyroid and other cancers typically occur in less than 10% of affected individuals and may develop later in life.

**Gender patterns:**

The search results do not indicate any gender-specific differences in FAP incidence, presentation, or severity. FAP is an autosomal dominant condition,[11] meaning it affects males and females equally. The condition is inherited from a parent regardless of the parent's gender, and both males and females have a 50% chance of inheriting the mutation if one parent is affected.

**Attenuated FAP (AFAP):**

A milder form called attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis exists, where individuals typically have fewer colon polyps (averaging 30) and develop cancer later in life.[3] This variant may affect the age of onset for some manifestations but does not show gender-specific patterns.

# Analysis of HPO Terms Related to Cleft Palate and Associated Conditions

## Overview of HPO Terms

The HPO terms provided include a mix of conditions directly related to cleft palate, secondary complications, and unrelated conditions. Let me analyze each category:

## Common and Less Informative Terms

**HP:0000175 - Cleft palate** is the primary condition itself and serves as the diagnostic criterion rather than an informative symptom. While essential for diagnosis, it is not rare or specific to a particular disease subtype.

**HP:0000164 - Abnormality of the dentition** and **HP:0000692 - Tooth malposition** are relatively common complications in cleft palate patients. Dental problems occur in children with clefts who are more prone to cavities and often have missing, extra, malformed, or displaced teeth.[3] These terms are informative for cleft palate but not specific to it, as dental abnormalities occur in many conditions.

**HP:0000689 - Dental malocclusion** is similarly common in cleft palate cases, where teeth and jaws don't line up evenly.[3] This is a frequent secondary finding rather than a distinguishing feature.

**HP:0000750 - Delayed speech and language development** occurs in many developmental conditions beyond cleft palate. While associated with cleft palate, it is not specific to this condition.

## Rare and Highly Informative Terms

**HP:0000175 - Cleft palate** combined with **HP:0008872 - Feeding difficulties in infancy** creates a highly specific clinical presentation. The feeding difficulties in cleft palate are distinctive because infants cannot generate intraoral pressure to extract milk via suction.[4] This combination is particularly informative for cleft palate diagnosis in newborns.

**HP:0010294 - Palate fistula** (oronasal fistula) is a more specific complication that can occur as an unrepaired defect or post-surgical complication.[15] This term is more informative for identifying specific cleft palate cases or surgical outcomes.

**HP:0001611 - Hypernasal speech** is a characteristic speech pattern specific to cleft palate when the palate is unrepaired or inadequately repaired. Because babies use the palate to form sounds, a cleft palate can affect speech development, and speech may have a nasal sound.[5] This is highly informative for cleft palate diagnosis in older children.

**HP:0040262 - Glue ear** (middle ear fluid) is a common but relatively specific complication of cleft palate. Babies with cleft palate are especially at risk of developing middle ear fluid and losing hearing.[5] While not rare in the general population, its association with cleft palate is strong.

**HP:0000405 - Conductive hearing impairment** often results from glue ear in cleft palate patients and is informative for identifying this complication.

## Unrelated Terms

**HP:0030041 - Schmorl's node**, **HP:0002385 - Paraparesis**, and **HP:0100651 - Type I diabetes mellitus** are not related to cleft palate and appear to be included in error. These conditions do not have established associations with cleft palate.

## Age and Gender Patterns

**Age-specific patterns:**

Cleft palate is a congenital condition present at birth, making it identifiable immediately or shortly after birth.[11] Feeding difficulties manifest within the first days to weeks of life.[2] Speech and language delays become apparent around 12-24 months of age as children begin to develop language.[5] Dental problems become evident as primary and permanent teeth erupt, typically between 6 months and 6 years of age.[3] Hearing loss may be detected through newborn hearing screening or later as middle ear complications develop.[5]

**Gender patterns:**

The search results do not provide specific information about gender differences in the prevalence of cleft palate or its associated complications. Cleft palate affects both males and females, though some research suggests slight variations in prevalence by gender depending on the specific type of cleft, but this information is not detailed in the provided sources.

hpo_input.definition: "Pierre Robin malformation is a sequence of developmental malformations characterized by micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia), glossoptosis and cleft palate." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Microcephaly
hpo_input.definition: "Head circumference below 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender." [PMID:15806441, PMID:19125436, PMID:25465325, PMID:9683597]

hpo_input.name: Epicanthus
hpo_input.definition: "A fold of skin starting above the medial aspect of the upper eyelid and arching downward to cover, pass in front of and lateral to the medial canthus." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Long philtrum
hpo_input.definition: "Distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border more than 2 SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border." [PMID:19152422]

hpo_input.name: Micrognathia
hpo_input.definition: "Developmental hypoplasia of the mandible." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Anteverted nares
hpo_input.definition: "Anteriorly-facing nostrils viewed with the head in the Frankfurt horizontal and the eyes of the observer level with the eyes of the subject. This gives the appearance of an upturned nose (upturned nasal tip)." [PMID:19152422]

hpo_input.name: Ptosis
hpo_input.definition: "The upper eyelid margin is positioned 3 mm or more lower than usual and covers the superior portion of the iris (objective); or, the upper lid margin obscures at least part of the pupil (subjective)." [PMID:19125427]

hpo_input.name: Impaired ocular abduction
hpo_input.definition: "An impaired ability of the eye to move in the outward direction (towards the side of the head)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Brachydactyly
hpo_input.definition: "Digits that appear disproportionately short compared to the hand/foot. The word brachydactyly is used here to describe a series distinct patterns of shortened digits (brachydactyly types A-E). This is the sense used here." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Intellectual disability
hpo_input.definition: "Intellectual disability, previously referred to as mental retardation, is characterized by subnormal intellectual functioning that occurs during the developmental period. It is defined by an IQ score below 70." []

hpo_input.name: Hypotonia
hpo_input.definition: "Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:21418198]

hpo_input.name: Growth delay
hpo_input.definition: "A deficiency or slowing down of growth pre- and postnatally." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Talipes equinovarus
hpo_input.definition: "Talipes equinovarus (also called clubfoot) typically has four main components: inversion and adduction of the forefoot; inversion of the heel and hindfoot; equinus (limitation of extension) of the ankle and subtalar joint; and internal rotation of the leg." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:32491773]

hpo_input.name: Short nose
hpo_input.definition: "Distance from nasion to subnasale more than two standard deviations below the mean, or alternatively, an apparently decreased length from the nasal root to the nasal tip." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199, PMID:19152422]

hpo_input.definition: "The presence of skeletal muscular atrophy (which is also known as amyotrophy)." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Neurogenic muscle atrophy, especially in the lower limbs

hpo_input.name: Aplasia/Hypoplasia of the tongue

hpo_input.name: Abnormal palate morphology
hpo_input.definition: "Any abnormality of the palate, i.e., of roof of the mouth." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Abnormality of the roof of the mouth

hpo_input.name: Ventriculomegaly
hpo_input.definition: "An increase in size of the ventricular system of the brain." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Cerebral calcification
hpo_input.definition: "The presence of calcium deposition within the cerebrum." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]
synonym: Abnormal deposits of calcium in the brain

hpo_input.name: Frontal balding
hpo_input.definition: "Absence of hair in the anterior midline and/or parietal areas." [PMID:19125436]

hpo_input.name: Maculopapular exanthema
hpo_input.definition: "A skin rash that is characterized by diffuse cutaneous erythema with areas of skin elevation. It may evolve to vesicles or papules as part of a more severe clinical entity. Different degrees of angioedema with involvement of subcutaneous tissue may also appear." [PMID:19398898]

hpo_input.name: Atypical behavior
hpo_input.definition: "Atypical behavior is an abnormality in a person's actions that can be controlled or modulated by the will of the individual. While abnormal behaviors can be difficult to control, they are distinct from other abnormal actions that cannot be affected by the individual's will." []

hpo_input.name: Thrombocytopenia
hpo_input.definition: "A reduction in the number of circulating thrombocytes." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hydronephrosis
hpo_input.definition: "Severe distention of the kidney with dilation of the renal pelvis and calices." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Hypersomnia
hpo_input.definition: "Excessive sleepiness or feeling of sleepiness, or difficulty staying awake despite having had adequate sleep, which persists over several days." [PMID:32901432]

hpo_input.name: Myopathy
hpo_input.definition: "A disorder of muscle unrelated to impairment of innervation or neuromuscular junction." [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0736-9199]

hpo_input.name: Gingival overgrowth

| **HP:0001611 - Hypernasal speech**            | Less common; specific to structural or neurological causes affecting nasal airflow | Informative for cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency syndromes | Typically children with cleft palate or related anomalies |
| **HP:0200153 - Agenesis of lateral incisor** | Relatively common dental anomaly; less specific alone | Informative for syndromes with tooth agenesis (e.g., ectodermal dysplasia) | Present from birth; no strong gender bias |
| **HP:0011452 - Functional abnormality of the middle ear** | Common in children with otitis media or Eustachian tube dysfunction; less specific | Informative when part of syndromes with hearing loss or craniofacial anomalies | Primarily children |

| **HP:0000405 - Conductive hearing impairment** | Common in children with middle ear infections; less specific | Informative when linked to syndromes with ear malformations or chronic otitis media | Mostly children; can occur at any age depending on cause |
| **HP:0012443 - Abnormal brain morphology**   | Rare; highly informative for neurological and developmental disorders | Very informative for specific syndromes with brain malformations | Congenital or developmental; affects all ages depending on disorder |
| **HP:0004325 - Decreased body weight**        | Common symptom in many conditions; less specific | Informative when part of syndromic or metabolic disorders | All ages; often children in growth disorders |
| **HP:0001824 - Weight loss**                   | Common symptom; less specific | Informative in context of systemic diseases or malignancies | All ages |
| **HP:0000689 - Dental malocclusion**           | Very common in general population; less specific | Informative if part of syndromes with craniofacial abnormalities | Mostly children and adolescents during dental development |
| **HP:0100681 - Esophageal duplication**        | Rare congenital anomaly; highly informative | Informative for congenital foregut malformations | Congenital; usually diagnosed in infancy or childhood |
| **HP:0200119 - Acute hepatitis**                | Common clinical condition; less specific | Informative for specific infectious, toxic, or autoimmune diseases | All ages; some viral hepatitis types have age or risk group predilections |
| **HP:0000840 - Adrenogenital syndrome**         | Rare genetic disorder; highly informative | Informative for congenital adrenal hyperplasia syndromes | Congenital; affects both genders but clinical presentation differs by sex |

**Summary of Key Points:**

- **More common and less informative terms** tend to be symptoms or findings frequently seen in the general pediatric population or in multiple disorders, such as *Abnormality of dental eruption*, *Recurrent otitis media*, *Delayed speech*, *Dental malocclusion*, and *Conductive hearing impairment*. These are often nonspecific and require additional context for diagnosis.

- **Rare and informative terms** are often congenital anomalies or specific functional abnormalities that strongly suggest particular syndromes or genetic disorders, such as *Primary failure of tooth eruption* (a subtype of abnormal dental eruption), *Orofacial cleft*, *Esophageal duplication*, *Adrenogenital syndrome*, and *Abnormal brain morphology*.

hpo_input.name: Abnormal facial shape
